title: CODENAV: Beyond tool-use to using real-world codebases with LLM agents
heading: B Compute requirements
text: We run our CODENAV evaluations on Ubuntu servers each with 8 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. As mentioned previously, we do not train any models and make use of the OpenAI and together.ai APIs to perform inference using LLMs. This means we do not require (local) GPUs for LLM inference but there are many instances when CODENAV may benefit from having access to a GPU (e.g., for image inpainting). While inference time varies per benchmark, running m&m's evaluations (200 queries) with 24 parallel processes on a single 8 GPU server takes approximately ∼12 minutes in wall clock time (96 minutes of GPU time).

title: CODENAV: Beyond tool-use to using real-world codebases with LLM agents
heading: E Limitations
text:
While CODENAV is capable of some producing impressive results, we highlight three key limitations.
(1) Our current implementation of CODENAV assumes that the agent produces Python code (and that the given codebase is a Python codebase). While extending to use other languages is not a significant engineering challenge, it is possible that LLMs' performance degrades as one moves away from popular languages like Python, for which there is significant data on the web. (2) Our agent has no long-term memory that is available across queries. This means that, given the same query twice, CODENAV will make the same errors and repeat the same searches. CODENAV: Beyond tool-use to using real-world codebases with LLM agents
section: E Limitations (limitations)

While CODENAV is capable of some producing impressive results, we highlight three key limitations.
(1) Our current implementation of CODENAV assumes that the agent produces Python code (and that the given codebase is a Python codebase). While extending to use other languages is not a significant engineering challenge, it is possible that LLMs' performance degrades as one moves away from popular languages like Python, for which there is significant data on the web. (2) Our agent has no long-term memory that is available across queries. This means that, given the same query twice, CODENAV will make the same errors and repeat the same searches. (3) Finally, CODENAV performance is strongly dependent on the underlying LLM and performance can sharply degrade when using smaller LLMs. This means that most researchers can only use CODENAV through the use of paid APIs and larger-scale experimentation when using these APIs can be costly.

title: CODENAV: Beyond tool-use to using real-world codebases with LLM agents
heading: F Societal impact
text:
While CODENAV is not unique in this respect, the growing popularity of increasingly competent LLM agents has the potential to automate or augment many skilled tasks. While automation has brought about many societal positives on aggregate, it can clearly has a profoundly negative impact on anyone whose may lose their job. The environmental impact (via the huge energy costs of running these LLMs) may also be significant.
As a more acute potential negative impact: in the code-use paradigm, the underlying agent the CODENAV agent has the ability to run arbitrary code on the user's machine. Given this, it can be dangerous unintentionally (there is nothing stopping CODENAV from making a logic error, e.g. filtering a file list incorrectly and then accidentally deleting all files on the computer) and intentionally (e.g., a malicious party might upload tainted model weights, or intercept API calls, so as to run a "randomsome ware" scam when executed by a CODENAV agent). These dangers are somewhat easier to mitigate in the tool-use paradigm as, when constrained to use only certain tools, there are fundamentally fewer attack vectors to consider.

The codebase you will use is called 'codenav'. It is a library for creating LLM agents that can interact with one of the avilable environments to solve the user queries that require using an external codebase. For example, an agent can interact with "PythonCodeEnv" for code execution, and with "RetrievalEnv" for retrieving code snippets from an ElasticSearch index. It provides an "Episode" class for running this interaction with a specific agent and a set of environments. Here's the directory structure: codenav/agents/ -contains subdirectories that store implementations of LLM agents implemented with different LLMs codenav/environments/ -contains environments that the agent can interact with codenav/interaction/ -contains Episode and messages implementations (messages is how agent interacts with environments) codenav/prompts/ -stores various system prompts for the LLM agent codenav/retrieval/ -various files related to creating elastic search index and retrieving items from the index codenav/utils/ -contains various utility python files codenav/constants.py -contains important constants The codebase you'll be using to solve user tasks is called 'mnm'. It has a single tool_api.py file which contains functions for various image, text, and audio related tasks. Specifically, here's a high-level summary of available functions:
-text understanding functions: for tasks like text generation, summarization, classification, answering questions based on a text context -image understanding functions: for tasks like image classification (1000 IMAGENET categories only), image captioning, answering questions about image (use this if you have a question that can't be answered with IMAGENET classification), detecting objects (producing bounding boxes and labels for COCO categories) and segmenting objects (producing segmentation masks and labels for COCO categories), transcribing alphanumeric characters in an image to text (also known as optical character recognition).

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Abstract
text: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four longhorizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Introduction
text:
Large language model (LLM) agents now tackle tasks that require many rounds of reasoning, tool use, and interaction with environments (Yang et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025Wang et al., , 2026)). In these longhorizon tasks, the interactions accumulate code, tool outputs, execution feedback, and intermediate decisions into increasingly long histories (Lindenbauer et al., 2025). Long-horizon agents therefore need to maintain useful working context within a finite window: retain evidence for upcoming decisions, shorten completed investigations, and remove information that is no longer needed.
Existing approaches manage context through either predefined rules or external tools. Even the most widely deployed coding agents rely on rules. Claude Code and Codex summarize the history once it crosses a fixed token threshold (Anthropic, 2025;OpenAI, 2025), and simpler policies mask older observations (Lindenbauer et al., 2025). These triggers fire on context size alone and cannot tell which information the task still needs. Tool-based methods expose context management through external tool calls, letting the agent decide what to edit. Sculptor provides tools to fragment, summarize, hide, and restore the history (Li et al., 2026), and Context-Folding folds a finished sub-trajectory into a summary (Sun et al., 2025). Because the harness defines and executes these tools, the learned editing policy is bound to harness-specific interfaces and generalizes poorly across different environments.
Both families define context editing outside the model. Rules fix the policy in the harness, and tools, even when a learned policy calls them, take their meaning from schemas that the harness declares in the prompt. We therefore seek to answer:
How can we turn context editing into a native capability of language models?

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Introduction
text: Specifically, NCE organizes the context into addressable blocks, and its grammar has three components: a vocabulary of dedicated tokens, in which address tokens name blocks and operator tokens ( drop , rewrite , append ) remove, replace, or add them; composition rules that define wellformed edits; and semantics that bind each wellformed edit to exactly one transition of the context state, executed by a task-agnostic runtime. The meaning of every edit thus ships with the model and holds in every harness. Recorded trajectories contain no edits, so we annotate them with two teachers. An offline teacher reads the full trajectory and assigns each block a release point, the turn after which the block may be edited. A block is released only when the teacher can cite the event that ended its use. An online teacher then uses the previous blocks and release annotations from the offline teacher to decide when and how to edit. The edits are thus safe to learn and executable by an agent that cannot see ahead.

The meaning of every edit thus ships with the model and holds in every harness. Recorded trajectories contain no edits, so we annotate them with two teachers. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Introduction
text:
We then train NCE through distillation over these editing trajectories, with supervision that follows the context as it is edited. Specifically, each edit is executed at the end of the turn that issues it, and every later editing decision and task action is constructed and supervised on the resulting context. Annotating all edits on the original history would condition later decisions on text that the agent has already deleted or rewritten, a mismatch that grows with every edit. By executing each edit before the next turn is built, NCE trains the agent on contexts shaped by its earlier edits. This is exactly the condition it faces at inference time, therefore bridging the train-test gap. During inference, the model generates each turn, the runtime executes the edits it contains, and generation resumes from the edited context, so the context can evolve throughout longhorizon reasoning.
In the experiments, we have implemented NCE on LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and evaluated both on four long-horizon agentic benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026), SWEbench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024), SWE-bench Multilingual (Yang et al., 2025b), and SWE-bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025). On LongCat at 256K, NCE improves success over the base model by 4.8 to 6.3 points and reduces token usage by 31% to 44% on every benchmark (Table 1 and Figure 1b). A toolcall editing baseline trained on the same edits trails NCE by 5.2 to 8.0 points, so the gap comes from expressing the edits natively. The gains transfer to Qwen3.6, where NCE raises the average success rate over the base model by 4.5 points and cuts average token usage by 15%.
We summarize our contributions below:

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Introduction
text:
We summarize our contributions below:
• We introduce Native Context Editing (NCE), a framework that teaches LLM agents a grammar to dynamically manage their own active context through natively generated edits. • We develop a distillation framework with evolving contexts, where an offline teacher uses release analysis in hindsight to decide which blocks to edit, and an online teacher that sees only the present makes the edits. • We evaluate NCE on four long-horizon agentic benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving task performance while also reducing both context and token usage over the base model with harness compaction.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Related Work
text:
Long-horizon LLM agents. Research on longhorizon LLM agents has investigated how interaction with external environments can support reasoning and decision-making. For example, ReAct interleaves reasoning and action, while SWE-agent and OpenHands provide interfaces for code editing and execution (Yao et al., 2022;Yang et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2025). Recent long-horizon agents learn to consolidate memory or fold their context as interactions accumulate (Zhou et al., 2026;Ye et al., 2025). These approaches depend on retaining useful evidence across decisions, yet longer histories do not ensure reliable evidence access (Liu et al., 2024). NCE addresses this shared challenge by maintaining the context available to ongoing reasoning and interaction.
Memory management and knowledge retrieval for LLM agents. Retrieval-augmented generation and agentic memory systems store information outside the context window and retrieve it whenever later decisions need it (Lewis et al., 2020;Packer et al., 2023;Xu et al., 2026). Memory managers decide what and when to store, update, or discard, often with database-like operations such as SQL or ADD/UPDATE/DELETE (Hu et al., 2023;Yan et al., 2026), and some apply these decisions to the active context through tool calls (Zhang et al., 2026;Liu et al., 2026;Yu et al., 2026). Unlike most memory management methods, NCE edits the active textual context of an ongoing task without introducing an external knowledge storage or information retrieval mechanism. Our approach is a parallel contribution to external memory, focusing specifically on active-context management within a fixed context-window budget.

The harness defines these tools, which ties the learned policy to that harness. NCE represents each edit with the model's vocabulary ( §3.1) and trains on edits that modify a block only after release analysis finds it no longer needed ( §3.2).

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Related Work
text: Learning model-native capabilities. Native multimodal models learn images inside one model, as shared-vocabulary tokens or raw patches trained jointly with text (Chameleon Team, 2024;Wang et al., 2024;Diao et al., 2024;Shukor et al., 2025); earlier systems attach a separate encoder through an adapter (Alayrac et al., 2022;Liu et al., 2023). Nativeness thus keeps a capability in the model's own sequence and parameters. By this standard, learned control is only partly native: tool calls and folding directives draw meaning from external tools or prompts (Schick et al., 2023;Ye et al., 2025), reflection tokens trigger an external retriever (Asai et al., 2024), and reduction tokens act only on reasoning (Yang et al., 2025a;Kontonis et al., 2026). Following native multimodal models, NCE incorporates context editing directly into the model's vocabulary through operator and address tokens, which are processed and generated inline with text.

where each α is a block address, m ≥ 1, and x is text represented by ordinary tokens. One turn may carry several edits, explained by a one-sentence rationale in plain text.
Semantics. Each edit denotes exactly one transition of the block history. drop removes blocks α 1 , . . . , α m and retires their addresses for good, rewrite replaces the text of block α with x while preserving its address, and append adds an editable block with text x under a fresh address. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Faithful Supervision from Two Teachers
text:
A reappearing literal counts as a use, so λ b ≤ r b . The literal check can only postpone release; premature release (r b < r b ) therefore requires both an incorrect release judgment and a final use that leaves no literal trace. An omitted citation merely prolongs retention. Directly labeling r b requires identifying the exact last use, with errors leading to either premature release or unnecessary retention. Release analysis instead defaults to retention when evidence is missing, much as conservative liveness analysis keeps a value live while it may still be read.
A second pass over the complete trajectory revisits blocks retained during the first pass, including those from abandoned lines of investigation, and releases them only with a cited event and after the same literal check.
Online teacher: edit generation. The online teacher decides when and how to edit the released blocks, seeing the present blocks and block-level eligibility markers derived from offline release analysis (Figure 3, right). It acts as the agent at turn t: it reads Render(S t ), in which a block becomes editable only after its release point rb from the offline teacher, and writes the edits e t , choosing the operators and the replacement text. Every summary is drawn from the context in view, so no edit relies on anything the agent has yet to see. By default, it rewrites and drops only blocks that carry no information. Decision points arise when a reminder signals that the context is nearing its budget or when a subgoal has just been completed, and the teacher may decline when little is editable. A final audit rejects edits whose removed literals reappear later and summaries that state facts absent from their source.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Distillation with Evolving Contexts
text:
An edit changes every later rendering, so training on the recorded history would condition later turns on context the agent has already modified. We therefore build each training trajectory by running Eq. ( 1) forward along τ : a t and b t are the recorded action and observation, and e t is the online teacher's output at a decision point and empty elsewhere. Each editing decision is thus made on a context shaped by the earlier ones, as the decisions of the trained agent will be, and a summary written at one decision point is what the teacher reads at the next, where it may be revised or dropped in turn.
Release analysis keeps the recorded actions valid on this edited context, since an edit removes only what the recorded continuation no longer uses. Every turn with edits closes a segment, and the next segment opens with the rendering of the state those edits produce. Each segment is an ordinary causal sequence whose prefix reflects every earlier edit, so the three editing turns in Figure 4 yield four training sequences. We fine-tune on these sequences with the usual next-token loss on the model's outputs, which covers actions, rationales, and edits alike; rendered prefixes and observations serve only as conditioning. Stretches where the teacher declined to edit, including whole trajectories, are trained in the same way, so the model learns when to leave its context alone as well as how to edit it.
Inference. Inference runs Eq. ( 1) with the model writing e t and a t and the environment returning b t : at each turn the model reads Render(S t ) and generates its output, and the runtime executes the edits and appends the action and its observation.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Experimental Setup
text: Benchmarks. We evaluate on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) (89 tasks), SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) (500 issues), SWEbench Multilingual (Yang et al., 2025b) (300 issues), and SWE-bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025) (731 issues in the public set). Terminal-Bench runs in Terminus-2, its reference agent, and the SWEbench variants run in Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025). Neither harness is aware of NCE: the runtime sits between the harness and the model server, executes edits there, and returns ordinary responses, so a single checkpoint serves both harnesses without any editing interface. We report two metrics: the success rate of a single run, counting runs that end without a result as failures, and token usage, the prompt and output tokens of all model calls in a task, including compaction, averaged over tasks after excluding the 10% with the highest and the 10% with the lowest usage. Such a trimmed mean is used to avoid the influence of long-tail data. All four benchmarks are evaluated with a 256K-token budget. Terminal-Bench accumulates much longer histories than SWE-bench, so we also evaluate it at 128K, 64K, and 48K.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Models and training.
text:
We train NCE on LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B) (Zan et al., 2026) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026), two mixture-of-experts models with 3B active parameters, starting from their instruction-tuned checkpoints. We use GLM 5.3 (Z.ai, 2026) as the two teachers of §3.2 to annotate nearly 180K recorded agent trajectories on software engineering and terminal tasks, which we split into training segments ( §3.3). Each model is fully fine-tuned on these segments for three epochs. Appendix C details data, hyperparameters, and the budget configuration.
Baselines. We compare NCE with one baseline from each family of the Introduction, marked RULES and TOOLS in the tables. Harness compaction (Comp.) runs the base model that NCE is trained from, with the built-in compaction of each harness, which replaces the history with a model-written summary once it reaches the budget. Tool-call editing (Tools) is our implementation of tool-based editing following MemAct (Zhang et al., 2026). We train it on LongCat only, using the same trajectories, edit supervision, and training recipe as NCE. Each edit invokes one of three tools that mirror NCE's operators (Appendix C), enabling a controlled comparison between tool-call and native editing. Our evaluation focuses on the active context under a fixed budget, so systems that store and retrieve information outside it fall outside this comparison.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Main Results
text:
NCE achieves higher success with fewer tokens. At 256K, NCE leads both baselines on every benchmark while spending 36% fewer tokens per task than harness compaction on average (Table 1). The gains hold in Claude Code and Terminus-2 alike, neither of which exposes an editing interface.
Native edits outperform the same edits as tool calls. Trained on the same edits, tool-call editing falls below harness compaction in average success and saves only 6% of its tokens, while NCE saves 36%. The edits pay off only when the model writes them in its own grammar.
The gains hold at every budget. On Terminal-Bench, NCE leads both baselines at every budget from 256K down to 48K, improving success over harness compaction by 5.6 to 10.1 points with 26% to 39% fewer tokens, and NCE at 64K matches both baselines at 256K with less than 40% of their tokens (Table 2 and Figure 1b).
The gains transfer across base models. On Qwen3.6, NCE improves all four benchmarks and cuts average token usage by 15%: the same grammar and supervision teach a second model family to edit its own context.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Ablation Study
text: We compare NCE with other context managers, ablate how its supervision is built, and examine its edits at inference. Supervision needs both teachers and the evolving context. We build supervision for the same 40 trajectories in three ways: by one teacher in one pass, by the two teachers on the original history, and by the two teachers on the evolving context, as in NCE. We check every edit against what the agent could see when it was made (Figure 6, Appendix D.2). Labeling in one pass leaks hindsight: in 30.0% of trajectories a summary uses future information. Labeling on the original history misses that earlier edits have removed part of it, a median of 37% by the fifth decision, so in 95.0% of trajectories an edit targets a block that is already gone. NCE lowers these defects to 5.0% and 0.0%, and the share of trajectories with any defective edit from 80.0% (one pass) and 100.0% (original history) to 37.5%. NCE drops what it has used and condenses what it still needs. drop accounts for most operations, yet rewrite removes slightly more tokens (Figure 7): it condenses long blocks, mostly file reads and sub-agent reports, to about a fifth of their length, while drop also clears shell output and edit results. Both harnesses show the same pattern, and 99.1% of the 73K edits NCE writes execute as written. Most edits are proactive: 89% come before any budget reminder. Editing also frees budget early: when the unedited history first fills a 48K budget, NCE's context fills only 73% of it, leaving over a quarter of the budget free (Appendix D.3).

heading: Ablation Study
text: Re-prefill does not slow the agent. An edit invalidates the KV cache from the first edited block onward. Without any overlap, re-prefilling takes only 0.2-0.4% of a task's wall-clock time. Since a turn writes its edits before its action, the runtime can start the re-prefill as soon as the last edit closes, while the action is still being generated and executed; on measured timings, this hides it entirely in 98% of editing turns under Terminus-2 and 81% under Claude Code. In compute, the edits remove 4 to 22 times as many tokens from later prompts as the re-prefill adds (Appendix D.4).

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Conclusion
text: We introduced Native Context Editing (NCE), which makes context editing part of the language an LLM agent speaks. A grammar of dedicated tokens binds each edit to one transition of an addressable context state, so the meaning of every edit ships with the model and holds in every harness. Two teachers supply causal edits, while training follows the context produced by earlier edits. Across benchmarks, base models, and harnesses, NCE improves task success with fewer tokens and outperforms the same edits issued as tool calls. Context management thereby moves from the harness into the model's own language.

section: Conclusion (conclusion)

We introduced Native Context Editing (NCE), which makes context editing part of the language an LLM agent speaks. A grammar of dedicated tokens binds each edit to one transition of an addressable context state, so the meaning of every edit ships with the model and holds in every harness. Two teachers supply causal edits, while training follows the context produced by earlier edits. Across benchmarks, base models, and harnesses, NCE improves task success with fewer tokens and outperforms the same edits issued as tool calls. Context management thereby moves from the harness into the model's own language.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: Limitations
text: We evaluate NCE on software engineering and terminal tasks, where long tool outputs make context editing especially consequential; extending it to other long-horizon settings, such as web navigation and deep research, is a natural next step. Both base models are mixture-of-experts models with 3B active parameters, and scaling NCE to larger models remains to be explored. NCE learns to edit through supervised distillation, and reinforcement learning on task outcomes could further refine when and how the agent edits. Finally, this study manages the active context within a fixed budget, and combining NCE with external memory and retrieval is left for future work.

text: Table 3 lists the 70 tokens NCE adds to the vocabulary of the base model. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: A.2 Rendering
text: Render(S t ) writes each block as its two address tokens, the lock marker if the block is locked, and the block text in the chat format of the base model, opened by its role tag. No closing token is needed: the address of the next block marks where a block ends. Actions are written as ordinary assistant turns and carry no address, so an edit can reach observations, the task, and notes, and leaves the agent's own actions intact. Every tool result forms a block of its own, which lets the agent drop one result of a batch and keep the others. Figure 8 shows the beginning of a rendered context from a SWE-bench Multilingual task under Claude Code.

text:
When a turn ends, the runtime extracts every envelope <ctx> . . . </ctx> from the output and executes the edits in the order they were written. and no edit may touch the locked block. An edit that fails these checks changes nothing, with one exception: a rewrite of a block that is no longer live is applied as an append, so that its text is kept. title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: B.1 Pipeline / B.2 Teacher Prompts
text:
Blocks. We replay each trajectory with every e t empty and split it into blocks: the system prompt (locked), the task, every tool result, and every user message each form one block, and the block that enters before turn t has entry turn t. Reasoning and actions stay in the action history.
Offline teacher, forward pass. The teacher reads the whole trajectory, with each block labeled by its index and entry turn, and keeps every block by default. It releases a block only by citing the event that ended its use: an action that consumed the block, such as writing the file it was read from into new code, or a later observation that superseded it, such as a full read of a file that a search result only pointed to. Each release names the turn after which the block may be edited and states its cause in one sentence that names the turn and the action.
A release has one of two strengths: to summary, when the fact that the block existed and its conclusion still help navigation, and to drop, when the block carries no information, such as an operation receipt or an empty search result. The forward pass also marks at most two subgoal milestones per trajectory, which later become decision points.
Literal check. For each released block, we extract its rare literals: paths of at least four characters, identifiers containing an underscore, integers of five or more digits, hexadecimal strings of eight or more characters, decimals with four or more fractional digits, and four-digit numbers in linenumber position, such as 1589: in a search result.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: B.1 Pipeline / B.2 Teacher Prompts
text:
A literal is rare if it is at least four characters long and occurs at most eight times in the whole trajectory. We then scan every action after the cited turn, including tool-call arguments. If a literal reappears, the release moves to the last turn where one reappears, and a drop becomes a summary. Identifiers are traced only for drops, since a summary keeps them. Two further clamps only postpone as well: a block read from a file is not released before the last turn that edits that file, and a block that serves as the blueprint of the final solution is not released before the turn that writes the solution out.
Offline teacher, second pass. The forward pass is conservative and keeps blocks such as the outputs of abandoned lines of investigation. A second pass collects candidates from the kept blocks in three ways: the teacher nominates blocks that, looking back over the finished trajectory, sit on an abandoned or superseded branch, with recall as the goal; a mechanical rule adds tool results whose rare literals stop reappearing at least three turns before the end; and injected reminders and bare continuation messages are added as well. A strict review then judges every candidate. A release must name the turn and action that ended the use of the block, and the review must find no residual dependency in a turn-by-turn scan of the rest of the trajectory, covering literals copied into later tool arguments (such as a line offset), later code checked against the block, and candidate options of an open decision. When the reviewer claims that a later block supersedes a candidate, we verify mechanically that the distinctive lines of the candidate appear in that block and reject the release otherwise. Approved releases pass the same literal check.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: B.1 Pipeline / B.2 Teacher Prompts
text:
Decision points. Each trajectory is assigned a context budget W from 32K, 48K, 64K, and 128K, the largest tier under which its peak context crosses the soft line while its incompressible floor still fits.
Replaying the trajectory turn by turn with exact token counts, we create a decision point when (i) the context first reaches 0.70W , which inserts a soft reminder that the agent may decline; (ii) it reaches 0.95W , which inserts a hard reminder that it may decline only when nothing is editable; or (iii) a milestone of the forward pass is reached.
Each trigger has a cool-down of two turns, and a milestone fires only if the last edit lies at least two turns back. At soft and milestone decision points, if the editable blocks together hold less than 8% of the current context, the teacher is not called and the turn becomes a declined decision. The reminder text contains no numbers, and the teacher never sees token counts.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: B.1 Pipeline / B.2 Teacher Prompts
text:
Online teacher. At a decision point the teacher plays the agent at turn t. It sees the trigger and every block still in context, each marked editable if t > rb and off-limits otherwise; it does not see release points, release reasons, or anything after turn t. Editing is all or nothing: once the teacher edits, it disposes of every editable block, rewriting by default, dropping only blocks without information, and appending a note when several blocks share a conclusion that the note consolidates. Every fact in a summary must come from the block it replaces. The teacher writes the one-sentence rationale that precedes the edits in training. If the edits free less than 8% of the context at a soft or milestone point, the whole decision is discarded and the turn is trained as a decline. The edits execute immediately, so the next decision point sees the rewritten blocks; a summary is editable again only if it is still long.
Final audit. The audit rejects an edit when (i) a number, path, identifier, or quoted string in a summary or note does not occur in its source block, or in the trajectory for a note; (ii) a literal that the edit removes reappears in a later action without having appeared in a summary or in visible output first; or (iii) the editing turn frees less than 3% of the context. It discards a trajectory when a hard reminder ends without an edit, or when more than six turns, and more than 15% of all turns, carry edits. About 4% of annotated trajectories are discarded.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: C Experimental Details
text:
Harnesses. The SWE-bench variants run in Claude Code (version 2.1.7) and Terminal-Bench 2.0 runs in Terminus-2 on Harbor. Both harnesses send ordinary chat requests to the NCE runtime, which serves them as described in Appendix A.5; neither harness needs any change to its prompts or tool definitions.
Context budgets. For a budget W , the compaction threshold of each harness is set to W : Claude Code through its auto-compaction setting and Terminus-2 through its context limit. Terminus-2 counts its own copy of the history, which keeps the text NCE has edited away, so it also compacts NCE runs once that copy reaches W . section: D Analysis (results)

This appendix details the ablations of Section 4.3: context management (D.1), building supervision (D.2), the edits NCE writes at inference (D.3), and the cost of re-prefilling after an edit (D.4).

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: D.1 Context Management
text: Methods. All five methods run on Terminal-Bench 2.0 under a 128K budget. The four baselines use the LongCat base model from which NCE is trained. Harness compaction is the built-in mechanism of Terminus-2: once the history reaches the budget, the harness asks the model for a summary, lets a fresh instance ask questions about it, and continues from the summary, the questions, and their answers. The other three baselines run inside the runtime in place of harness compaction and always keep the system prompt and the task description. The sliding window drops the oldest turns once the prompt exceeds the budget, down to 75% of the budget, and leaves a one-line marker in their place. The fixed memory state drops turns the same way and adds a memory block of at most 4,096 tokens, which the base model rewrites from the previous memory and the dropped turns at every eviction. Prompt compression has the base model compress every tool output longer than 1,024 tokens to at most 256 tokens once it is older than the two most recent turns, and falls back to the sliding window when the prompt still exceeds the budget. NCE keeps harness compaction as in Table 2; since the harness counts its own copy of the history, it also compacts some NCE tasks.

heading: D.2 Building Supervision
embed_text:
Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
section: D.2 Building Supervision (other)

Designs. We compare three ways to build editing supervision on 40 trajectories sampled from our long-trajectory training pool, stratified by source and by the number of editing decisions (26 terminal tasks and 14 software engineering issues, 97 decisions in total). All three use the same teacher model, decide at the same turns, and receive the same trigger signals; the decision turns are those at which the production pipeline edited. One teacher, one pass reads the whole trajectory and writes the edits of every decision in a single response; its prompt states that the agent at decision turn t has seen only the blocks and actions up to t and requires every summary to use that information alone. Two teachers, original history keeps the release points of the offline teacher and runs the online teacher at every decision on the unedited history. Two teachers, evolving context is NCE: each decision is made on the context that the earlier edits produced. The two two-teacher designs share their first decision, since no edit precedes it, and differ only from the second decision on.
Defects. We execute the edits of each design in order on the recorded trajectory and check every edit against what the agent could see at that moment. A literal is a path, file name, identifier with an underscore or an inner capital, number with at least four digits, decimal number, IPv4 address, or hexadecimal hash, of at least five characters, that occurs in fewer than 2% of 1,000 reference trajectories; the frequency filter removes strings such as os.path that an agent can write from general knowledge. An edit at turn t
• uses future information if its text contains a literal that first appears in the trajectory after turn t and is absent from the action of turn t;

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: D.3 Editing at Inference
text:
We read every turn the NCE runtime served in the LongCat runs of Tables 1 and2. An operation is one envelope <ctx> . . . </ctx> ; an editing turn contains at least one operation that executes. Table 7 reports each benchmark at 256K and Figure 14 summarizes the analysis.
Token cost. We count the tokens processed per task as the sum of prompt and output tokens over all model calls, including compaction calls, and average them over tasks with a 10% trimmed mean. At 256K, NCE processes 64% of the tokens of harness compaction on average across the four benchmarks, and on Terminal-Bench the ratio stays between 61% and 74% at every budget.
Editing behavior. Editing turns make up 1.7% of all turns and 8.1% of output tokens, and the edits themselves take 5.7% of output tokens. A task receives 45 operations in 1.9 editing turns on average, drop accounts for 71% of operations, and an editing turn removes 12.7K tokens on average. Of the 73,148 edits the model writes, 99.1% are well formed, address live blocks, and execute as written; the rest mostly address a block that an earlier edit already removed or repeat an edit verbatim. Tighter budgets raise the share of reminded edits: on Terminal-Bench, edits issued without a reminder fall from 72% at 256K to 27% at 48K, and editing turns rise from 2.9% to 5.0% of turns.
Compaction. Because the edited context grows more slowly, the harness rarely needs to compact.
Under Claude Code at 256K, it compacts in 3 of the 1,531 SWE-bench tasks of NCE (0.2%), against 14 of 1,531 under tool-call editing (0.9%) at the same threshold.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: D.3 Editing at Inference
text:
Under Claude Code at 256K, it compacts in 3 of the 1,531 SWE-bench tasks of NCE (0.2%), against 14 of 1,531 under tool-call editing (0.9%) at the same threshold.
Evidence. Edits rarely remove evidence the agent still needs. We trace the rare literals of every block an drop or rewrite removes, with the literal definition of Appendix D.2, through the agent's later actions. Of the removed literals, 1.4% reappear in a later action, and 0.45% reappear while absent from the agent's context. Only 1.2% of drop and rewrite operations remove a literal that the agent later writes without seeing it, and 0.2% when only paths, numbers, and hashes count. Most of these are framework names the model writes from knowledge, such as django.core, or paths a rewritten sub-agent report left out.
Budget. Edits free a quarter of the budget before compaction is due. On Terminal-Bench, Terminus-2 compacts once the unedited history reaches the budget, and NCE's context is always smaller than that history, so we compare the two only before the first harness compaction of each task, where neither side has been compacted. When the unedited history first fills a budget of 48K, 64K, or 128K, the context NCE maintains fills a median of 73%, 69%, and 73% of it (Figure 14a): by then NCE has freed over a quarter of the budget on its own. Over the same turns, edits lower the peak context of a task by a median of 19%.

title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
heading: D.4 Re-prefill After an Edit
text:
An edit changes the rendered context from the first edited block onward, so the KV cache of everything after that block must be recomputed. Edits execute when the turn ends, and every token of the next prompt except the new observation is then known. A runtime can therefore issue the re-prefill as a separate request before the harness returns the observation. We measure how much time this reprefill costs and how much of it fits into time the model server would otherwise leave idle for this agent.
Re-prefill length. For each editing turn we compare the next prompt with the sequence held in the prefix cache, the previous prompt followed by the model's output. The re-prefill spans from the first differing token to the start of the new observation; the observation itself is excluded because every method must prefill it. Turns without edits differ only in the turn delimiter, a single token, which confirms the comparison. The model edits old blocks, and the oldest blocks sit right after the task, so an edit invalidates most of the context: the median re-prefill is 23K to 58K tokens on Terminal-Bench (86-97% of the prompt) and 13K to 22K tokens on SWE-bench (45-55%, behind roughly 18K tokens of Claude Code tool declarations that are never edited).

Hiding the re-prefill. A turn writes its edits before its action, so the runtime knows the new context as soon as the last edit closes, while the model still writes the action and the harness then executes it. The idle time available to the re-prefill therefore runs from the last edit of the turn to the next request. We estimate its decoding part from the output tokens after the last edit and the measured decoding time per token, and take the rest from the harness timestamps. Starting at the last edit, the re-prefill fits entirely in 98% of editing turns under Terminus-2 and 81% under Claude Code (Table 8, Figure 15). These shares are computed from the measured timings of our runs.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Abstract
text: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce EpiSEM-Bench, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Introduction
text:
Large language model (LLM) agents use tools to read documents, inspect resources, and execute operations on a user's behalf (Yao et al., 2022, 2024, Lu et al., 2025). Before sending a payment, sharing a file, or deleting a resource, the agent needs to establish that the operation is permitted in the current environment. This decision depends on facts returned by its tools, such as an authorization limit, a recipient's access rights, or the dependencies of a running service. A missing fact can change the agent's decision even when the tool response contains no false statement.
Existing benchmarks evaluate tool-use capability, action safety, and robustness to adversarial observations (Zhang et al., 2024, Debenedetti et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2026b). AgentDojo evaluates task utility and security using executable checks (Debenedetti et al., 2024). Missing evidence poses a different intervention that requires no attacker instruction, and the remaining observations can all be true. An evaluation of this problem needs to follow the decision from available facts to consequential action. It must establish whether the agent distinguishes permission from prohibition, how that behavior responds to missing evidence, and whether the agent can actively recover the facts needed to proceed appropriately. Task completion alone rewards execution in the permissible case. Avoidance of unsafe execution alone can reward refusal in every case.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Introduction
text: To address these challenges, we introduce the Epistemic Safety under Evidence Missingness Benchmark (EpiSEM-Bench), which separates the world's safety conditions from the evidence visible to the agent. It contains 300 task pairs comprising 600 worlds, with 50 pairs in each of six domains and 60 task families. The suppression inventory contains 1,363 facts, comprising 944 critical and 419 irrelevant, with two to seven critical facts per task. The two worlds in a pair share the request and tools, but differ in the state that makes the target operation prohibited or permissible. An executable oracle judges actions against the complete state. Evidence annotations identify every ordinary-tool exposure of a fact. Suppression therefore persists throughout the rollout. Critical facts enter the safety rule, such as the payment authorization limit. Irrelevant facts, such as a cost-center display label, affect neither legality nor the action parameters. These design choices support three stages of evaluation. Complete evidence first establishes legitimate completion and avoidance of prohibited actions, measured by Full Safe-World Success (SWS) and Full Unsafe Commit Rate (UCR). In Suppressed Evidence (SE), selected facts remain unavailable through ordinary tools. Critical UCR identifies tasks with unsafe execution under critical omission, while Safety Boundary Margin (SBM) characterizes the minimum observed omission needed for failure. In Recoverable Evidence (RE), the same omissions apply, but the agent can actively query an independent audit source. Recovery UCR measures unsafe execution with this opportunity, and Paired Useful Recovery (PUR) requires evidence acquisition followed by restraint in the prohibited world and completion in its permissible twin.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Introduction
text:
The six metrics are intended to be read together. Full SWS supplies the utility context for safety, Critical UCR and SBM describe observed omission vulnerability, and Recovery UCR and PUR distinguish avoiding unsafe action from using restored evidence successfully. Our ten-model evaluation shows why this joint interpretation matters. High completion can coexist with prohibited execution, strong restraint can coexist with refusal after permission is established, and recovery access can be beneficial without being used consistently. The resulting profiles reveal different strengths and failure modes that a single score would conceal. Our contributions are:
• An executable benchmark for missing-evidence safety. We introduce EpiSEM-Bench, which removes selected true facts from tool observations while preserving the world's safety conditions. Matched prohibited and permissible tasks expose both unsafe execution and excessive refusal. Avoiding all action therefore cannot stand in for useful safety.
• A protocol for safety boundaries and evidence recovery. The matched worlds, omission intervention, and recovery opportunity yield six core measurements spanning complete-evidence behavior, omission vulnerability, and useful recovery. Their joint interpretation distinguishes task completion, avoidance of unsafe execution, and evidence-guided action. Recovery calls and action sequences explain whether failures arise before acquisition or after the facts have been restored.
• A ten-model evaluation with reproducible analyses. We find that the model with the highest observed safety boundary does not achieve the highest paired recovery score, that recovery gains coexist with task-level regressions, and that obtaining evidence does not ensure appropriate action. Domain, family, and interaction-cost analyses locate variation in these outcomes. Retained task definitions and rollout records support regeneration of the reported results.

• A ten-model evaluation with reproducible analyses. We find that the model with the highest observed safety boundary does not achieve the highest paired recovery score, that recovery gains coexist with task-level regressions, and that obtaining evidence does not ensure appropriate action. Domain, family, and interaction-cost analyses locate variation in these outcomes. Retained task definitions and rollout records support regeneration of the reported results.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Related Work
text:
Evaluating tool-using agents. ReAct couples reasoning with tool actions (Yao et al., 2022). τ-bench and τ 2 -bench assess task completion under domain policies (Yao et al., 2024, Barres et al., 2025), while ToolSandbox models stateful tool dependencies (Lu et al., 2025). Safety benchmarks assess risky execution (Ruan et al., 2024, Zhang et al., 2024, Levy et al., 2026, Vijayvargiya et al., 2026a), while AgentHarm targets malicious requests (Andriushchenko et al., 2025). When2Call evaluates whether to call tools, ask for clarification, or report inability to answer (Ross et al., 2025). EpiSEM-Bench varies safety-relevant evidence in matched prohibited and permissible worlds.
Security in external observations. InjecAgent and AgentDojo evaluate tool-response injections (Zhan et al., 2024, Debenedetti et al., 2024). MCP-SafetyBench tests attacks involving real tool servers (Zong et al., 2026), and AgentDyn evaluates dynamic workflows (Li et al., 2026). IHEval tests instruction-priority conflicts (Zhang et al., 2025). Task Shield checks alignment with user goals (Jia et al., 2025), while MELON compares tool calls under original and masked user prompts (Zhu et al., 2025). Our intervention preserves instructions and retained facts while suppressing safety evidence, exposing unsafe execution of the original request.
Missing information and recovery. AgentNoiseBench perturbs observations (Wang et al., 2026b), while ReliabilityBench injects infrastructure faults (Gupta, 2026). AbsenceBench evaluates omitted-information recognition (Fu et al., 2025). Controlled instruction underspecification is studied in Long-Horizon Augmented Workflows (LHAW) and related work (Pu et al., 2026, Ji et al., 2026), while clarification is studied in coding and tool-use settings (Vijayvargiya et al., 2026b, Edwards and Schuster, 2026, Suri et al., 2026). AgentAbstain pairs tasks requiring action with closely matched tasks requiring abstention (Liu et al., 2026). EpiSEM-Bench combines paired outcomes, persistent atom-level suppression, minimum observed failure cardinality, and optional authoritative recovery to evaluate evidence-dependent decisions and useful action after restoration.

heading: EpiSEM-Bench
text:
EpiSEM-Bench is designed around the gap between a truthful observation and sufficient evidence for action.
The evaluator retains the complete state to judge legality, while the agent receives the request and tool observations. This separation allows a safety-relevant fact to disappear from view without making the prohibited operation permissible. Figure 1 shows the overview of EpiSEM-Bench.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Evidence atoms and suppression
text:
An evidence atom represents one fact about an object in the environment. Its annotation includes an identifier, subject, predicate, world-specific value, source, and the ordinary-tool responses that expose it. Critical atoms contain facts relevant to the task's safety rule. Irrelevant atoms contain facts that determine neither action legality nor the parameters required for the target operation.
A mask specifies the atoms to suppress. The observation projection removes every annotated exposure of these atoms throughout the rollout, including those arising from repeated ordinary reads. It leaves the private state, safety rule, user request, tool schemas, action semantics, and unmasked values unchanged. The remaining responses contain true facts, without injected instruction or replacement assertion. Atom identities and exposure structure are shared across twins. The mask can therefore be applied in both worlds.
Fact-level suppression preserves the operational context around the missing evidence. Removing an entire tool response could also remove the amount, recipient, or resource needed to execute the task, mixing missing safety evidence with inability to perform the operation. Annotated exposures allow us to remove the selected facts while retaining other true information. Applying the mask throughout the rollout also prevents repeated reads from inadvertently restoring them, so the intended evidence deficit persists across the agent's ordinary-tool choices.
We construct tasks from the private state and executable rule before specifying evidence, exposure maps, tools, and the user goal. Validation checks schema consistency, exposure paths, and opposite oracle labels across the twins. Other annotated facts describe workflow context or redundant evidence and remain outside the critical/irrelevant omission inventory. Appendix A.2 illustrates the intervention on a concrete payment request.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Optional evidence recovery
text:
In SE, selected facts are removed from ordinary tool responses and remain unavailable even if the agent repeats its reads. RE retains the same omissions but adds an independent evidence-recovery tool that returns all omitted facts and their authoritative values upon a valid query. Recovery changes what the agent can observe, not the underlying state or whether an action is permitted. The agent needs to decide whether and when to seek the missing evidence, as well as how to act once it is available.
Evidence is restored only when the agent makes a valid audit query. Making the tool available does not automatically supply the missing facts. The agent can actively use this tool to establish whether the requested operation is permitted, then withhold it in the unsafe world or carry it out in the safe twin. RE therefore evaluates whether agents initiate verification, obtain the missing evidence, and use it to guide the consequential action. SE tests decisions while the evidence deficit remains unresolved, giving Critical UCR and SBM. RE tests whether the agent actively resolves that deficit and adjusts its action to the recovered facts, giving Recovery UCR and PUR. Returning all omitted facts on a valid query makes the subsequent decision directly observable: once the query succeeds, the agent has the evidence needed to distinguish the twins. We compare SE and RE under identical nonempty omission masks. The full-evidence baseline supplies complete ordinary observations without a recovery tool. Trajectories distinguish failure to seek evidence from premature execution, unsafe action after recovery, and refusal despite permission to proceed.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Reporting safety, utility, and recovery
text:
Let N denote the total number of matched unsafe/safe task pairs, with N = 300 in our benchmark. We report six core metrics to characterize safety, utility, and evidence recovery. Full SWS and Full UCR establish the agent's completion and safety behavior with complete evidence. Critical UCR and SBM describe which tasks exhibit unsafe execution under SE and where their observed omission boundaries lie. Recovery UCR and PUR assess safety with recovery access and whether active restoration supports the appropriate outcome in both RE twins. All six are reported as percentages. Supplementary measures of failure frequency, evidence acquisition, action timing, and safe-world outcomes explain the behavior underlying this core profile.
Unsafe execution and legitimate completion. UCR is the fraction of tasks with at least one commit prohibited by the complete-world oracle. The numerator is the number of affected tasks, and the denominator is all N tasks. Full UCR uses the unsafe-world full-evidence baseline. Critical UCR considers all completed unsafe-world SE rollouts with nonempty critical-evidence masks. Recovery UCR applies the same rule in RE, including execution without a recovery call. SWS requires legal target-goal completion in the safe twin without an invalid action. Full SWS uses the complete-evidence baseline.
Omission failure frequency. As a complementary measure, Critical Omission Failure Rate averages the fraction of unsafe rollouts among each task's completed critical-omission conditions in SE, then averages these fractions across all 300 tasks. Unlike Critical UCR, which records whether a task ever fails, this measure describes how frequently its tested omissions lead to unsafe execution.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Safety Boundary Margin.
text:
For each task pair i ∈ {1, . . . , N}, let c i be the number of critical atoms and m i the minimum cardinality of a critical mask with an observed unsafe SE rollout. After the full-evidence baseline, we inspect critical omission combinations in increasing size, reusing completed rollouts and evaluating untested conditions as needed, until an unsafe witness is found or all combinations have been tested. A full-evidence failure gives m i = 0. If no critical subset yields an unsafe commit under its retained rollout, we assign the sentinel m i = c i + 1. SBM normalizes these boundaries and averages them over all task pairs:
All omission combinations of smaller cardinality are tested before a larger one is accepted as the boundary, without assuming that removing more evidence always increases risk. A higher SBM indicates a larger average normalized failure boundary, with a value of one assigned to tasks with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. SBM measures resistance to unsafe execution. An agent that always refuses can attain a maximal SBM without completing any permissible task. We thus interpret SBM alongside SWS and PUR.
The procedure is detailed in Appendix B.

heading: Safety Boundary Margin.
text:
The procedure is detailed in Appendix B.
Strict and paired recovery. Strict unsafe recovery requires restoration of all omitted atoms, no invalid action or prohibited commit, and a final abstention or escalation. Strict safe recovery requires restoration followed by legal target-goal completion, with no invalid action. PUR requires both outcomes under the same nonempty critical omission mask in RE. Let q i ≥ 1 be the number of completed nonempty critical masks shared by both RE twins of task pair i. For j ∈ {1, . . . , q i }, let p ij equal one when both twins satisfy strict recovery under the jth such mask, and zero otherwise. PUR averages these joint outcomes within each task and then across tasks:
Refusing both twins or executing both twins gives p ij = 0, since one of the two required outcomes fails. SWS allows legal completion without restoration, while strict recovery requires restoration explicitly. Each successful pair includes agent-initiated evidence acquisition, withholding the prohibited operation, and completing its permissible counterpart. Recovery-call rates and the two worlds' outcomes show which steps agents complete or fail.
Evidence acquisition and action behavior. Attempt records whether an agent makes a valid recovery query. Premature commit records whether it executes the target operation before recovering the missing facts. Every valid recovery query returns all omitted facts. Attempt therefore indicates that the evidence was obtained. Premature commit includes execution without any recovery query. In safe-twin rollouts without legal completion, stopping or escalating is counted as false abstention. Remaining failures, including invalid or unfinished episodes, are classified as other non-completions. Recovery, behavioral, and omission SWS rates first average the applicable conditions within each task and then weight the N tasks equally.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Safety Boundary Margin.
text:
Joint interpretation of the metrics. The measurements form a profile rather than independent claims of agent quality. Full SWS and Full UCR establish whether successful execution is accompanied by appropriate restraint. Critical UCR identifies affected tasks, while SBM supplies the observed boundary information that an affected-task count does not contain. Recovery UCR and PUR distinguish safety with a recovery opportunity from evidence acquisition followed by correct behavior in both worlds.
Joint interpretation resolves otherwise ambiguous successes. Refusing every operation can give zero UCR and maximal SBM, but gives neither legitimate completion nor PUR. High SWS can instead accompany execution without regard to permission. Low Recovery UCR alone also leaves open whether the agent verified the facts or simply avoided acting. PUR requires active verification and the appropriate paired outcome, while acquisition and action records explain unsuccessful pairs. Reading the six metrics together therefore evaluates safety, usefulness, and evidence-dependent decisions without treating any one as a substitute for the others.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Evaluation
text:
The ten-model evaluation follows three stages. Full SWS and Full UCR assess completion and safety under complete evidence. Critical UCR and SBM measure vulnerability to missing evidence, while Recovery UCR and PUR evaluate evidence recovery. Behavioral partitions and radar profiles further reveal distinct failure modes and model strengths.
Experimental setup. We evaluate the ten models listed in Table 1, including GPT-6-Luna and Claude-Haiku-5.5, using the same tasks, tool schemas, system instruction, and tool-use evaluation framework. The evaluated serving configurations are documented in Appendix E. Every model completes 6,052 fixed evaluation conditions: 600 full-evidence unsafe/safe baselines and 5,452 single-atom omissions, comprising all 1,363 critical and irrelevant atoms in both worlds and settings. These conditions remain complete even when the model fails with full evidence.
To determine safety boundaries, we inspect critical omission combinations in the unsafe world under SE in increasing cardinality, reusing completed conditions and evaluating untested masks until an unsafe witness is found or coverage is exhaustive. The first unsafe mask receives counterpart evaluations in the safe world and RE. All completed nonempty critical omissions enter the metrics. Paired comparisons align the same task, world, and mask, while PUR aligns the RE twins. The adaptive procedure produces different condition sets, whose coverage is reported in Table 7.

heading: Evaluation
text:
Omission failures also differ in scope and recurrence. Figure 2(a) distinguishes tasks that fail under at least one tested omission from the average fraction of tested conditions producing unsafe execution. For GPT-6-Luna, these rates are 21.0% and 7.9%: vulnerability reaches roughly one in five tasks, but unsafe execution is less frequent across its retained conditions. Qwen3-14B's high values on both measures instead indicate failures spanning nearly all tasks and recurring across many tested omissions. Table 8 thus distinguishes occasional failures within affected tasks from broadly recurrent unsafe behavior. SBM characterizes where an observed failure boundary lies. The decomposition in Figure 4 separates tasks that already fail with complete evidence, tasks that first fail after suppression, and tasks that remain without an unsafe commit through exhaustive critical omission testing. These categories explain different sources of a low margin: unsafe decisions can be present before any fact is removed, or arise when safety evidence becomes unavailable. GPT-6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash illustrate why similar full-evidence safety can coexist with different boundary profiles, while Qwen3-14B's low margin largely reflects failures already present at baseline. heading: Paired useful recovery. / GLM-4.7-Flash
text:
Resistance to omission and useful recovery are distinct strengths in the evaluated model profiles. GPT-6-Luna has the highest SBM, whereas DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash more often recovers evidence and reaches the required outcome in both worlds. PUR combines agent-initiated verification with permissionsensitive action: the restored facts must support withholding the prohibited operation and completing its permissible counterpart. Its difference from the safety and completion measures shows why neither restraint nor goal achievement alone captures this sequence. Figure 2(c) shows that GPT-6-Luna more often succeeds only in the unsafe twin than in both twins. False abstention limits useful recovery: stopping prohibited actions must be paired with completing permissible ones, as shown in Appendix D.4.
Figure 2(d) exposes the complementary problem: legal completion without evidence restoration. Qwen3-14B has a task-averaged safe RE completion rate of 94.7%, but a strict safe recovery rate of only 15.4%. GLM-4.7-Flash shows the same qualitative pattern. Many successful operations therefore occur while the missing facts remain unresolved. These models also frequently commit in prohibited worlds, indicating that high safe-world completion can reward execution without adequate verification. The paired criterion tests whether the agent actively establishes permission instead of relying on a hidden state that happens to permit its action.
Task variation and cost. Recovery performance varies across domains and task families, so aggregate strengths do not extend uniformly across workflows. Active recovery also increases interaction cost without ensuring useful action. Detailed analyses of task structure and interaction cost are provided in Appendix D.

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: Conclusion and Discussion
text:
EpiSEM-Bench evaluates agent safety under missing evidence through matched worlds, controlled omission, and optional recovery. Across ten models, robustness to evidence omission does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Effective recovery requires agents to obtain evidence and use it for both restraint and legitimate completion. Combining the six metrics with recovery records identifies whether agents fail to seek missing facts or fail to use them after acquisition, providing targets for improving safety without sacrificing utility. These findings highlight the importance of jointly evaluating safety and utility.
In this work, the six metrics must be interpreted jointly: avoiding unsafe execution can reflect indiscriminate refusal, while completing permissible tasks can reflect execution without verification. Matched worlds and recovery records distinguish these behaviors from agents that actively obtain evidence and act according to permission. Figure 3 shows distinct capability combinations. GPT-6-Luna combines strong restraint and a high safety boundary margin with more limited legitimate completion and PUR. Qwen3-14B, Gemma-4-31B-IT, and GLM-4.7-Flash achieve high legitimate completion rates but perform poorly on safety and paired recovery. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash achieves higher PUR than GPT-6-Luna despite having a lower SBM. Robustness to missing evidence and useful recovery therefore capture different strengths. These profiles suggest that agents could improve by verifying permission before committing, using recovered facts to guide actions, and completing legitimate tasks once permission is established. The benchmark evaluates whether such changes improve both safety and utility, complementing policy-violation detection (Wen et al., 2025), executable enforcement, and provenance mechanisms (Wang et al., 2026a, Debenedetti et al., 2026).

title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
heading: B. Safety Boundary Evaluation Procedure
text:
This procedure determines the observed safety boundary defined in Section 3.4 from retained unsafe-world SE rollouts. For task pair i, c i is the number of critical atoms and m i is the returned boundary value, with c i + 1 reserved for no observed failure. The procedure is:
1. Complete the full-evidence SE baseline in both worlds and all scheduled single-atom critical and irrelevant omissions in both worlds and settings. 2. If the unsafe-world baseline contains an unsafe commit, set m i = 0. 3. Otherwise, inspect critical omission combinations in increasing cardinality, reusing completed rollouts and evaluating untested conditions as needed. Stop at the first unsafe witness and set m i to its size. 4. If every critical subset has been tested without an unsafe commit, set m i = c i + 1.
The recorded ordering seed, scenario identifier, and atom identifiers determine a hash-based ordering within each cardinality. For an unsafe witness, the corresponding safe-world and RE conditions are retained for additional outcome comparisons.
To verify the returned boundary, suppose a nonempty witness has cardinality k. Every critical mask of cardinality less than k has been tested without an unsafe commit. The minimum observed failure cardinality is therefore at least k. The retained witness contains an unsafe commit. Thus, the minimum is at most k. These two bounds give m i = k. A full-evidence failure instead gives m i = 0, since no mask has negative cardinality. This argument does not require monotonicity. A larger omission may produce a trajectory without an unsafe commit. Tasks have at most seven critical atoms and hence at most 128 critical subsets, including the empty mask. The no-failure sentinel is assigned only after all subsets have been tested without an unsafe commit.

heading: C.2. Failure scope, frequency, and matched recovery
text:
Critical UCR describes how widely failures occur across tasks, while Critical Omission Failure Rate describes their frequency within the retained conditions, with tasks weighted equally. A task with one unsafe rollout contributes one to the UCR numerator but contributes its unsafe fraction to the frequency measure.
Table 9 compares SE and RE using completed critical masks shared by both settings in the corresponding world. UCR change marks each task unsafe if any shared mask fails. SWS change averages legal completion over shared masks within each task. These aligned comparisons hold the tested omissions fixed rather than subtracting aggregates with different coverage.
All ten models have a negative UCR change, ranging from -45.3 to -0.7 percentage points. Nine models have a positive SWS change, while MiMo-V2.5-Pro decreases by 0.6 points.

title: ENVACE: INTERNALIZING ENVIRONMENT DY-NAMICS VIA WORLD REHEARSAL FOR AGENTIC RE-INFORCEMENT LEARNING
heading: Abstract
text: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, τ 2 -Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales.
