title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Results
text: Enumeration vs. Selection. Throughout the solve process, each LLM enumerates many potential candidates, reasons through those candidates, and then runs the most promising of the candidates through an oracle tool call. We investigate whether or not LLMs are capable of enumerating passing molecules but fail at the reasoning and selection step. In order to do so, we use GPT5.4 mini to extract every SMILES string mentioned in each of the agent's traces for the Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly tasks. We then, using the task instance's evaluation pipeline, evaluate all of the molecules that the agent did not perform an oracle call on -this set of molecules represents the molecules which the agent hypothesized could be strong candidates, but considered to be inferior. We then calculate the overall recovered success rate on SMDD-Bench had the LLM selected the best candidate from its enumeration and report the values in Table 4. More details on how we performed this experiment can be found in Appendix G. Scaffold hopping sees a significant increase in recovered rate for Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT5.4 -indicating that the agents are not as capable at reasoning through binding interactions of chemically different analogues without first performing oracle calls. On the other hand, fragment assembly, a task requiring a deep understanding of how the binding pocket and surrounding chemistry affects the 3D geometry of the small molecule binding pose, sees very minimal overall improvement. Interestingly, MiniMax M2.7 nearly doubles its success rate for the Lead Optimization task, indicating its ability to enumerate solutions and inability to select from the enumerations.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Related Work
text:
SMDD-Bench evaluates LLM agents on challenging, real-world small molecule drug design tasks.
Existing chemistry and molecular benchmarks -ChemBench [Mirza et al., 2025], MolecularIQ [Bartmann et al., 2026], SmolInstruct [Yu et al., 2024], QCBench [Xie et al., 2025], and MuMOInstruct [Dey et al., 2025] -are restricted to single-turn question answering on relatively simple chemistry tasks and do not evaluate complex agentic systems on real-world problems. Prior work on multi-turn iterative molecular optimization [Chennakesavalu et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2024] Beyond single-turn QA, prior LLM agents for drug design and discovery [Ock et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026a,b, Zhang et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024] either report results on a few hand-selected successes or use ad hoc, non-standardized evaluation setups, often retrofitting datasets built for de novo molecular generation such as ZINC, Therapeutics Data Commons, GuacaMol, PMO, and MOSES [Tingle et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2021, Brown et al., 2019, Gao et al., 2022, Polykovskiy et al., 2020]. Adjacent domains like computational biology have produced agentic benchmarks such as DeepResearch Bench [Du et al., 2025], BioProBench [Liu et al., 2025c], BioLP-Bench [Ivanov, 2024], ABC-Bench [Liu et al., 2025a], Lab-Bench [Laurent et al., 2024], BixBench [Mitchener et al., 2025], and CompBioBench [Nair et al., 2026], but no prior work evaluates LLMs on agentic small molecule drug design.
The primary contributions of SMDD-Bench compared to previous work are as follows: (1) the first standardized benchmark for evaluating long-horizon, multi-turn, small molecule drug design agents on a chemically diverse array of challenging drug discovery tasks;
(2) support for five relevant, realworld task types: 2D Pharmacophore Identification, Interaction Point Discovery, Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly; and (3) guaranteed solvability for all tasks, including the Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly tasks via the existence of a held-out witness molecule which passes all evaluation requirements.

Prior work on multi-turn iterative molecular optimization [Chennakesavalu et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2024] Beyond single-turn QA, prior LLM agents for drug design and discovery [Ock et al., 2026, Li et al., 2026a,b, Zhang et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024] either report results on a few hand-selected successes or use ad hoc, non-standardized evaluation setups, often retrofitting datasets built for de novo molecular generation such as ZINC, Therapeutics Data Commons, GuacaMol, PMO, and MOSES [Tingle et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2021, Brown et al., 2019, Gao et al., 2022, Polykovskiy et al., 2020]. Adjacent domains like computational biology have produced agentic benchmarks such as DeepResearch Bench [Du et al., 2025], BioProBench [Liu et al., 2025c], BioLP-Bench [Ivanov, 2024], ABC-Bench [Liu et al., 2025a], Lab-Bench [Laurent et al., 2024], BixBench [Mitchener et al., 2025], and CompBioBench [Nair et al., 2026], but no prior work evaluates LLMs on agentic small molecule drug design.
The primary contributions of SMDD-Bench compared to previous work are as follows: (1) the first standardized benchmark for evaluating long-horizon, multi-turn, small molecule drug design agents on a chemically diverse array of challenging drug discovery tasks;
(2) support for five relevant, realworld task types: 2D Pharmacophore Identification, Interaction Point Discovery, Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly; and (3) guaranteed solvability for all tasks, including the Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly tasks via the existence of a held-out witness molecule which passes all evaluation requirements.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Discussion and Conclusion
text: We present SMDD-Bench, the first agentic benchmark evaluating LLM agents on challenging, longhorizon, real-world small molecule drug design. SMDD-Bench tests scientific and chemical reasoning across diverse chemistries, task types, and protein targets, alongside domain-specific tool-calling capabilities, with every task instance generated to be guaranteed-solvable. An agent can perform lead optimization on properties unseen at training time, understand the failure modes of specific oracles, selecting the right tool for a given task, and adhere to constraints (such as maintaining protein-protein contacts when designing a PROTAC) that were never specified during training. title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Discussion and Conclusion
text: Reliance on Boltz2 and ADMET-AI. Boltz2 and ADMET-AI are imperfect oracles. However, in SMDD-Bench we treat these oracles as the ground truth within the "world" of the benchmark, analogous to an agent requesting wet lab assays. As a result, we deliberately provide a limited number of oracle calls to reflect the sparsity of real-world wet lab experiments. To enforce that the Boltz2 and ADMET-AI predicted distributions are the operative ground truth, all PDB-sourced complexes are re-folded via Boltz2 and re-scored by ADMET-AI during task generation, so the agent only sees structure-activity relationships and property distributions produced by these oracles. SMDD-Bench is intended as a testbed for developing training frameworks calibrated to the Boltz2 and ADMET-AI distributions. The same frameworks can later be interfaced with an autonomous laboratory, where the oracle becomes a real wet lab that synthesizes, characterizes, and tests candidates, allowing agents to be re-trained under the true distribution of real-world structure-activity relationships.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B Details on Task Type Generation / B.1 2D Pharmacophore Identification
text:
In the following section, we provide the specific details for generating the task instances for each task type.
B.1 2D Pharmacophore Identification. Each instance of this task type asks the agent to identify a 2D pharmacophore that distinguishes a set of active molecules from a set of inactive molecules for a given protein target. Tasks are generated procedurally from ChEMBL.
Activity data extraction We restrict to direct binding assays by requiring standard_type ∈ {IC 50 , K i }, standard_units = nM, standard_relation = '=', and confidence_score ≥ 8.
Only targets with target_type = 'SINGLE PROTEIN' are considered.
Compound normalization and deduplication. SMILES are canonicalized via RDKit. We discard multi-component salts/mixtures, molecules with exact molecular weight greater than 900 Da, and entries that fail RDKit parsing. Multiple measurements of the same canonical compound are collapsed by taking the per-compound median activity in nM.
Active/inactive labeling Compounds with median activity below 1,000 nM (IC 50 /K i < 1 µM) are labeled active; compounds with median activity above 10,000 nM (> 10 µM) are labeled inactive. Compounds in the 1-10 µM ambiguous zone are discarded, providing a 10× potency gap between the two classes that excludes borderline molecules. Targets with fewer than 30 actives or fewer than 30 inactives after filtering are not eligible.
Diverse subset selection For each class, ten visible exemplars are selected via the MaxMin algorithm operating on Morgan fingerprints (radius = 2, 2048 bits, seed = 42) [Ashton et al., 2002]. The remaining compounds form a held-out evaluation set that the agent never sees. MaxMin selection forces the visible exemplars to span chemical space, allowing the agent to see the most chemically diverse spread of actives as possible.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B Details on Task Type Generation / B.1 2D Pharmacophore Identification
text:
Agent inputs and outputs Each generated task directory contains: actives.smi and inactives.smi (the 10 visible exemplars per class, given to the agent), protein.fasta (the target sequence). The agent is required to emit solution.py defining check_pharmacophore(smiles: str) -> bool, which is run on every molecule of the held-out evaluation set during scoring.
Design rationale Using ChEMBL-measured inactives rather than synthetically constructed decoys (e.g. DUD-E) ensures that negatives are experimentally verified non-binders that may share scaffolds with the actives, ruling out solutions that rely on coarse topological dissimilarity. Providing both classes to the agent and requiring generalization to a held-out set forces extraction of a genuine substructural pattern rather than memorization of the visible exemplars.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B.2 Interaction Point Discovery
text:
Each instance of this task type asks the agent to predict, given a single apo-like protein structure and a pocket center, the 3D coordinates and pharmacophoric type of the three interaction points most likely to be conserved across diverse binders of that pocket. Tasks are generated procedurally from the RCSB PDB [Berman et al., 2000].
Ensemble construction For each specified target from the PDB, we fetch up to 500 unique X-ray crystal structures with resolution better than 2.5 Å. The first structure containing a drug-like ligand is taken as the reference; common crystallization additives (glycerol, PEG, DMSO, sulfate, and similar) are explicitly blacklisted. Within that reference structure, the largest non-blacklisted ligand by heavy-atom count is selected as the reference ligand. The reference receptor is stripped of all heteroatoms, waters, and ions to produce receptor.pdb, and the centroid of the reference ligand defines the pocket center provided to the agent.
Local structural alignment All ensemble members are superimposed onto the reference using only the C α atoms of residues within 12 Å of the pocket center. Restricting the alignment to the local pocket suppresses contributions from global protein motion and induced fit -minimizing potential global variance in the 3D reference frame.
Pharmacophore feature extraction For each aligned structure, we select the ligand whose centroid lies closest to the reference pocket center (within 12 Å); waters, the same blacklist of crystallization additives and common ions used during reference selection, and small fragments (fewer than six heavy atoms) are excluded from candidacy. RDKit is then used to assign each atom or functional group of the chosen ligand to one of six pharmacophoric families: hydrogen-bond donor, hydrogen-bond acceptor, aromatic, hydrophobic, cation, or anion. Features further than 12 Å from the pocket center are discarded to exclude allosteric binders and crystallographic artifacts.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B.2 Interaction Point Discovery
text:
Consensus clustering Clustering proceeds in two stages. First, DBSCAN [Ester et al., 1996] is run independently per pharmacophore family at ε = 1.0 Å on the 3D points of that family alone, so that, e.g., donor and acceptor densities never collapse into a single cluster regardless of spatial proximity.
A cluster is retained only if it is supported by at least 15% of the unique structures contributing to the ensemble; the conservation score of a cluster is the fraction of unique PDB entries supporting it. Cross-family relationships between surviving clusters are handled separately during ground-truth point selection.
Ground-truth point selection Surviving clusters are post-processed to yield a physically valid, non-redundant ground-truth set: (i) clusters within 2 Å of any heavy atom of the reference receptor are discarded as sterically clashing with the reference protein conformation given to the agent; (ii) clusters of different types (e.g. donor and cation arising from a basic amine, or donor and acceptor from a hydroxyl) whose centroids lie within 2 Å are merged into a single point with a set-valued type label, reflecting and allowing for chemical ambiguity in the agent output. The full set of N ≥ 3 surviving consensus points constitutes the ground truth.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Agent inputs and outputs / Design rationale
text:
The agent is provided receptor.pdb (the reference protein with all ligands and solvent removed) the pocket center coordinates and the 12 Å pocket radius where all interaction points are within. The agent must emit solution.csv with exactly three rows of the form x, y, z, type, where type is drawn from {Donor, Acceptor, Aromatic, Hydrophobic, Cation, Anion}.
Evaluation Predicted points are matched against the N ground-truth points by optimal bipartite assignment [Kuhn, 1955] on Euclidean distance, restricted to type-compatible pairs: a prediction is type-compatible with a ground-truth point if its label is in the ground-truth label set, with an additional aromatic/hydrophobic equivalence at scoring time, reflecting that aromatic ring features and hydrophobic features are partially co-tagged by RDKit and that the ground-truth construction may assign only one of the two labels at a position where both are chemically reasonable. This choice was made out of evaluation leniency. A match is counted if the assigned distance is below 2.5 Å. The task score is (number of matched predictions) / 3, and the task is considered solved only when all three predictions match (score = 1.0).
Design rationale. The local-pocket alignment, conservation threshold, and steric clash filter were designed to ensure that the targets are simultaneously experimentally grounded, chemotype-agnostic, empirically solvable, and medicinally useful in the specific receptor conformation handed to the agent.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B.3 Scaffold Hopping / Pocket definition
text:
Each instance of this task type asks the agent to propose a novel small molecule that binds the same protein pocket as a given reference ligand and reproduces its protein-ligand interaction pattern, while presenting a chemically distinct scaffold. Tasks are generated procedurally from the RCSB PDB and ChEMBL, and every task is constructed around an explicit witness molecule that is known and evaluated a priori to satisfy the evaluation criteria -thus guaranteeing the solvability of the task instance.
Target and canonical structure selection Targets are sourced from a curated pool of ∼300 (UniProt, PDB, ligand) triplets spanning diverse protein families, grouped by UniProt identifier.
For each UniProt, the PDB entry with the best X-ray resolution is chosen as the canonical receptor; its FASTA sequence and a single fixed pocket definition are reused throughout downstream steps.
Pocket definition. The binding pocket is defined as the set of residues with any heavy atom within 6 Å of the canonical ligand. This pocket, expressed as (chain, SEQRES position) pairs, is held fixed for all downstream Boltz2 cofolding runs and is also handed to the agent as part of the task specification.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Candidate ligand collection
text:
For each target we assemble a candidate ligand pool from two sources: (i) all ligands co-crystallized with the same UniProt across the PDB, with bond orders corrected via Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) templates and deduplicated by canonical SMILES; and (ii) ChEMBL actives against the target with reported IC 50 /K i /K d below 10 µM, pre-filtered to remove unparseable structures, molecules above 1,000 Da, and metal-containing species.
Scaffold-diversity pre-filter Bemis-Murcko scaffolds are extracted for every candidate, and for each unordered ligand pair we compute the Maximum Common Substructure (MCS) of the two scaffolds [Bemis and Murcko, 1996]. A pair is retained only if the MCS covers less than 65% of the heavy atoms of the larger scaffold; the symmetric denominator ensures the filter does not depend on the eventual reference/witness role assignment.
Crystal-PLIP pre-ranking For pairs in which both members appear as PDB co-crystals, each source structure is superimposed onto the canonical receptor using C α atoms of pocket residues within 12 Å, and a protein-ligand interaction fingerprint is extracted with PLIP [Salentin et al., 2015]. Pairs are then ordered by descending crystal interaction-fingerprint similarity, with PDB-PDB pairs prioritized over pairs involving ChEMBL-only ligands. This ranking concentrates downstream compute on pairs that are most likely to clear the interaction-similarity gate during the co-folding screen.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Candidate ligand collection
text:
Co-folding screen For each target, the top-ranked unique candidate ligands are co-folded with the canonical receptor using Boltz2 [Passaro et al., 2025], constrained to the fixed pocket definition with 10 diffusion samples per ligand. From the resulting ensemble of 10 conformations, we extract: (i) the Boltz2-predicted binding probability across samples; (ii) per-sample PLIP interaction finger-prints, where each interaction is coarsened to a (chain, residue, broad type) tuple over six interaction families (HBond, Aromatic, Ionic, Halogen, Metal, Hydrophobic); and (iii) a consensus interaction fingerprint defined as the set of tuples present in at least 60% of the diffusion samples. Any ligand whose predicted binding probability falls below 0.75 is discarded. The consensus interaction fingerprint is required during evaluation to offset variance induced by Boltz2-predicted binding poses.
Witness validation and role assignment A pair is promoted to a task only if both members survive the binding gate and the set Tanimoto between their consensus interaction fingerprints exceeds 0.75. Within a surviving pair, the ligand with the higher predicted binding probability is assigned as the reference (the molecule provided to the agent to hop away from) and the other becomes the witness (the hidden molecule whose existence guarantees the solvability of the task instance). We retain at most three tasks per UniProt target and require distinct reference molecules across tasks of the same target, preventing one well-behaved reference from dominating the benchmark.
Agent inputs and outputs The agent is given: complex.pdb (the Boltz2-predicted reference complex, with the ligand on chain L), reference.sdf (the reference ligand conformer extracted from the Boltz2 complex), protein.fasta (the canonical protein sequence), and the target ligand identifier and pocket contact residue list used during the task generation process. The agent is required to emit solution.smi containing a single SMILES string. The witness molecule is never exposed to the agent.

Agent inputs and outputs The agent is given: complex.pdb (the Boltz2-predicted reference complex, with the ligand on chain L), reference.sdf (the reference ligand conformer extracted from the Boltz2 complex), protein.fasta (the canonical protein sequence), and the target ligand identifier and pocket contact residue list used during the task generation process. heading: Candidate ligand collection
embed_text:

section: Candidate ligand collection (other)

Evaluation A submission must clear five gates: (1) the SMILES is parseable by RDKit;
(2) the Morgan fingerprint Tanimoto (radius = 2, 2048 bits) between the agent's molecule and the reference is below 0.5; (3) the Bemis-Murcko scaffold MCS, normalized by the heavy-atom count of the larger of the two scaffolds, is below 0.65; (4) the agent's molecule, co-folded under the same Boltz protocol used during generation (10 diffusion samples, identical pocket constraint), produces a consensus interaction fingerprint whose set Tanimoto with the reference's consensus fingerprint exceeds 0.75; and (5) the predicted binding probability of the agent's molecule across the same diffusion samples exceeds 0.7. Gates 1, 2, and 3 enforce 2D novelty; gates 4 and 5 enforce 3D mimicry, ensuring the scaffold hopped molecule adheres to the same pharmacophore, and binding competence.
Design rationale Every task is anchored to a concrete witness molecule that has already cleared the same evaluation pipeline the agent will be scored against, ensuring the existence of at least one solution for the task instance. The 2D-dissimilarity and 3D-interaction-similarity criteria rule evaluates for a true scaffold hopped molecule and that the submitted molecule matches the binding mode of the original reference molecule. High predicted binding probability of the submitted molecule is also enforced. We score interaction similarity against a consensus fingerprint over the 10-sample diffusion ensemble rather than against the single most confident pose to ensure robustness against variance in the Boltz2 poses. Requiring a tuple to appear in at least 60% of samples discards interactions that are artifacts of any one diffusion draw and retains only those the model is confident enough to recover under structural perturbation.

For each target we aggregate experimentally reported actives from ChEMBL, BindingDB, and PubChem, deduplicated by canonical SMILES. No PAINS [Baell, 2016] or Brenk/NIH alerts [Brenk et al., 2008, Limban et al., 2018] Table 7: List of ADMET properties used as optimization objectives and hold-constant constraints. title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Agent inputs and outputs
text:
Design rationale Deriving objectives and hold-constant sets from the actual reference-witness property delta, rather than imposing a fixed objective list per target, produces tasks that provably solvable. The high-Tanimoto pairing constraint enforces that the task captures local lead-series chemistry rather than de novo design, which is the regime in which the multi-objective trade-offs are most relevant. Because the entire hard-constraint panel and the ADMET model are applied identically at generation and at evaluation, the agent is scored under the exact filter that defined task feasibility, and any submission that clears the gates is at least as good as a known real molecule on every property the task names.
We investigate the indicators of the difficulty of the Lead Optimization tasks in Section D.1.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B.5 Fragment Assembly
text:
Each instance of this task type asks the agent to design a single drug-like molecule that incorporates one or two given 3D molecular fragments at their specified poses inside a protein binding pocket, covalently links them when more than one is provided, and binds the target well. As in the previous two task types, every task instance is constructed around an explicit witness molecule -here, the known active from which the fragments were carved -that has already been verified to satisfy every gate the agent will be scored against, guaranteeing the solvability of the task instance.
Target and active selection Targets are sourced from UniProt entries that have at least two PDB entries containing distinct, non-buffer ligands of at least 10 heavy atoms, after filtering crystallization additives. For each (UniProt, PDB, ligand) triplet, the ligand SMILES is reconstructed via Chemical Component Dictionary templates and the binding pocket is defined as the protein residues with any heavy atom within 6 Å of the ligand.
Witness co-folding Each candidate active is co-folded against its source protein with Boltz2 [Passaro et al., 2025] under pocket constraints derived from the crystal pose, with the affinity head enabled and 10 diffusion samples. Only chains that participate in pocket contacts are retained for the co-fold; coligands and unrelated chains are excluded. Actives are kept only if their predicted binding probability exceeds 0.75. The resulting predicted log 10 (IC 50 ) is recorded as the witness affinity baseline against which the agent's submission will be scored.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: B.5 Fragment Assembly
text:
Fragment generation Surviving actives are decomposed via BRICS [Degen et al., 2008] into chemically reasonable fragments at retrosynthetically meaningful bonds. Each fragment is retained only if it (i) contains at least 6 heavy atoms after dummy-atom removal, (ii) makes at least one PLIP [Salentin et al., 2015] protein-ligand interaction with the receptor when scored on the witness's docked pose, and (iii) lies within 4 Å of the protein. The first criterion ensures the fragment is large enough to be a meaningful pharmacophore rather than a methyl-scale stub; the second and third together guarantee that the fragment is genuinely engaged with the pocket rather than solvent-exposed.
Pair sampling for two-fragment tasks When a task instance is to contain two fragments, the pair is drawn from a single source active and is required to have a closest-heavy-atom distance of at least 6 Å, this prevents the fragments from being spatially close enough to admit a short or simple linker.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: Agent inputs and outputs
text:
The agent is given: pocket.pdb (the witness's Boltz2-predicted protein structure with the witness ligand stripped), one fragment_i.sdf per fragment (the 3D pose of each fragment as it sat in the witness's Boltz2 docked complex), the binding affinity baseline target for the submited molecule, and the full hard-constraint panel also used in the Lead Optimization task (see Table 6). The agent is required to emit solution.smi containing a single SMILES string. The witness is never exposed to the agent.
Evaluation A submission must clear five gates: (1) the SMILES is valid; (2) every fragment SMARTS pattern is a substructure of the agent's molecule; (3) the fragments admit a disjoint substructure assignment (no shared atoms across fragments) and are pairwise connected by a covalent path in the agent's molecule; (4) the agent's molecule clears the same hard-constraint panel specified in Table 6; and (5) Boltz2 co-folding of the agent's molecule against the source receptor under the same pocket constraint and 10 diffusion samples produces (a) a predicted binding probability above 0.7, (b) a predicted log 10 (IC 50 ) no more than 0.1 log units worse than the witness baseline, and (c) a per-fragment 3D pose RMSD below 2.0 Å. RMSD is computed by SMARTS-matching each fragment against the docked agent ligand, extracting the 3D coordinates of the matched atoms, aligning the docked complex to pocket.pdb by Kabsch superposition on the C α atoms of the pocket residues, and selecting the best-aligned diffusion sample for the comparison.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: C Minimalist Agent Setup
text:
To isolate model capability from harness engineering, all baseline runs use a deliberately minimalist ReAct loop. The agent sees only the obfuscated task description and the tool schemas. All tools run in an isolate docker container with an isolated filesystem. The standard agent configuration can be found in Table 8.
Tools. The agent is provided four tools: (i) python(code): executes Python in the sandbox with RDKit, OpenBabel, PLIP, BioPython, NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn preinstalled;
(ii) predict_boltz(smiles, protein_sequences, ...): runs Boltz-2 co-folding with affinity prediction; (iii) predict_admet(smiles): runs ADMET-AI property predictors and returns all the values of all properties of the molecule in a single call; The Boltz/ADMET oracles live in an isolated venv that the agent's python tool cannot import, forcing all oracle calls through the budgeted interface.
Sandbox. Each task runs in a fresh smdd-agent container on an internal Docker network with no external routing; the only reachable endpoint is api.colabfold.com:443 via an nginx TCP-passthrough sidecar (required by Boltz's MSA server). Task files (e.g. complex.pdb, reference.sdf) are obfuscated to remove target names, PDB codes, and ligand three letter codes to suppress data-leakage shortcuts via memorized identifiers.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: C.1 Selecting Oracle Calls
text:
By default, across all evaluations, we set the total number of available Boltz2 calls to 8 and the number of ADMET-AI calls to 15. Note that a single ADMET-AI call returns all 8 ADMET properties for the inputted SMILES string. The complete reasoning behind only providing the LLM with a limited number of oracle calls is outlined in Section 6. In short, our goal is to treat the oracle calls as though they were ground truth, real-world wet lab experiments, hence the limited number of oracle calls.
Ultimately, SMDD-Bench can be considered a testbed for developing the right training strategies and agent harnesses for SMDD agents -even though agents trained on SMDD-Bench adhere to the Boltz2/ADMET-AI distribution of binding affinities, structures, and properties. Afterwards, the agents can be trained using those same strategies with a wet-lab-in-the-loop -where the oracle calls are directly made to an automated wet lab, performing the synthesis and then the pertinent assays completely autonomously.
The amount of Boltz2 and ADMET-AI calls must be tight enough to reward oracle-efficient reasoning instead of brute-force enumeration but generous enough such that a competent agent is not bottlenecked by oracle access.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: C.1 Selecting Oracle Calls
text:
The amount of Boltz2 and ADMET-AI calls must be tight enough to reward oracle-efficient reasoning instead of brute-force enumeration but generous enough such that a competent agent is not bottlenecked by oracle access.
In order to determine a standard number of oracle calls, we performed a sweep across oracle budget choices using a small calibration subset. We constructed the calibration split of 25 tasks drawn proportionally from each task type, with a minimum of one task per type (each task yielding max(1, ⌊25 • n t /N ⌋), where n t is the number of tasks of type t and N the total benchmark size). The Lead Optimization task instances were sampled stratified by problem complexity, defined as the sum of the number of optimization objectives and the number of hold-constant constraint, such that the calibration set spans the full difficulty range of the task type.
We swept each oracle independently while pinning the other to a generous ceiling:
• Boltz sweep: ADMET budget fixed at 35; Boltz budget varied over {5, 8, 12}.
• ADMET sweep: Boltz budget fixed at 12; ADMET budget varied over {15, 25, 35}.
The shared end-point (boltz = 12, admet = 35) was reused, giving five distinct (B, A) configurations in total. All other agent-harness settings were held at their defaults; the agent model used for calibration was GPT5.4.
For each sweep, we computed the per-type pass rate at every budget level and selected the "knee" of the plot, where the increase in performance began to saturate as the number of oracle calls increased.

heading: D.1 Indicators of the Difficulty for Lead Optimization Tasks
text:
We find that the number of optimization objectives and hold constant constraints are not indicative of the difficulty of a Lead Optimization task instance, as seen in Figure 10, where the difficulty of a task instance is defined by the average success rate of the 7 evaluated frontier LLM agents. This may be a byproduct of the greedy task generation algorithm used to generate Lead Optimization task instances -for every pair of molecules, all conserved and optimized properties of a molecule within the pair are used to create the task instance. Therefore, properties with synergistic effects can be simultaneously co-optimized via the same local molecular edit.
Rather than the number of optimization objectives and hold-constant constraints, we find that tasks with a large number of properties with clashing effects to be the greatest indicator for task difficulty. The incompatible, clashing property pairs can be found in Table 14 [Waring, 2010, Gleeson, 2008, Leeson and Springthorpe, 2007, Varma et al., 2009]. These properties are chemically anti-correlatedstandard local modifications intended to optimize for one property result in the degradation of the other. As a result, molecular modifications are typically multi-step and more complex in nature compared to task instances with fewer incompatible property pairs.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: D.2 Analysis on inter-agent submission diversity
text:
As seen in Figure 12, we find, perhaps intuitively, that an increase in the number of turns an LLM takes to solve a task is correlated with the increasing difficulty of the task (as indicated by success rate). We also observe that, as the LLM agents require more turns for more challenging tasks, the pairwise Tanimoto similarity between successful submissions of different LLMs for the same task increases while the fraction of unique molecules also increases. This is a surprising result, indicating that, for challenging tasks, the successful agents are converging onto the same narrow region in chemical space but via different approaches -leading to successful submissions with high Tanimoto similarity but also high unique fraction.
Conversely, simpler tasks lead to a low fraction of unique molecules; most likely resulting from the agents identifying and attempting the same set of straightforward strategies which passed the oracle calls on an early turn count.

heading: E Selecting SMDD-Bench Lite
text:
Running the full 502-task benchmark is expensive in wall clock time and GPU compute requirement (see Table 10). As a result, we introduce the SMDD-Bench Lite subset, a 100 task instance representative subset of SMDD-Bench, making faster model and harness iteration faster and more unified.
Lite preserves the per-type mix of the full benchmark as seen in Table 15. The mean success rate across all agents plotted against the specific incompatible pair. There is no relationship between the difficulty of the task and the specific pairing. Selection proceeds independently within each task type, and combines stratified sampling with a greedy representativeness/diversity objective. For each task we define a stratum used as a difficulty/discrimination proxy:
• Lead optimization: the tuple (n opt , n hold ) of the number of optimisation objectives and hold-constant properties. • 2D Pharmacophore ID, Interaction Point Discovery, Scaffold Hopping, Fragment
Assembly: the integer success rate of the task across the seven evaluated models, Stratum allocation. Given a per-type budget k and stratum sizes {n s }, we allocate k slots across strata in proportion to n s using the largest-remainder (Hamilton) rule: each stratum gets ⌊k • n s /N ⌋ slots, and the remaining slots are awarded to the strata with the largest fractional parts, breaking ties by stratum key.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: F Selecting SMDD-Bench Diversity
text:
During a lead optimization campaign, one potential use case involves running many SMDD agents on the same task in parallel in order to achieve a diverse spread of successful molecules. In order to test this, we develop the SMDD-Bench Diversity subset, a standardized 20 instance subset of SMDD-Bench meant for each task instance to be run multiple times.
In order to select the SMDD-Bench Diversity subset, we seek to find the most challenging consistently solvable instances. Task instances that are too simple are trivially solvable with minimal molecular edits. Task instances which are too challenging may be out of reach for the current frontier LLMs.
We first rank all Lead Optimization task instances solvable by 5/7 LLMs and rank them by turn count. We use turn count as a proxy for ranking the difficulty and chemical solution space of a task instance, following insight from Appendix D.2. We then hand-select the 20 instances with the highest average turn counts across the 7 LLMs while ensuring target diversity (no single target dominates the subset). This selection strategy ensures the tasks are at the edge of the realm of solvable tasks for current frontier LLM agents. Note that, across the SMDD-Bench Diversity runs outlined in Table 3, none of the LLMs failed a task instance all 10 times the task instance was run.

title: SMDD-Bench: Can LLMs Solve Real-World Small Molecule Drug Design Tasks?
heading: G Enumeration vs. Selection Details
text:
A failure on SMDD-Bench can come from two qualitatively different shortcomings of the agent: (i) the agent never enumerated a passing molecule at all, or (ii) the agent enumerated a passing molecule somewhere in its trajectory but never selected it to be tested by an oracle call. The enumeration vs. selection experiments are designed to disentangle these shortcomings: for every failed task, we extract and evaluate every SMILES string enumerated by the agent but not selected for an oracle call. We define a "recovered" task to be one whose original submission fails evaluation but where at least one trajectory-resident SMILES would have passed the full evaluator.
We run the experiment for all seven evaluated models and the three generation-style task types: Scaffold Hopping, Lead Optimization, and Fragment Assembly. 2D Pharmacophore Identification and Interaction Point Discovery are excluded because their outputs are not molecules. In order to extract the SMILES string, we compact each trajectory to only the reasoning trace, LLM output, and python interpreter input before feeding the compacted trajectory to GPT5.4-mini-high.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Abstract
text: Post-training compression reduces the computational and memory costs of large language models (LLMs), enabling resource-efficient deployment. However, existing compression benchmarks only focus on language modeling (e.g., perplexity) and natural language understanding tasks (e.g., GLUE accuracy), ignoring the agentic capabilities-workflow, tool use/function call, long-context understanding and real-world application. We introduce the Agent Compression Benchmark (ACBench), the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating how compression impacts LLMs' agentic abilities. ACBench spans (1) 12 tasks across 4 capabilities (e.g., WorfBench for workflow generation, Needle-in-Haystack for long-context retrieval), ( 2) quantization (GPTQ, AWQ) and pruning (Wanda, SparseGPT), and (3) 15 models, including small (Gemma-2B), standard (Qwen2.5 7B-32B), and distilled reasoning LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill). Our experiments reveal compression tradeoffs: 4-bit quantization preserves workflow generation and tool use (1%-3% drop) but degrades real-world application accuracy by 10%-15%. We introduce ERank, Top-k Ranking Correlation and Energy to systematize analysis. ACBench provides actionable insights for optimizing LLM compression in agentic scenarios. The code can be found in https://github.com/pprp/ACBench.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Introduction
text:
Large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020;Chiang et al., 2023;OpenAI, 2023;Team, 2024a) have demon-Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025. Copyright 2025 by the author(s). strated transformative capabilities in domains ranging from code synthesis (Roziere et al., 2023) and scientific research (Li et al., 2024d) to multi-agent collaboration (Wang et al., 2024a;b;Li et al., 2023a;Wu et al., 2024b). Despite these advances, their practical deployment remains hindered by prohibitive computational and memory costs (Samsi et al., 2023b;Stojkovic et al., 2024). Post-training compression techniques-notably pruning (Sun et al., 2024c;Dong et al., 2024b) and quantization (Park et al., 2024;Dong et al., 2024c)-address this challenge by reducing model size by up to 4× while preserving performance on standard benchmarks like perplexity and arithmetic tasks (Zhang et al., 2024d).
Existing compression evaluations focus narrowly on singleturn language modeling (e.g., WikiText-2 perplexity) and natural language understanding (NLU) tasks (e.g., GLUE accuracy) (Gong et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2024a;Wang et al., 2025a;Lai et al., 2025). However, real-world agentic applications-such as robotic control (Li et al., 2023a) and financial analytics (Yang et al., 2023a)-demand capabilities that transcend these static benchmarks. Specifically, compressed LLMs must retain (1) multi-step planning (e.g., API call sequences in WebShop), (2) long-context coherence (e.g., 40k-token retrieval in Needle-in-Haystack), (3) adaptive reasoning across conversational turns in workflow, and (4) seamless tool integration (e.g., external API). Prior work (Li et al., 2024e) evaluates quantized models on NLU tasks but overlooks the interplay between compression and these agentic capabilities-a critical oversight given their centrality to deployment scenarios requiring multi-turn interactions.

(3) Impact of different compression approaches: The relative effectiveness of quantization versus pruning methods, and their potential complementarity, remains unexplored in the context of agent tasks. A comprehensive comparison is needed to guide optimal compression strategy selection. Specifically, we evaluate three categories of LLMs: (1) Small language models (<7B parameters) like Phi-3.5 (Abdin et al., 2024), MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024), and Megrez (Infinigence, 2024); (2) Standard models (7B-32B parameters) including Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5, and Mistral-7B; and (3) Distilled Reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1-Distilled series. For agent tasks, we systematically evaluate four core agentic capabilities (Action Execution, Workflow Generation, Long-Context Understanding, and Real-world Application) that enable complex workflow execution while maintaining coherent behavior across extended interactions. To investigate the effects of compression configuration, we evaluate two mainstream compression methods: quantization (including GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2023)) and pruning (including SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023a) and Wanda (Sun et al., 2024b)).
To facilitate systematic analysis of compression impacts, we introduce three novel analytical tools: (1) Efficient Rank (Roy & Vetterli, 2007;Wei et al., 2024) leverages rank-based techniques to capture the distribution of model logits more efficiently. This tool helps identify the structural changes in the model's decision-making process induced by compression. (2) Top-K Ranking Correlation can measure the ranking consistency between the top-k logits of compressed and uncompressed LLMs, providing insights into how well the compressed model preserves the original model's confidence in its predictions. (2) Energy-based Analysis, inspired by Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection techniques (Lee et al., 2018;Liu et al., 2020), evaluates the distributional shifts in logit energies between the compressed and uncompressed models.

heading: Preliminaries
text:
In this paper, we mainly focus on quantization and weight pruning as presented in Figure 1(b), with additional experiments on distilled DeepSeek-R1 series. Additionally, we design three metrics to measure the gap between compressed and uncompressed LLMs.
Quantization reduces the memory and computational demands of neural networks by mapping full-precision values (e.g., 16-bit floats) to lower-bit integer representations. The affine transformation
preserves the dynamic range of the original tensor X FP16 , where N specifies the target integer bit-width (e.g., 8 bits), S is the scaling factor, and Z aligns the integer zero-point with the floating-point range. In this paper, we mainly focus on GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2023).
Weight Pruning removes redundant parameters to create sparse weight matrices, reducing model size and inference latency. Unstructured sparsity is achieved via element-wise masking:
where τ governs the sparsity level. For hardware efficiency, structured pruning eliminates entire channels using the L 1norm i |W c,i | to identify less salient features, trading finer granularity for better computational alignment. In this paper, we mainly focus on SparseGPT (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023a) and Wanda (Sun et al., 2024b) with unstructured and 2:4 semi-structured settings.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Agentic Taxonomy
text:
Since there are already several benchmarks (Li et al., 2024e;Yang et al., 2024a;Gong et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2024a;b) that focus on the capabilities of LLMs like in-context learning, commonsense multi-step reasoning, mathematical multi-step reasoning, instruction following, and selfcalibration. However, the agentic capabilities of open-sourced LLMs have not been well-studied. To fill the gap, we focus on the distinct characteristics of agentic capabilities in this paper. To study the influences of compression on the agentic capabilities of LLMs, we mainly focus on the capabilities that can be influenced by compression. We classified the agentic capabilities into four main ones as shown in Figure 1(c) and Table 1:
(1) Action Execution includes function call and tool use (Chen et al., 2023c). Function call denotes that the agent can employ the user predefined functions to enhance the capabilities, while tool use denotes that the agent can use the external tools to enhance the capabilities. We focus on the six key capabilities: plan, reason, retrieve, understand, instruct, and review.
(2) Workflow Generation enables agents to break down complex tasks into executable sequences of steps (Wang et al., 2024a;b). heading: Statistical Analysis of Compression Effects
text: Efficient Rank Analysis. We visualize the ERank (Wei et al., 2024) of LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B in Figure 2. We separately evaluate the ERank under varying weight quantization levels (W2, W3, W4, W8, W16) and KV Cache precisions (KV4, KV8, KV16). Our findings indicate that both models exhibit similar trends in their effective rank across these configurations. Specifically, the ERank decreases as the quantization precision reduces, suggesting a loss of information and structural complexity in the weight matrices. This behavior highlights the impact of quantization on the intrinsic dimensionality of the models' representations, which may contribute to the performance trade-offs observed in downstream tasks. As shown in Table 2, this relationship holds across model scales -from 125M to 6.7B parameters, where we observe ERank values ranging from 13.898 to 17.877 for 4-bit quantized models. Notably, the ERank values correlate positively with model accuracy, with larger models generally maintaining higher ERank values post-compression. For instance, the 6.7B model achieves the highest ERank of 17.877 and correspondingly strong accuracy of 0.360, while the 2.7B model shows a lower ERank of 13.898 despite having comparable accuracy. This suggests that larger models may be more robust to compression, maintaining their structural complexity better. The Diff-ERank metric, measuring the change in effective rank after compression, also shows a consistent trend, increasing with model size from 1.410 to 2.280, indicating that larger models undergo more significant structural changes during compression while still preserving performance.

text: Top-K Ranking Consistency Analysis. We quantitatively assess the discrepancy between compressed and uncompressed LLMs through top-k ranking consistency metrics. As depicted in Figure 4, we evaluate the ranking consistency using both Kendall's Tau and Spearman Correlation coefficients. Our analysis reveals a notable pattern: as k decreases from 10 to 3, the ranking consistency exhibits increasing instability and degradation. This finding is particularly significant for LLM text generation, where the top-3 tokens are crucial as they represent the most probable next-token predictions. This degradation in ranking consistency for the most probable tokens provides a potential explanation for the observed performance deterioration in downstream tasks when using compressed LLMs. Additionally, Figure 5 demonstrates the strong Spearman correlation between perplexity and Top-k ranking correlation metrics across different model sizes and quantization levels, validating the metrics' ability to capture meaningful performance characteristics. Energy-based Analysis. We visualize the distribution of energy scores of compressed and uncompressed LLMs for a series of tokens. As shown in Appendix C.7, we observed that the quantized LLM has a distinct energy distribution compared with uncompressed ones in the initial stage, while they begin to merge in the subsequent stage. The higher negative energy means high confidence in the prediction. The results show that in the initial decoding stage of the compressed LLM, the confidence distribution is polarized, with some over-confidence on certain tokens and some underconfidence on others. During the late decoding stage, both compressed and uncompressed LLMs regard tokens as low confidence. As shown in Table 2, we observe consistent energy scores across different model sizes, indicating that this behavior is inherent to the compression process rather than model scale dependent.

heading: Model Compression Significantly Impacts Structured
text:
Output Generation. Our experimental results in Table 8 demonstrate significant performance variations between JSON and string format outputs under different compression techniques. The analysis reveals that model performance consistently degrades more severely when generating JSONstructured outputs compared to string formats. As evidenced in Figure 3, this performance disparity is particularly pronounced in both InternLM2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B architectures.
Quantization Preserves Tool Use Capabilities Better Than Sparsification Methods. The empirical evidence presented in Table 8 indicates that quantization approaches, specifically GPTQ and AWQ, maintain model performance more effectively than sparsification techniques such as SparseGPT and Wanda. However, it is noteworthy that Wanda (Sun et al., 2024c) achieves comparable performance to quantization methods when implemented with unstructured pruning parameters.
Tool Use Capabilities Vary Significantly Across Model Architectures. From Table 8, the experimental results reveal substantial performance differentials among model architectures, with InternLM2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B demonstrating superior tool use capabilities compared to Mistral-7B. This observation suggests that architectural advancements in newer models contribute significantly to enhanced tool use proficiency.
Distillation from a reasoning model lead to performance degradation in agent scenarios. Despite the theoretical advantages of incorporating explicit reasoning processes, our experiments with the DeepSeek-R1-Distilled variant of Qwen2.5-7B reveal a degradation in performance. As shown in Table 8, we observe a substantial decline in average accuracy from 70% to 43.6%, contradicting conventional expectations regarding the benefits of knowledge distillation.
Compression Strategy Recommendations. Based on our empirical analysis, quantization emerges as the most effective compression approach for maintaining tool use capabilities across diverse scenarios. When available, GPTQ with 4-bit precision or FP8 representation demonstrates superior performance characteristics. For applications requiring sparsification, our findings suggest that Wanda with 2:4 sparsity patterns provides an optimal trade-off between model performance and compression efficiency.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Effects of Compression
text:
Model Compression Shows Minimal Impact on Workflow Generation Capabilities. Our experimental results, as presented in Table 10, demonstrate that most compression methods maintain model performance within a 5% degradation margin, with only magnitude-based pruning showing significant performance deterioration. This resilience suggests that workflow generation tasks primarily rely on high-level planning capabilities that remain largely intact under compression. Among the evaluated architectures, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B demonstrate notably superior performance compared to InternLM2.5-7B, indicating that architectural differences may be more influential than compression effects.
Robust Performance Maintained for OS and Webshop Tasks Under Compression. Our analysis reveals that models maintain approximately 80% performance across all compression methods for operating system and e-commerce tasks. This robustness likely stems from the structured nature of these domains and the relatively constrained action space. Based on these findings and considering the compute efficiency trade-offs, we recommend GPTQ and AWQ as optimal compression choices for these applications.
Model Size Influences Compression Sensitivity in Specialized Tasks. In Alfworld and Lumos tasks, which require fine-grained language understanding and complex reasoning, we observe a clear correlation between model size and compression resilience. Smaller architectures, such as Qwen2.5-3B, experience substantial performance degradation of up to 50% under GPTQ and AWQ compression. In contrast, larger models like Qwen2.5-32B maintain their performance under quantization, occasionally showing slight improvements. This suggests that larger models possess redundant capacity that helps preserve critical capabilities under compression.

Fur-thermore, we observe that the uncompressed Megrez-3B demonstrates insufficient capability for workflow generation tasks, highlighting the importance of architectural design beyond parameter count.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Effects of Compression
text:
Compressed LLMs face significant challenges in handling most real-world scenarios. Through comprehensive evaluation detailed in Table 9, we assessed various quantization and pruning techniques applied to 7B LLMs. The results demonstrate that these compressed models generally exhibit substantial degradation in real-world task performance. Among the compression methods evaluated, only AWQ and Wanda maintained acceptable performance levels, while alternative approaches showed marked deterioration in capability across multiple task domains.
DeepSeek-R1-Distilled model series exhibited minimal progress and success rates in practical applications. As illustrated in Table 9, the distilled models experienced a significant degradation in functional performance across practical tasks. For instance, the progress rate on the Pddl benchmark for the DeepSeek-R1-Distilled-Qwen2.5-7B model dropped markedly from 33% to 1%. In contrast, smaller models such as Qwen2.5-3B, when enhanced with AWQ, achieved a 23% progress rate. This stark performance gap can be attributed to two key factors. First, the DeepSeek-R1 teacher model used for distillation lacked robust agentic capabilities in its training, particularly for tool use and practical task execution. As a result, the distillation process could not effectively transfer these crucial agentic skills to the student model. Second, the limited model capacity creates an inherent trade-off during distillation -when the process prioritizes core reasoning skills like mathematical problem-solving, it necessarily deprioritizes the preservation of agentic capabilities like function calling and tool manipulation. As presented in Figure 8, we compare the undistilled Qwen2.5-7B with its distilled counterpart across LongBench, T-Eval, WorfBench, and AgentBoard, revealing consistent degradation in practical task performance despite improvements in traditional reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the need to develop distillation techniques that can better balance the preservation of both abstract reasoning and practical agentic capabilities.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: Impact Statement
text:
The findings of this work have significant implications for the future development and deployment of LLMs in realworld agentic applications. By systematically evaluating the impact of compression techniques on key agentic capabilities, our work sheds light on the complex trade-offs involved in compressing LLMs while preserving their performance in critical tasks such as planning, reasoning, tool use, and long-context understanding.
The introduction of the Agent Compression Benchmark (ACBench) provides a foundational tool for the evaluation of compressed models in agentic settings, an area that has been largely overlooked in prior research. This benchmark paves the way for more targeted research into optimizing LLM compression for specific agent tasks, helping to bridge the gap between state-of-the-art compression methods and the practical requirements of real-world deployments.
Our comprehensive comparison of quantization and pruning techniques highlights the importance of selecting appropriate compression configurations based on the specific needs of agentic tasks. The novel analytical tools we introduce, including ERank, Top-k Ranking Correlation and Energy, provide new insights into the internal workings of compressed models and enable a more granular understanding of the impact of compression on model performance and decision-making.
This work has the potential to influence the design of more efficient LLMs, allowing for their deployment in resourceconstrained environments where computational and memory resources are limited. Furthermore, the ability to maintain agentic capabilities even in compressed models will facilitate the broader adoption of LLMs in practical applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and interactive AI agents. By providing a systematic framework for evaluating and optimizing compressed LLMs, we hope to contribute to the ongoing efforts to make AI models more accessible and capable in real-world scenarios, paving the way for their integration into a wide range of industries and applications.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: A.1. LLM Compression
text:
Broadly speaking, LLM compression comprises various techniques such as quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, low-rank decomposition, and more. These methods aim to reduce the size and computational requirements of large language models without substantially sacrificing their performance. By employing these compression strategies, researchers and practitioners can make LLMs more accessible and deployable in resource-constrained environments, thereby broadening their applicability across different platforms and devices.
Pruning. Pruning (Frantar & Alistarh, 2023b;Sun et al., 2024c;Shao et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2024d;Dong et al., 2024b;Tang et al., 2020;Dong et al., 2024a;Lai et al., 2025) involves systematically removing less important parameters or connections within a large language model (LLM) to reduce its size and computational requirements. This technique helps enhance the model's efficiency without significantly compromising its performance by eliminating redundancies. Pruning can be categorized into several types, including unstructured pruning (Sun et al., 2024c;Shao et al., 2024), which targets individual weights, and structured pruning (Molchanov et al., 2019;Ma et al., 2023;Kim et al., 2024), which removes entire neurons, channels, or layers. Additionally, dynamic pruning (Zhang et al., 2024d;Han et al., 2015) methods adjust the sparsity level during training or inference, allowing for more flexible compression tailored to specific deployment needs.
Research has shown that judicious pruning can maintain or even sometimes improve model generalization by removing overfitting parameters.

Quantization. Quantization (Park et al., 2024;Frantar & Alistarh, 2022;Lee et al., 2024;Du et al., 2024a;Kim et al., 2023;Lin et al., 2023;Dong et al., 2024c;Gu et al., 2025;Du et al., 2024b;Li et al., 2024f) reduces the precision of the model's weights and activations from high-precision formats (like 32-bit floating-point) to lower-bit representations (such as 8-bit integers). This reduction in numerical precision helps decrease the model's memory footprint and speeds up inference times, making LLMs more deployable in resource-constrained environments. Quantization can be applied in various forms, including uniform quantization, which uses the same scale for all weights, and non-uniform quantization, which allows different scales for different layers or weight groups. Advanced techniques like quantization-aware training (QAT) integrate the quantization process into the training phase, enabling the model to better adapt to lower precision and mitigate performance degradation. Research in post-training quantization (PTQ) explores methods to quantize pre-trained models without retraining, preserving accuracy while achieving significant compression.

title: Can Compressed LLMs Truly Act? An Empirical Evaluation of Agentic Capabilities in LLM Compression
heading: A.1. LLM Compression
text:
Knowledge Distillation. Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015b;Li et al., 2024b;2023b;Liu et al., 2023c;Tian et al., 2022) is a process where a smaller, student model is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger, teacher model. By transferring the knowledge from the teacher to the student, the resulting compressed model retains much of the performance and capabilities of the original while being more efficient in terms of computation and memory usage. This technique involves training the student model using a combination of the original training data and the outputs (such as logits or probability distributions) produced by the teacher model. Various distillation strategies, including teacher-student learning and self-distillation, have been developed to optimize the efficiency and effectiveness of the process. Recent advancements focus on multi-teacher distillation, where multiple teacher models contribute to the training of a single student model, enhancing the diversity and robustness of the compressed model.
Low-Rank Decomposition. Low-rank decomposition techniques (Yuan et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2024b;Wang et al., 2024e;2025b) aim to approximate the weight matrices of LLMs with lower-rank matrices, effectively reducing the number of parameters and computational operations required during inference. By decomposing large matrices into products of smaller matrices, these methods exploit the inherent redundancy and low-rank structure present in many neural network architectures. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) is a widely used technique for low-rank approximation, where a matrix is factorized into three components with reduced dimensionality. Other methods, such as tensor decomposition and matrix factorization, have also been explored to facilitate efficient compression. Low-rank decomposition not only diminishes the model size but also accelerates inference by simplifying the mathematical operations involved, making it a valuable tool for deploying LLMs in real-time applications.

heading: A.2. LLM-based Agents
text:
Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents like MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023), AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), AgentVerse (Chen et al., 2023b), and MegaAgent (Wang et al., 2024b) are sophisticated AI systems that leverage the powerful natural language understanding and generation capabilities of LLMs as their core reasoning engine to perform complex, autonomous tasks through interaction with their environment. These agents typically integrate LLMs with additional components such as planning modules, tool use capabilities, and memory systems to create more versatile and capable autonomous systems. The combination of these elements allows LLM-based agents to not only generate human-like text but also engage in goal-directed behavior, adapt to dynamic environments, and utilize external resources to achieve specified objectives.
LLM-based agents operate by receiving inputs or prompts that define their goals or tasks (Chen et al., 2024a;2023a;Tesfatsion, 2023;Wen et al., 2024;Chan et al., 2024;Park et al., 2023), processing this information through the LLM to generate plans or actions (Chen et al., 2023a;Wang et al., 2024b;c), and then executing these actions in their environment.
For instance, an LLM agent designed for web navigation might interpret user queries, plan a sequence of web interactions to gather information, and utilize browser automation tools to execute these interactions effectively. Similarly, an LLM agent tasked with information gathering can autonomously search, retrieve, and synthesize data from various sources to provide comprehensive insights or summaries.

heading: A.3. Reasoning
text:
External tool integration involves several key components:
Selection of Appropriate Tools. LLMs must be capable of determining which tools are best suited for a given task. This involves understanding the requirements of the task and matching them with the functionalities offered by available tools.
For instance, a task requiring numerical computations might prompt the use of a calculator API, while a task involving data retrieval might utilize a database query tool (Qin et al., 2023b;Shi et al., 2024;Schick et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2023b;Zhang et al., 2023a).
Constructing Valid API Calls. Once an appropriate tool is identified, the LLM must be able to construct valid API calls to interact with the tool. This requires understanding the syntax and parameters of the API, as well as the ability to format requests correctly (Qin et al., 2023b;Tang et al., 2023a;Shi et al., 2024). Proper API call construction ensures that the tool is utilized effectively and returns the desired outcomes.
Interpreting Tool Outputs. After executing an API call, the LLM needs to interpret the output provided by the external tool. This involves parsing the returned data, understanding its structure, and integrating it with the ongoing task or response generation (Zhang et al., 2023a;Schick et al., 2023). Effective interpretation enables the LLM to provide coherent and contextually appropriate results based on the tool's output.
Recent developments have shown significant progress in enhancing LLMs' tool use capabilities. Techniques such as tool-specific fine-tuning (Schick et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2023b;Tang et al., 2023a;Shi et al., 2024), where models are trained on the usage patterns of specific tools, have improved the accuracy and reliability of tool interactions. Additionally, the incorporation of contextual understanding allows LLMs to dynamically select and switch between tools based on the task requirements and the context in which the task is being performed.

heading: A.6. Retrieval Augmented Generation
text:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an advanced technique that enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by integrating external knowledge sources during the generation process. Unlike traditional LLMs that rely solely on the information encoded within their parameters, RAG leverages a retrieval component to fetch relevant documents or data from expansive databases or knowledge bases (Jeong et al., 2024;Soudani et al., 2024;Gao et al., 2023a;Chen et al., 2024b;Asai et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2023d;Yu et al., 2024). This approach addresses the limitations of fixed-parameter models, enabling them to access up-to-date and domain-specific information dynamically.
The architecture of RAG typically comprises two primary components: a retriever and a generator (Jeong et al., 2024;Wang et al., 2023d). The retriever utilizes dense or sparse retrieval methods to identify and extract pertinent information related to a given query or prompt from the external corpus. Techniques such as dense vector representations (Pan et al., 2024), which encode semantic similarities, or traditional keyword-based approaches, can be employed to optimize the retrieval process.
Once the relevant documents are retrieved, the generator, often powered by transformer-based architectures, assimilates this information to produce coherent and contextually accurate responses.
One of the significant advantages of RAG is its ability to mitigate issues related to factual inaccuracies and hallucinations commonly observed in generative models. By grounding the generation process in retrieved factual data, RAG models can produce more reliable and verifiable outputs. This is particularly beneficial for applications in areas such as healthcare, legal, and scientific research, where precision and accuracy are paramount.

heading: A.7. Long Context
text:
Processing and understanding long contexts is a formidable challenge in the realm of large language models (LLMs).
Traditional transformer architectures, while effective in handling short to moderately long sequences, face scalability issues as the input length increases. This limitation arises primarily due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention mechanisms, which hampers efficiency and computational feasibility for extended texts.
To overcome these challenges, several innovative approaches and architectural modifications have been proposed to enhance the long-context capabilities of LLMs:
Sparse Attention Mechanisms Sparse attention reduces the computational burden by limiting the scope of attention to a subset of tokens rather than considering all possible token pairs. Techniques such as Longformer's sliding window attention and BigBird's combination of global and random attention patterns enable models to process longer sequences efficiently while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
Memory-Augmented Networks Memory-augmented models incorporate external memory structures that allow the model to store and retrieve information across longer spans. Transformer-XL, for instance, introduces a recurrence mechanism that reuses hidden states from previous segments, effectively extending the context window without a proportional increase in computational resources.
Hierarchical Models Hierarchical approaches decompose the processing of long texts into multiple levels of abstraction. By first encoding smaller chunks of text (e.g., sentences or paragraphs) and then aggregating these encodings at a higher level, models can capture long-range dependencies more effectively. This method not only enhances comprehension but also facilitates better information retention across lengthy documents.
Receptive Field Modifications Adjusting the receptive field of the attention mechanism allows models to maintain a broadened scope of context without incurring significant computational costs. Techniques like dynamic attention span, where the model learns the optimal span of attention based on the input, contribute to more flexible and efficient long-context processing.

heading: B.4. Details of Long Context Understanding Experiments
text:
LongBench: LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the long-context capabilities of LLMs. It consists of 12 tasks across five categories: Single-Doc QA, Multi-Doc QA, Summarization, Few-shot Learning, and Synthetic tasks. The benchmark features documents ranging from 2K to 32K tokens in length. Single-Doc QA tasks include NarrativeQA and Qasper, which test comprehension of long narratives and scientific papers. Multi-Doc QA encompasses HotpotQA and MultiNews, evaluating cross-document reasoning. The summarization tasks (e.g., GovReport, QMSum) assess models' ability to distill key information from lengthy documents. Few-shot learning tasks test the model's capacity to learn from examples within extended contexts, while synthetic tasks measure specific capabilities like information retrieval and counting in long sequences. The benchmark spans diverse domains including healthcare, legal, scientific research, and creative writing, providing a comprehensive evaluation of long-context understanding.
LongGenBench: LongGenBench (Liu et al., 2024a) is a synthetic benchmark designed to evaluate long-context generation capabilities of language models. Unlike existing long-context benchmarks that focus primarily on retrieval-based tasks (e.g., locating specific information within large input contexts), LongGenBench specifically targets a model's ability to produce coherent, contextually accurate, and structurally sound text over extended outputs. The benchmark supports customizable context length configurations and evaluates models on generating single, unified long-form responses. This fills an important gap in long-context evaluation by providing a standardized framework for assessing generation rather than just retrieval capabilities. The benchmark enables systematic analysis of how different model architectures handle the challenges of maintaining coherence and accuracy in long-form text generation.

heading: B.5. Details of Workflow Generation Experiments
text: In this paper, we employ WorfBench (Qiao et al., 2024) to evaluate the workflow generation capabilities, which encompass planning and reasoning processes. WorfBench is a comprehensive benchmark containing 18k training samples, 2146 test samples, and 723 held-out tasks across four types of scenarios: function call, problem-solving, embodied planning, and open-grounded planning. The benchmark features multi-faceted scenarios and complex graph-structured workflows, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks that focus only on linear workflows. WorfBench is accompanied by WorfEval, a systematic evaluation protocol that uses subsequence and subgraph matching algorithms to accurately quantify workflow generation abilities. This evaluation framework has revealed significant gaps between linear and graph planning capabilities in current LLMs, with even advanced models showing up to 15% performance differences. The benchmark's diverse scenarios and evaluation metrics make it particularly suitable for assessing both the quality of generated workflows and their practical applicability in real-world tasks.

The benchmark features multi-faceted scenarios and complex graph-structured workflows, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks that focus only on linear workflows. WorfBench is accompanied by WorfEval, a systematic evaluation protocol that uses subsequence and subgraph matching algorithms to accurately quantify workflow generation abilities. This evaluation framework has revealed significant gaps between linear and graph planning capabilities in current LLMs, with even advanced models showing up to 15% performance differences. The benchmark's diverse scenarios and evaluation metrics make it particularly suitable for assessing both the quality of generated workflows and their practical applicability in real-world tasks.

text:
Table 3 presents a comparative analysis of the AWQ and GPTQ quantization methods applied to two large language models (LLMs), InternLM2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B, across various long-context understanding tasks sourced from LongBench.
For InternLM2.5-7B, the application of the AWQ results in significant performance enhancements across most evaluated tasks. Specifically, in Single-Doc QA tasks such as NrtvQA, Qasper, and MF-en, AWQ boosts the scores from 0 to 25.08, 29.27 to 45.16, and 22.92 to 47.72, respectively. Similarly, in Multi-Doc QA and Summarization tasks, AWQ consistently improves performance metrics, with notable increases in TriviaQA (from 48.1 to 84.69) and Code Completion (from 50 to 99.5). In contrast, the GPTQ method yields more modest improvements. While GPTQ enhances some scores, such as Qasper from 29.27 to 30.16 and MF-en from 22.92 to 30.04, the gains are less pronounced compared to AWQ. Additionally, GPTQ shows slight decreases in certain areas, such as Lcc, which drops from 58.2 to 56.62.
Examining Qwen2.5-7B, both AWQ and GPTQ quantization methods demonstrate varying levels of performance enhancement. AWQ provides consistent, albeit smaller, improvements across most tasks. For example, Qasper increases from 13.12 to 14.18, and MF-en decreases slightly from 30.29 to 26.12. On the other hand, GPTQ offers substantial performance gains in several areas, notably increasing Qasper from 13.12 to 38.94 and MF-en from 30.29 to 47.53. However, similar to InternLM2.5-7B, GPTQ also results in slight performance declines in specific tasks, such as a reduction in Lcc from 62.28 to 57.44.
