title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Abstract
text: Modern large language model (LLM) agents can use external tools to help users solve complex tasks. However, for problems that require learning from long-term historical events or from previous agent-environment interactions, LLM agents are required to use memory mechanisms to store and retrieve experiences. While sophisticated memory systems exist for dialogue agents, few studies have empirically examined how to improve agents' tool-using capabilities through past user-agent conversations. We propose MemToolAgent, a framework that improves tool use through memory management. Our approach contains a memory extraction module that processes past experiences into structured memory entries, and a retrieval module that dynamically selects a subset of the stored memory entries. This enables more personalized and accurate responses aligned with user preferences and feedback without requiring LLM fine-tuning. In summary, this work has three main contributions: (1) a unified memory entry format that improves both general-purpose and personalized tool use without LLM fine-tuning, (2) a reflection-based memory extraction that uses environment and user feedback to distill wrong executions into critiques to store, and (3) a retrieval module that chooses how many past experiences to use based on the memory similarity distribution. MemToolAgent achieves 29%, 80%, and 17% relative improvements compared to strong baselines on the WorkBench, NESTFUL, and PEToolBench benchmarks, respectively.

heading: Introduction
text:
Combining powerful LLMs with additional components like memory systems, workflow mechanisms, APIs, and other tools to create LLM agents is an emerging trend. These agents are designed to solve complex tasks that require sequential reasoning and multi-step planning. In this context, tools are functions utilized by agents to interact with their environment. title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Introduction
text:
Integrating memory into an LLM agent supports two main types of tasks: personalized and generalpurpose tool use, as shown in Figure 1. Users utilize the same tools in particular ways, such as using different input parameters, or they might use different tools to achieve the same goal. In scenarios where the agent has access to tools with similar functionalities, it requires user context to correctly execute the task. Storing the past interactions in the memory allows for better personalization. For instance, personalization can resolve the tool-level ambiguity if "create a ticket" could refer to Zendesk ticket creation or Jira issue creation. Regarding general-purpose tool use, there are common error patterns in tool use agents, such as dependency violation, parameter hallucination, and premature tool calling. Having past experiences in memory can help the agent use the correct parameters for tools and use the tools in the correct order. For example, this is useful in scenarios where the agent utilizes the same set of tools for a group of users to solve generic tasks like forwarding emails.
Our work offers three main contributions: (1) a unified memory entry format of storing past experiences for better general-purpose and personalized tool use performance without LLM fine-tuning, (2) an environment and user feedback-based reflection approach for memory writing to distill failed past experiences into critiques, and (3) a retrieval module based on similarity distribution that dynamically selects relevant memory entries to guide the agent for the current task.

heading: Related Work
text: There has been a growing interest in memory management for LLM agents in recent years. A related earlier idea is Case-based reasoning (CBR) (Aamodt and Plaza, 1994) where systems retrieve and use similar past cases (experiences) to solve new problems. MemGPT (MemoryGPT) (Packer et al., 2023) introduces an OS-inspired memory hierarchy with two memory types called the main context and the external context. More recent work includes graph-based architectures to organize the information more flexibly and expressively. In Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), the memory is modeled as a directed knowledge graph to express complex relationships. This allows dynamic and more advanced storage and retrieval. A-MEM (Agentic Memory) (Xu et al., 2025b) proposes a memory based on the Zettelkasten knowledge management system. The memory entries are linked as interconnected networks, and the existing entries are updated based on new experiences. Similarly, Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025) and Cognitive Weave (Vishwakarma et al., 2025) are based on temporally aware knowledge graphs and Spatio-Temporal Resonance Graphs, respectively.

heading: Related Work
text:
M em p (Fang et al., 2025) is a procedural memory framework that extracts both fine-grained instructions and high-level abstractions from past agent trajectories. Memento (Zhou et al., 2025) stores past experiences in an episodic memory, learns and continually updates a case-selection policy based on environmental feedback. Training-Free GRPO (Cai et al., 2025) is a training-free alternative to agentic RL that optimizes an experience library consisting of natural-language experiential knowledge. TOOLMEM (Xiao et al., 2025) stores memories of tool capabilities from previous interactions and helps the agent select the most suitable tool for a given task at inference. ReMem agents (Wei et al., 2025) combine reasoning, action, and memory refinement and actively exploit, prune, and reorganize their memory while solving the current task.
There are in-context learning (ICL) approaches closely related to agents with memory. For example, STE (Wang et al., 2024a) creates tool use trajectories based on a trial-and-error approach offline and stores them in a static memory for inference. Unlike the related work, MemToolAgent addresses both personalized and general-purpose tool use. It proposes a general memory entry format and stores and leverages detailed information like tool trajectories and a reflection/critique about the execution. Importantly, MemToolAgent also incorporates user feedback as a signal to improve the quality of memory entries.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Method: MemToolAgent
text:
MemToolAgent consists of two main components: the memory retrieval and memory extraction modules. Figure 2 illustrates the general overview of our proposed approach. Memory entries, i.e., past experiences, are retrieved from the memory based on the semantic similarity between the query and the entries. Dynamic "n" Top-n Embedding-based Retrieval is proposed for retrieval. Instead of retrieving a fixed number of memory entries for each query, the number of entries to retrieve is dynamically determined based on the cosine similarities between the embeddings of memory entries' queries and the test query. Then, the entries are used as incontext learning to guide the agent for the current task.
To add a new entry to the memory based on the current query, an LLM-based "Memory Extraction" module provides a reflection/critique of the execution, which is then stored in the memory with the query and user feedback.
MemToolAgent specifies what to store in memory with a general memory entry format. Each memory entry m is represented as a tuple m = (q, a, f, r) where:
• q: the user query • a = {a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n }: the sequence of tool calls executed by the agent
• f ∈ {0, 1}: binary user feedback indicating task success (f = 1) or failure (f = 0)
• r: reflection or critique generated by the memory extractor when f = 0 (otherwise r = ∅)
With binary user feedback, we simulate the scenarios where the user does not know anything about the underlying tools/APIs and gives feedback based on the outcome. However, this feedback could easily be replaced by any other type of feedback, such as text or score. Figure 3 illustrates an example memory entry with reflection.

heading: Memory Retrieval: Dynamic "n" Top-n
text:
Embedding-based Retrieval
Retrieving a fixed number of memory entries for every query is not optimal since some queries might not have relevant memory entries, while there might be many similar entries for other queries.
Prior work (Taguchi et al., 2025;Xu et al., 2025c) in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses the trade-off between missing information with too small k and adding redundancy with too large k, where k is the number of retrieved documents. These methods dynamically decide the number k and show that the optimal amount of retrieved context varies across queries. Adaptive-k (Taguchi et al., 2025) selects "k" as the largest adjacent similarity-score gap.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Memory Retrieval: Dynamic "n" Top-n
text:
Our Dynamic "n" approach has four main steps illustrated by the Algorithm 1. The first two steps are calculating the cosine similarity values between the query and memory entries and sorting them in descending order. The third step calculates a first-order derivative estimate of sorted similarities based on a sliding window approach where x is an array of sorted similarities, and R is considered as the "radius" of the derivative estimate. The final step is finding the peaks, i.e., sudden drops in similarity, ideally showing a class boundary. The peak corresponds to our "n" value for Dynamic "n" retrieval. The entire process is inspired by the concept of finding "knees" for designing systems (Satopaa et al., 2011). The find_peaks * function from the SciPy library is utilized for peak finding. Figure 4 illustrates an example. The blue line shows the sorted similarity values, while the red line shows the first derivative estimation. As observed, the locations where there are local maxima, i.e., a peak, correspond to locations with a sudden drop in similarity. Dynamic "n" retrieval has three parameters, namely R, prominence, and the peak number. R is a smoothing parameter, and larger R values result in smoother derivative estimates. Prominence is a parameter of the find_peaks function to filter important peaks based on comparison of neighboring values. The peak number is simply which peak to select. Similarity curves can be noisy, have multiple knees and multi-step drops rather than huge gaps. We hypothesize that finding peaks based on the derivative estimate rather than raw similarity values results in a more robust approach than Adaptivek. Dynamic "n" robustly finds points of change or cluster boundaries on noisy similarity curves, while Adaptive-k finds the biggest drop and works well only when the curve has one clean knee.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Memory Extraction Module
text:
The agent needs to apply experience to the current task based on the user feedback and the context. An important observation from our experiments is that agents struggle to effectively learn from retrieved negative experiences when they are presented as raw execution traces. We hypothesize this is because the agent must simultaneously understand what went wrong in the past example while solving the current task. To make the agent's work easier, a "Memory Extraction" module is proposed. It reflects on the context and user feedback to understand what was wrong. For wrong executions, the reflection/critique is added to the memory instead of the raw context, which might be too complicated and contain irrelevant parts. Doing the reflection as a separate step helps the agent focus only on the current task and learn from its mistakes.
The memory extraction module is an LLM E that takes the following as input: (1) current query q, (2) set of available tools T = {t 1 , t 2 , . . . , t m }, (3) agent's response (actions) a = {a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a n } including tool calls, (4) environment feedback e including tool responses, (5) user feedback f ∈ {0, 1}, and (6) retrieved semantically similar memory entries M ′ ⊂ M. The module outputs a reflection/critique r = E(q, T , a, e, f, M ′ ).

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Benchmarks
text:
WorkBench is an outcome-centric tool use benchmark that evaluates agents on workplace tasks such as sending emails and scheduling meetings. It includes five databases and 27 tools. WorkBench tasks are from different domains like Analytics, Calendar, etc. The evaluation metric is accuracy, which is defined as the percentage of tasks where the outcome from the agent's actions matches the expected outcome. The correct outcome means the correct changes in the database values.
WorkBench queries were created based on predefined templates such as 'Delete an email from person X' or 'Schedule a meeting with person Y'. There are 10 queries per template. Since the benchmark has no train-test split, one query from each template is used to populate the memory. This ensures that there is at least one directly relevant memory entry for each test query. This setup is used to show the advantages of using the memory. The test set consists of 108 Analytics, 99 Calendar, 72 CRM, 81 Email, and 189 Multi-domain tasks.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Benchmarks
text: NESTFUL benchmark evaluates LLMs on nested sequences of tool calls, where the output of one tool call is used as input for the next tool call. It includes 1891 test queries based on MathQA (Amini et al., 2019) and StarCoder2-Instruct (Wei et al., 2024) benchmarks. The first 500 tasks are used as test set while the next 500 tasks are used to populate the memory. The benchmark uses five evaluation metrics, which are F1 scores for tool and parameter generation, Partial Sequence Matching, Full Sequence Matching, and Win Rate. Partial Sequence Matching measures how many predicted APIs with their argument-value pairs match the gold API sequence, Full Sequence Matching evaluates whether the model produces the exact full sequence, and Win Rate assesses whether the predicted APIs lead to the gold answer when executed. PEToolBench is a personalized tool orchestration benchmark. Each query comes with an instruction history consisting of 80-100 past user queries, where each past query includes a binary rating (1 for correct/desired execution, 0 otherwise). For our experiments, this instruction history forms the memory, where each memory entry consists of a past query, its corresponding tool call, and binary user feedback. Test queries are designed such that the agent must rely on user preferences from memory for correct tool execution. section: Benchmarks (experiments)

NESTFUL benchmark evaluates LLMs on nested sequences of tool calls, where the output of one tool call is used as input for the next tool call. It includes 1891 test queries based on MathQA (Amini et al., 2019) and StarCoder2-Instruct (Wei et al., 2024) benchmarks. The first 500 tasks are used as test set while the next 500 tasks are used to populate the memory. The benchmark uses five evaluation metrics, which are F1 scores for tool and parameter generation, Partial Sequence Matching, Full Sequence Matching, and Win Rate. Partial Sequence Matching measures how many predicted APIs with their argument-value pairs match the gold API sequence, Full Sequence Matching evaluates whether the model produces the exact full sequence, and Win Rate assesses whether the predicted APIs lead to the gold answer when executed. PEToolBench is a personalized tool orchestration benchmark. Each query comes with an instruction history consisting of 80-100 past user queries, where each past query includes a binary rating (1 for correct/desired execution, 0 otherwise). For our experiments, this instruction history forms the memory, where each memory entry consists of a past query, its corresponding tool call, and binary user feedback. Test queries are designed such that the agent must rely on user preferences from memory for correct tool execution. A subset of 591 queries is used as the test set after filtering the queries with sufficiently long instruction histories (at least 80 past queries). This makes sure that the agent needs a memory rather than using the full history in context. The benchmark uses two evaluation metrics: Tool Accuracy, which evaluates the model's ability to call the appropriate tool based on user preferences, and Parameter Accuracy, which assesses whether the model generates the correct parameters.

Hard Preference Guiding and Simple Ranking for PEToolBench. Table 4 demonstrates the effectiveness of simple ranker and Hard Preference Guiding ideas through ablation studies. The original approach for PETool-Bench provides the agent with the entire instruction history, which is not optimal, as irrelevant queries can make the task more challenging. Embeddingbased Retrieval_v1 improves this by retrieving only the top-10 semantically similar queries from memory. Retrieval_v2 builds on v1 by introducing a simple ranker that separates memory entries by rating (1 vs. 0) in the system prompt to emphasize user preferences. This is a small modification for personalization tasks. Although it substantially increases the tool accuracy, there is a decrease in parameter accuracy. This is due to binary feedback, which only provides correct/incorrect information.
Negative feedback causes the agent to consider correct parameters as incorrect, as the tool itself can be incorrect even with correct parameters.
Error analysis revealed cases where the agent selected tools despite negative user preferences from the memory. To address this, we introduce an alternative baseline called Hard Preference Guiding which removes tools with a rating of 0 from the system prompt. This is a substitute for the memory extraction module's approach of providing user preferences as soft guidance. It provides a costefficient alternative to the LLM-based memory extraction module, eliminating the need for additional LLM calls during memory addition. Hard Preference Guiding extends MemToolAgent w/o memory extractor and improves Tool Accuracy from 0.72 to 0.84, as shown in Table 4. Although less general than memory extraction, Hard Preference Guiding is effective for scenarios like PEToolBench and could be used as a complementary approach.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Conclusion
text: MemToolAgent is a memory framework that enhances the tool-using capabilities of LLM agents by using past experiences. The results show significant improvements across multiple benchmarks in both personalized and general-purpose tool use scenarios. The main contributions of the framework include (1) a retrieval mechanism that dynamically determines the number of relevant memory entries to retrieve, (2) a memory extraction module that generates reflections on incorrect executions to help avoid similar mistakes, and (3) an overall effective approach for both general-purpose and personalized tool use based on user and environment feedback.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
heading: Limitations
text:
Despite the improvements in general-purpose and personalized tool use performance achieved by MemToolAgent, several limitations remain for future work. One limitation is the cold-start problem of memory. Moreover, the benchmarks used contain fewer than 40 tools. However, there are typically more tools in real-life applications. As the number of tools increases, it is more challenging to cover the usage of all tools with memory. This could potentially make the cold-start problem more severe. Our experiments using synthetically generated queries show that even a simple approach can help the cold-start problem.
Another limitation emerges in conversational scenarios with multiple turns. The benchmarks used in our experiments are single-turn. For singleturn tasks, the memory retrieval is done once at the beginning of the conversation. This might not be optimal for multiple-user turn tasks where the agent needs to obtain the necessary information from the user across multiple turns. One possible solution is to extend MemToolAgent to retrieve from memory after each user turn, so that the agent can focus on the sub-task associated with that specific turn. title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: Abstract
text: LLM agents are increasingly equipped with skills to perform complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Although skills provide reusable procedural knowledge, agents may still execute them unreliably. Even when an agent has demonstrated the capability to complete tasks under the guidance of a skill, it may fail to do so consistently across similar tasks or repeated runs due to deviations from the skill procedure or incorrect execution of individual steps. Such instability limits the practical reliability of LLM agents. To address this problem, we propose SKILLSENTRY, a skill-oriented runtime assurance framework built upon a new domain-specific language (DSL) for representing runtime guidance for skill execution. SKILLSENTRY initializes the runtime guidance by combining a skill specification extracted from the corresponding skill document with execution experience mined from historical successful and failed traces. It then wraps around the agent execution loop to monitor and guide skill execution under the current guidance, while iteratively refining the guidance using newly collected traces. We evaluate SKILLSENTRY on 15 skills across two LLM agents, each paired with two backbone models, i.e., Claude Code with Claude-Haiku-4.5 and Claude-Opus-4.6, and Codex with GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.4. Our results show that SKILLSENTRY improves the task success rate of LLM agents by 24.1% across skills, on average, while exhibiting lower variability across repeated runs.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
Large language models (LLMs) [3,12,19,37] have shown strong capabilities in understanding user instructions, generating code, and solving complex reasoning questions. Building on these capabilities, LLM agents [4,21,27,28,36] further extend LLMs from passive text generation to autonomous task execution, i.e., planning intermediate steps, invoking external tools, observing execution feedback, and refining their actions [8,14,32,35,38]. As user tasks become more complex and diverse, skills [16,40,41] have emerged as an important abstraction for packaging reusable task-solving knowledge. A skill usually describes how an agent should complete a class of tasks through predefined steps, including high-level procedures, tool-use patterns, and task-specific constraints [30]. By providing such procedural guidance, skills help LLM agents reuse validated task-solving strategies, constrain the execution space, and improve their capability to complete complex tasks.
However, equipping an LLM agent with a skill does not guarantee reliable execution. Even when the LLM agent has demonstrated the capability to complete a task under the guidance of a skill before, it may fail to reproduce the correct execution consistently in later runs [13,33]. Such failures do not necessarily indicate a lack of fundamental model capability for task-solving. Rather, they often arise from the generative nature of LLM agent execution, where each action is produced from an evolving context of prior reasoning, tool feedback, and intermediate observations. Thus, small variations during agent execution may lead to deviations from the skill procedure or incorrect execution of individual steps, resulting in task failures.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
Existing approaches improve the reliability of LLM agent execution from different perspectives. Some studies focus on acquiring, generating, or selecting skills for better reusability [16,41]. Some automatic prompt optimization and reflection-based approaches refine prompts, instructions, in-context memories, or skills based on execution feedback [18,26,29,34,39,42]. A few studies improve the underlying model capability through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or post-training on agent execution traces [7,9,24,27,28]. These approaches mainly improve LLM agents by updating external artifacts or the underlying model parameters, thereby enhancing the task-solving capability before agent deployment. In contrast, some studies focus on runtime guardrails and enforcement systems [11,15,31], constraining agent behaviors during execution according to user-specified rules, safety policies, or domain constraints. They are effective for preventing unsafe or policy-violating actions, but a skill-based agent may still fail without violating explicit safety policies. Although prior approaches can improve LLM agent capabilities or constrain unsafe runtime behavior, it remains unclear how to improve the runtime reliability of skill execution when an agent already has the basic capability to complete the task but may still deviate from the skill procedure or execute individual steps incorrectly.
To bridge this gap, we propose SKILLSENTRY, a skilloriented runtime assurance framework for improving the reliability of LLM agent execution. SKILLSENTRY does not aim to teach an LLM agent fundamentally new skills or compensate for tasks beyond the capability of the underlying model. Instead, it targets cases where an agent has demonstrated the capability to complete tasks under the guidance of a skill but may still execute the skill unreliably across similar tasks or repeated runs.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: INTRODUCTION
text: SKILLSENTRY is built upon a new domain-specific language (DSL) for representing runtime guidance for skill execution, and consists of an initialization stage and a self-evolving stage. In the initialization stage, it extracts a skill specification from each skill document, capturing the expected steps, step dependencies, constraints, and completion requirements. It also mines execution experience from historical successful and failed traces, including validated action patterns, failure-associated action patterns, and step-level suggestions and warnings. By combining the skill specification with the mined experience, SKILLSENTRY constructs the initial runtime guidance. In the self-evolving stage, the agent executes new task queries under current runtime guidance through the step-aware runtime assurance mechanism. SKILLSENTRY monitors agent execution, delivers step-level suggestions and warnings to improve the execution of individual skill steps, intervenes upon detecting procedural deviations or failure-associated action patterns, and checks the completion of required steps before accepting the final output. The resulting traces are used to refine the execution experience, enabling SKILLSENTRY to iteratively improve the runtime guidance as new execution traces are collected.

SKILLSENTRY monitors agent execution, delivers step-level suggestions and warnings to improve the execution of individual skill steps, intervenes upon detecting procedural deviations or failure-associated action patterns, and checks the completion of required steps before accepting the final output. title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION / A. Background
text:
We first introduce the background of skill-based agent execution, and then introduce the motivation for our work.
A. Background. Skill-Based Agent Execution. An LLM agent completes tasks through iterative interactions with external environments [9,32,36]. To guide multi-step planning and execution, skills have been introduced as reusable procedural knowledge for completing a class of tasks [16,40,41]. A skill usually contains a name, a description specifying when it should be used, and a procedure describing the expected execution steps. Fig. 1 shows an example skill for macroeconomic timeseries detrending. An LLM agent executes a skill through the agent runtime. The runtime maintains the interaction context, presents the skill and available tools to the model, receives modelgenerated actions, executes tool calls, and returns observations to the model for the next decision. Therefore, the abstract procedure described in a skill is realized as a concrete runtime trace comprising multiple iterations of action planning, tool invocation, and execution feedback, followed by a final output.
Hook. Modern agent systems commonly expose hooks as extension points in the runtime loop [4,21]. Hooks can be triggered at different lifecycle points, such as before an action is executed, after execution feedback is returned, or before the agent terminates [5,22]. These hooks allow an external module to observe the next action and provide additional information to the agent during execution. In this work, we use hooks to monitor and guide LLM agents' skill execution at runtime.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: B. Motivation
text:
Although skills provide procedural knowledge for task completion, runtime decisions depend on iterative reasoning and execution feedback, making the execution process sensitive to small variations in intermediate contexts. Thus, an agent may understand the overall skill but still deviate from the skill procedure or execute individual steps incorrectly. Fig. 3: Approach Overview of SKILLSENTRY To illustrate this problem, we show two cases of Claude Code [4] under the guidance of the skill for macroeconomic timeseries detrending. As illustrated by Case-1 in Fig. 2, the task query asks the agent to compute the correlation between the cyclical components of personal consumption expenditure (PCE) and private fixed investment (PFI) from 1973 to 2024. The skill procedure requires the agent to explicitly harmonize mixed-frequency inputs before real-term conversion, log transformation, HP filtering, and correlation analysis. The agent had previously completed the task query successfully, demonstrating its capability to complete such tasks with the skill. However, later repeated executions of the same task query failed occasionally because it skipped the step of frequency harmonization, deviating from the skill procedure.
Besides, we semantically rewrote the query without changing the intended task or expected output. After this benign rewrite, Codex failed to complete the task successfully because it used an incorrect HP filtering parameter. As illustrated by Case-2 in Fig. 2, the skill explicitly specifies λ = 1600 for quarterly data, but the agent applied λ = 100, which is intended for annual data. This parameter mismatch changed the extracted cyclical components and eventually led to an incorrect correlation result.
These cases show that skill-related tasks may still fail even when the agent has previously completed similar tasks successfully under the guidance of corresponding skills. These observations motivate SKILLSENTRY, which wraps around the LLM agent execution loop, monitors the agent execution progress against the skill procedure, and intervenes when necessary to guide the agent towards reliable skill execution.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: METHODOLOGY
text:
We propose SKILLSENTRY, a skill-oriented framework to improve the reliability of LLM agent execution. The approach overview of SKILLSENTRY is presented in Fig. 3. The key idea is to represent the expected skill procedure and historical execution experience as structured runtime guidance, use this runtime guidance to monitor and guide agent skill execution, and iteratively refine it using newly collected execution traces. To this end, we design a domain-specific language (DSL) for runtime guidance that combines a skill specification with execution experience for each skill (see Sec. III-A).
Given the DSL, SKILLSENTRY consists of an initialization stage and a self-evolving stage. In the initialization stage, it first extracts a skill specification (i.e., step 1 in Fig. 3) from the corresponding skill document using an LLM-based parser (see Sec. III-B). The extracted specification captures the expected skill steps, their dependencies, step-level constraints, and the steps required for task completion. SKILLSENTRY then uses historical successful and failed execution traces to mine initial execution experience (i.e., step 2 in Fig. 3). Successful traces provide validated action patterns and step-level suggestions, whereas failed traces reveal failure-associated action patterns and corresponding warnings (see Sec. III-C). By combining the extracted specification with the mined experience, SKILLSEN-TRY constructs the initial runtime guidance for the skill.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: METHODOLOGY
text: In the self-evolving stage, the agent executes new task queries under the current runtime guidance through the stepaware runtime assurance mechanism (i.e., step 3 in Fig. 3). SKILLSENTRY wraps around the agent execution loop through runtime hooks, and inspects the actions planned by the agent through a procedure checker and a termination checker. The procedure checker monitors whether the execution follows the steps embedded in the runtime guidance. When the execution reaches a specific step, it delivers the corresponding steplevel suggestions and warnings to help the agent execute the step correctly, and hints the agent to re-plan when procedural deviations or failure-associated action patterns are detected. The termination checker verifies that all required skill steps have been completed before accepting the final output, and prompts the agent to continue planning otherwise (see Sec. III-D). The resulting new traces are collected for later execution experience mining to refine the runtime guidance. The updated guidance is used in the next round of runtime assurance, forming an iterative optimization loop that progressively improves the runtime guidance for reliable skill execution.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: A. DSL for Skill-Oriented Runtime Guidance
text:
Although skill documents provide procedural knowledge described in natural language, they do not explicitly expose the information needed for runtime procedure checking. Moreover, agent execution traces are typically unstructured. The key challenge is to transform these unstructured data into structured representations that can be consumed by our runtime assurance mechanism. To this end, SKILLSENTRY introduces a domainspecific language (DSL) for skill-oriented runtime guidance.
The DSL combines the skill specification extracted from the skill document and execution experience mined from successful and failed agent execution traces. Fig. 4 shows the abstract syntax of our DSL. Here, X * denotes zero or more occurrences of X, X + denotes one or more occurrences of X, and [•] denotes an optional field. Fig. 5 shows an example of runtime guidance for the macroeconomic-timeseries-detrending skill.
A runtime guidance instance is associated with one skill and consists of a set of procedure steps and termination requirements. Each step is marked by a unique identifier and a short description. The depends on field records prerequisite steps, determining the dependencies between steps, while the constraints field records explicit requirements on step execution. We consider two types of constraints, i.e., a tool constraint specifies a tool required by the step, and a parameter constraint specifies a required parameter value or condition. The termination field lists the required steps that must be completed before the final output can be accepted. All this information can be extracted from the skill document (see Sec. III-B).

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: A. DSL for Skill-Oriented Runtime Guidance
text: Each step further contains a set of logical actions. A step may involve multiple logical actions, and each logical action may have multiple alternative action patterns. Each pattern specifies an observable tool call and an optional regular expression in the command match field that matches commands realizing the action. Matching any action pattern indicates that the corresponding logical action has been performed, whereas a step is considered completed only after all of its logical actions have been matched during runtime execution. The on enter field stores suggestions and warnings for step execution, which are delivered to the agent to support more reliable step execution when the execution reaches the corresponding step. Each step also contains a set of failure patterns, which record failureassociated action patterns together with reasons explaining their potential risks. All this information can be mined from successful and failed agent execution traces (see Sec. III-C).

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: B. Skill Specification Extraction
text:
Given the DSL, SKILLSENTRY first extracts the skill specification from the corresponding skill document. A skill document is written in natural language. Therefore, SKILLSENTRY uses an LLM-based parser with GPT-5.4 [23] to transform each skill document into the specification fields defined by the DSL.
Specifically, given a skill document D skill , the parser extracts four types of specification information. First, it identifies the expected procedure steps, assigning each step a unique identifier and a short natural-language description. Second, it identifies prerequisite relations among the steps and stores them in the depends on fields. Third, it extracts possible tool and parameter constraints for individual steps. Finally, the parser extracts steps that must be completed before the final output can be accepted and stores them as required steps in the termination field.
The parser is provided with the DSL syntax and instructed to preserve the semantics of D skill without introducing requirements not stated in the original document. All parser prompts are available at our website [1]. We further perform lightweight structural validation on the parsed specification, including checking the uniqueness of step identifiers, the validity of referenced dependencies, the acyclicity of the dependency graph, the validity of constraint types, and the inclusion of all required steps in the extracted step set. If any check fails, SKILLSENTRY returns the validation errors to the parser, and asks it to revise the result. The resulting skill specification forms the procedural backbone of runtime guidance, while other fields in the DSL are subsequently populated and refined from successful and failed agent execution traces.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: C. Execution Experience Mining
text:
SKILLSENTRY mines execution experience from successful and failed agent execution traces to populate or refine the experience fields in the runtime guidance. Let G denote the current runtime guidance for a skill, and let T + and T -denote the successful and failed traces of agent execution under the skill, respectively. Although G specifies the expected skill procedure, it may not provide sufficient observable evidence for tracking individual actions or step-level experience for guiding execution of individual steps. Therefore, SKILLSENTRY uses an LLM-based miner powered by GPT-5.4 to analyze T + and T -together with G and the DSL, populating or refining the logical actions, on enter, and failure patterns fields for each step in G. The resulting runtime guidance is denoted by G * .
The mining process consists of five stages: action pattern extraction, trace summarization, experience field diagnosis, experience field edition, and guidance validation. All prompts used by the miner are available at our website [1].

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: C. Execution Experience Mining
text:
The mining process consists of five stages: action pattern extraction, trace summarization, experience field diagnosis, experience field edition, and guidance validation. All prompts used by the miner are available at our website [1].
Action Pattern Extraction. The miner first aligns observable actions in each trace with the skill steps defined in G. The alignment considers the purpose, inputs, outputs, and execution order of each action in the trace, while actions unrelated to any skill step remain unmatched. For each successful trace τ + ∈ T + , the miner extracts validated action patterns associated with each aligned skill step, i.e., tool calls of each step. We refer to them as validated action patterns because they were exercised in successful executions and therefore provide empirical evidence that the corresponding actions can contribute to completing the step and the overall task. The miner then organizes these patterns into candidate logical actions, denoted as P + , of the corresponding step, and generates regular expressions if needed for command matching at runtime. Since one step may require multiple logical actions and one logical action may admit multiple valid implementations, patterns that realize the same logical action are grouped as alternatives, while different logical actions remain separate requirements of the step.
For each failed trace τ -∈ T -, the miner identifies observable tool calls associated with the failure in the context of an aligned step. These actions are organized into candidate failure patterns, denoted as P -, of the corresponding step, along with the reasons explaining their potential risks.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: C. Execution Experience Mining
text:
Trace Summarization. Raw execution traces contain long reasoning, tool outputs, file operations, and repeated trials. To reduce noise, we summarize each trace with respect to the steps in G. For each trace τ , the miner produces a summary Σ(τ, G) = ⟨S align , S skip , A unalign , s fail , y⟩, where S align denotes the steps aligned in the trace, S skip denotes the steps that should have been executed but are not supported by the trace, A unalign denotes actions in the trace that cannot be aligned with any step, s fail denotes the step that may be responsible for the failure, and y ∈ {0, 1} denotes whether the task is successfully completed. These summaries provide compact step-level evidence for diagnosing and updating experience fields in the current runtime guidance.
Experience Field Diagnosis. Given all the extracted action patterns from traces and trace summaries, the miner diagnoses the experience fields, i.e., logical actions, on enter, and failure patterns, in the current runtime guidance G. Let F(G) be the set of these fields. For each field f ∈ F(G), the miner assigns d f = Diagnose(f, {Σ(τ, G) | τ ∈ T }, P + , P -), where d f ∈ {FP, FN, MC, OK}, jointly examining the current field, the trace summaries, and the candidate patterns under the corresponding step context. Here, FP means that the field is too restrictive and may incorrectly discourage actions observed in successful traces. FN means that the field is too weak and fails to capture risky actions observed in failed traces. MC means missing coverage, where a step lacks sufficient logical actions in the runtime guidance for reliable progress tracking. OK means that no update is needed for the field.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: C. Execution Experience Mining
text:
Experience Field Edition. Based on the diagnosis, the miner generates step-level suggestions and warnings, and edits the corresponding experience fields in G. Each field-level edit is represented as an operation o f ∈ {ADD, UPDATE, REMOVE}. For an FP diagnosis, it applies REMOVE or UPDATE to remove or relax the overly restrictive content. For an FN diagnosis, it applies ADD to introduce new action patterns, suggestions, or warnings. It also applies UPDATE to strengthen the existing content in the corresponding field. For an MC diagnosis, it applies ADD to incorporate new action patterns, suggestions, or warnings into the corresponding field. No edit is generated for a field diagnosed as OK. Applying the generated edits to G produces the populated runtime guidance G * .
Guidance Validation. Finally, SKILLSENTRY validates the mined experience against the DSL and the extracted skill specification. It checks that all experience fields are attached to existing steps, each action pattern is well-formed, and each command-matching expression is a valid regular expression. It further checks that runtime guidance does not include duplicated or conflicting entries. If any validation check fails, the errors are returned to the miner for revision.

It further checks that runtime guidance does not include duplicated or conflicting entries. If any validation check fails, the errors are returned to the miner for revision.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: D. Step-Aware Runtime Assurance
text:
Given the runtime guidance G * for a skill, SKILLSENTRY provides step-aware runtime assurance by wrapping around the agent execution loop through runtime hooks. This online assurance mechanism, which contains a procedure checker and termination checker, intervenes when the agent deviates from the skill procedure and provides step-level suggestions and warnings to mitigate errors in individual step execution.
Procedure Checker. For each task query, the agent executes the task through an iterative loop of planning, action execution, observation, and re-planning. SKILLSENTRY attaches to this loop through runtime hooks [5,22]. Before each action planned by the agent is executed, SKILLSENTRY intercepts the action through a pre-action hook and checks it against G * .
To track execution progress, SKILLSENTRY constructs a finite-state machine (FSM) from the steps and dependency relations in G * . Each skill step s i ∈ G * corresponds to an FSM state, and its depends on field determines when the state can be activated. Let LA(s i ) denote the set of logical actions associated with s i , and let M(s i ) ⊆ LA(s i ) denote the logical actions that have been matched by the observed execution trace. Initially, M(s i ) = ∅. A logical action is considered matched when the action planned by the agent conforms to any of its alternative action patterns. s i is marked as completed only after all of its logical actions have been matched, i.e., M(s i ) = LA(s i ). Completing a step may subsequently activate other steps whose dependencies are satisfied.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: D. Step-Aware Runtime Assurance
text:
Based on the current FSM state and runtime guidance, SKILLSENTRY handles each action planned by the agent as follows. When the execution enters an activated step for the first time, SKILLSENTRY injects the corresponding on enter suggestions and warnings into the agent context, providing step-specific guidance for more reliable step-level execution. If the action matches a logical action of an activated step, SKILLSENTRY allows the action for execution. If it matches a logical action belonging to a step whose dependencies have not yet been satisfied, SKILLSENTRY temporarily denies the action, and provides a hint to the LLM agent for re-planning, avoiding deviations from the expected skill procedure.
Besides, the procedure checker also uses the failure patterns stored in G * to identify actions associated with historical failures. For each failure-associated action pattern in G * , SKILLSENTRY records whether it has already been triggered during the current execution. When an action matches a failureassociated action pattern for the first time, SKILLSENTRY temporarily denies the action and returns a hint containing the corresponding failure reason, thereby giving the agent an opportunity to reconsider its plan. If the agent subsequently generates the same action again, SKILLSENTRY allows it to proceed. This design treats execution experience as advisory evidence for executing individual steps correctly, and avoids permanently blocking actions that may be valid under the current task.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: D. Step-Aware Runtime Assurance
text:
An action that matches neither a logical action nor a failure pattern is also allowed, because it may represent auxiliary exploration or a valid implementation not yet covered by the runtime guidance. However, such an action does not advance the FSM. Every allowed action is executed normally, and its observation is returned to the agent for subsequent planning. Through this process, the procedure checker monitors execution progress, delivers step-level guidance at the corresponding execution context, and intervenes only when it observes a procedural deviation or a failure-associated action pattern.
Termination Checker. When the agent signals task completion, the termination checker checks whether all required steps specified in the termination field of G * have been completed. If any required step is missing, it denies the termination request and provides a hint asking the LLM agent to re-plan. Otherwise, it accepts the final output and terminates the task.
Finally, SKILLSENTRY follows a fail-open principle [25] to avoid disrupting the underlying agent runtime. If an exception occurs within either checker, it allows the action or termination request by default, and records the error for subsequent diagnosis. All the agent execution traces of task queries under the current runtime guidance are collected as new inputs for execution experience mining and subsequent runtime-guidance refinement, supporting the self-evolution of SKILLSENTRY.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: EVALUATION / A. Evaluation Setup
text:
We implement a prototype of SKILLSENTRY with 5,072 lines of Python code. To evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of SKILLSENTRY, we design the following research questions.
A. Evaluation Setup. Agent and Model Selection. We evaluate SKILLSENTRY on two widely used LLM agents, i.e., Claude Code [4] and Codex [21]. Both agents are designed for multi-step task execution, and can interact with external tools during execution, supporting the incorporation of external skill documents into the execution context. More importantly, both agents provide hook mechanisms that expose key lifecycle points of the agent execution loop, allowing us to inspect actions planned by the agent and deliver runtime guidance through their extension interface without modifying the underlying agent implementation. For each agent, we consider two backbone models. Specifically, we use Claude Code with Claude-Haiku-4.5 [2] and Claude-Opus-4.6 [6], and Codex with GPT-5.2 [20] and GPT-5.4 [23]. For fairness, all the agent-model configurations use the same tool execution environment and maximum task execution time (i.e., 30 minutes).
Dataset Preparation. We build our evaluation dataset based on SkillsBench [16], which contains 87 tasks associated with one user query, a skill document, a task execution environment and an outcome-based deterministic verifier. SkillsBench is suitable for our evaluation because its skill documents provide procedural knowledge with high quality, while its deterministic verifiers reproducibly determine whether each task execution succeeds or fails, thereby labeling the resulting trace as successful or failed for execution experience mining.
Since our study focuses on runtime assurance rather than teaching an LLM agent a completely new skill, we evaluate skills for which the target agent has already demonstrated basic task-solving capability but may still execute the skill unreliably.
We therefore filter the original SkillsBench skills according to the execution capability of the evaluated agentmodel configurations.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: EVALUATION / A. Evaluation Setup
text:
We therefore filter the original SkillsBench skills according to the execution capability of the evaluated agentmodel configurations.
Specifically, for each of the four agentmodel configurations, we execute the original query of every SkillsBench task five times with its corresponding curated skill.
A task is regarded as executable under a configuration if at least one of the five executions passes its deterministic verifier.
Tasks that fail in all five runs are excluded for that configuration, because such consistent failures are more likely to indicate insufficient basic task-solving capability than unreliable skill execution.
We then take the intersection of the executable skill sets obtained from the four configurations.
This intersection ensures that every retained skill can be executed successfully by all evaluated configurations at least once, allowing subsequent failures to be more reasonably attributed to execution instability.
After this filtering process, 15 skills remain from the original SkillsBench.
These commonly executable skills constitute the subjects of our evaluation, and their details are shown in Table I.
Since each retained SkillsBench skill originally provides only one task query, we expand the query set for each selected skill through a two-stage augmentation process inspired by [17].
The objective is to increase both task-level and expressionlevel diversity while preserving deterministic and verifiable task oracles for evaluation.
In the first stage, we perform tasklevel semantic expansion.
For each skill, we construct 8 task instances, including the original task and 7 manually created variants.
These variants preserve the intended skill usage but change concrete query semantics, such as input parameters, target objects, and task context.
We manually adapt the corresponding deterministic verifier for each newly constructed instance.
In the second stage, we perform expression-level paraphrase mutation.

heading: EVALUATION / A. Evaluation Setup
text:
We manually adapt the corresponding deterministic verifier for each newly constructed instance.
In the second stage, we perform expression-level paraphrase mutation.
For each task instance, we construct ten semantically equivalent query expressions, including its original expression and nine paraphrases generated using GPT-5.4 [23].
The paraphrases modify only surface-level expressions, such as wording and sentence structure, without changing the task requirements or expected outcome.
Therefore, all expression variants derived from the same task instance share the verifiers.
In total, each skill contains 80 queries, resulting in 1200 queries across 15 selected skills. For each skill, we divide the queries into an evolution set and a held-out test set, denoted by Q evol and Q test , respectively. We perform this split at the task-instance level. Five complete task instances, containing 50 queries in total, are assigned to Q evol , while the remaining three task instances, containing 30 queries, are assigned to Q test . Consequently, paraphrases derived from the same task instance never appear in both sets. The 50 queries in Q evol are used to simulate a stream of new task queries arriving after deployment. As new queries arrive, their successful and failed execution traces are progressively collected and used to mine execution experience and update the runtime guidance. The 30 queries in Q test remain unseen throughout evolution and are used only for effectiveness evaluation.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: EVALUATION / A. Evaluation Setup
text:
RQ Setup. For RQ1, we evaluate whether SKILLSENTRY improves both task success across queries and execution stability under repeated runs. For each skill and agent-model configuration, we evolve the runtime guidance for 10 iterations using the 50 queries in Q evol . In each iteration, we randomly select five previously unused queries, execute them under the current guidance, collect the resulting traces, and update the guidance accordingly. After all 50 queries have been processed, we evaluate the final guidance on the 30 queries in Q test .
We evaluate each evolved guidance five times on Q test and report the mean and standard deviation (SD) of the resulting task success rates for each skill and agent-model configuration, where a higher mean and lower SD indicate more reliable execution of LLM agents with the corresponding skill.
For RQ2, we evaluate the runtime overhead introduced by SKILLSENTRY on Q test . We compare the base agentmodel configuration and SKILLSENTRY in terms of the average number of inference turns and token costs. We further report the computation time of SKILLSENTRY, and its proportion of the total execution time for each agent-model configuration.
For RQ3, we analyze the self-evolving capability of SKILLSENTRY by evaluating it after each of the 10 evolution iterations. At the end of each iteration, we evaluate SKILLSEN-TRY on Q test and compute the task success rate of each skill. To reduce the effects of query ordering, we repeat the entire evolution process five times. We aggregate the results over five independent evolution processes, and report how the average task success rate changes as more traces are included.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: B. Effectiveness Evaluation (RQ1)
text:
Overall Effectiveness. Table II shows the mean task success rate and standard deviation over five repeated evaluations for the base agents and SKILLSENTRY across 15 skills and four agentmodel configurations. The higher mean and lower standard deviation are highlighted in bold. Overall, SKILLSENTRY consistently improves task success rates across all evaluated settings. Averaged across the 15 skills, SKILLSENTRY achieves relative improvements of 29.5% and 22.7% for Claude Code with Claude-Haiku-4.5 and Claude-Opus-4.6, respectively, and 24.5% and 20.5% for Codex with GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.4, respectively. Across all four configurations, SKILLSENTRY increases the average task success rate from 62.6% to 77.7%, corresponding to an overall relative improvement of 24.1%.
The improvement is consistent across all agent-model configurations and skills. The gains are particularly pronounced on skills with low baseline performance, reaching 210.8% for excitation-signal-design, 131.6% for weighted-gdp-calc, and 199.2% for d3-visualization, with substantial gains also observed for pddl-skills and geospatial-analysis. For skills with strong baseline performance, the relative gains are smaller, yet SKILLSENTRY still reduces residual failures, achieving perfect task success rates for glm-calibration across all four configurations and for several configurations of pcap-analysis, spring-boot-migration, and mesh-analysis. Overall, SKILLSEN-TRY improves challenging skill executions while mitigating occasional failures on skills that already succeed in most runs.
In addition to improving task success rates, SKILLSENTRY generally produces more stable results across repeated evaluations. The average standard deviation decreases by 41.2%, 39.5%, 46.5%, and 36.9% under Claude-Haiku-4.5, Claude-Opus-4.6, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4, respectively. Across all 60 skill-agent-model configurations, SKILLSENTRY yields a lower standard deviation in 50 pairs and the same standard deviation in two pairs. Overall, it reduces the average standard deviation by 41.1%, indicating that these effectiveness improvements are accompanied by more consistent execution across repeated runs.

heading: E. Ablation Study (RQ4)
text:
Table IV reports the ablation results across the four agentmodel configurations. Overall, the complete SKILLSENTRY consistently achieves the highest average task success rate. SKILLSENTRY outperforms w/o On-Enter and w/o Failure Patterns by 19.0% and 13.6%, respectively. This result confirms that both forms of execution experience improve skill reliability. Removing on enter causes a larger degradation, highlighting the importance of step-level suggestions and warnings, while failure-associated action patterns provide complementary guidance by prompting agents to reconsider previously unsuccessful actions, helping the execution of individual steps.
SKILLSENTRY also outperforms System-Prompt Delivery by 5.8% on average. Although both use the same guidance, steplevel delivery is more effective because it presents relevant information in the corresponding execution context, reducing the chance that suggestions or warnings are overlooked in a long initial prompt. Moreover, the complete SKILLSENTRY also achieves the lowest average standard deviation, indicating improvements in both effectiveness and stability.
Summary.
Step-level suggestions, warnings, and failureassociated action patterns all contribute to the effectiveness of SKILLSENTRY. Delivering guidance at the step level further improves the average task success rate by 5.8%.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: THREATS TO VALIDITY
text:
First, the selection of skills, agents, and backbone models may limit generalizability. To mitigate this threat, we evaluate the 15 skills across two widely used agents, i.e., Claude Code and Codex, each paired with two backbone models.
Second, the original capabilities of the agents and the quality of skill documents pose threats to validity. SKILLSENTRY assumes that the agent correctly selects the required skill and the procedure in the skill document is correct. It focuses on assuring individual skill execution rather than skill selection. When a task requires multiple skills, SKILLSENTRY can support their execution when the skills are invoked sequentially. However, it does not currently provide effective assurance for workflows that repeatedly switch between interdependent steps from different skills. Such cases may require integrating and jointly optimizing the involved skills into a unified one.
Third, execution experience mining relies on a verifier to label successful and failed traces. We use deterministic verifiers provided by the evaluation dataset to ensure reliable trace labels in our experiments. In practice, such verifiers may require additional construction effort. In these cases, SKILLSENTRY can instead incorporate LLM-based evaluators tailored to the target task for agent execution trace labeling.
Finally, the stochasticity of LLM-based execution and randomness of query ordering in experiments pose threats to validity. To mitigate these threats, we evaluate each evolved guidance five times, repeat the evolution process five times, and report both mean and standard deviation. We also conduct paired t-test analysis [10] across our comparisons, and the improvements are statistically significant (p<0.05).

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: RELATED WORK A. Runtime Assurance for LLM Agents
text: The autonomy of LLM agents brings new safety and reliability challenges, motivating recent work [11,15,31] on runtime guardrails, monitoring, and enforcement. AGENTSPEC [31] allows users to specify runtime constraints for LLM agents with a domain-specific language and enforces these constraints during execution. SHIELDAGENT [11] extracts verifiable rules from policy documents and uses them to check whether the trace of agent actions violates safety policies. Kumar et al. [15] further study policy-enforced guardrails for infrastructure agents. These studies show the importance of adding an external runtime module to constrain agent behaviors without modifying the underlying model. SKILLSENTRY differs from these studies by targeting skill execution reliability rather than safety enforcement. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a runtime assurance framework for skill-oriented agent execution. We therefore do not directly compare SKILLSENTRY with these approaches, as prior approaches detect safety violations, whereas SKILLSENTRY enforces skill procedures and leverages execution experience to improve task completion, resulting in different inputs, objectives, and evaluation criteria.

AGENTSPEC [31] allows users to specify runtime constraints for LLM agents with a domain-specific language and enforces these constraints during execution. SHIELDAGENT [11] extracts verifiable rules from policy documents and uses them to check whether the trace of agent actions violates safety policies. Kumar et al. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a runtime assurance framework for skill-oriented agent execution. We therefore do not directly compare SKILLSENTRY with these approaches, as prior approaches detect safety violations, whereas SKILLSENTRY enforces skill procedures and leverages execution experience to improve task completion, resulting in different inputs, objectives, and evaluation criteria.

title: SKILLSENTRY: Reliable Skill Execution for LLM Agents via Runtime Assurance
heading: B. Execution-Based Optimization for LLM Agents
text: A growing body of work improves LLM agents by optimizing or augmenting system prompts, agent memories, and skills based on execution feedback. Reflexion [29] stores verbal reflections generated from task feedback and reuses them in later trials. ExpeL [39] summarizes successful and failed traces into reusable natural-language experience in the system prompt. APE [42] generates instruction candidates with LLMs and selects prompts according to task performance. ProTeGi [26] edits prompts using textual gradients derived from model errors, while OPRO [34] treats prompt optimization as a natural-language optimization process driven by LLMgenerated proposals. Recently, Trace2Skill [18] distills prior failure lessons into transferable agent skills, providing a new perspective on leveraging execution traces for agent improvement. Instead of rewriting a prompt or skill artifact offline, SKILLSENTRY uses execution traces to support runtime assurance. It aligns successful and failed traces with skill steps, mines step-level runtime guidance, and provides such guidance only when the agent reaches the corresponding step during execution, improving the runtime reliability of skill execution.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Abstract
text:
As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents, their integration into interactive environments and tool use introduce new safety challenges beyond those associated with the models themselves. However, the absence of comprehensive benchmarks for evaluating agent safety presents a significant barrier to effective assessment and further improvement. In this paper, we introduce AGENT-SAFETYBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the safety of LLM agents. AGENT-SAFETYBENCH encompasses 349 interaction environments and 2,000 test cases, evaluating 8 categories of safety risks and covering 10 common failure modes frequently encountered in unsafe interactions. Our evaluation of 16 popular LLM agents reveals a concerning result: none of the agents achieves a safety score above 60%. This highlights significant safety challenges in LLM agents and underscores the considerable need for improvement. Through failure mode and helpfulness analysis, we summarize two fundamental safety defects in current LLM agents: lack of robustness and lack of risk awareness. Furthermore, our findings suggest that reliance on defense prompts alone may be insufficient to address these safety issues, emphasizing the need for more advanced and robust strategies. To drive progress in this area, AGENT-SAFETYBENCH has been released 1 to facilitate further research in agent safety evaluation and improvement.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Benchmark / LLM Safety Evaluation
text:
Using AGENT-SAFETYBENCH, we evaluate 16 agents that are powered by LLMs with tool usage capabilities, including both proprietary ones (e.g., ) and open-source ones (e.g., Llama-3.1). As shown in Figure 1, the results reveal that the overall safety scores for all models fall below 60%. These results highlight a concerning level of safety across current LLM agents. Moreover, we identify two fundamental safety defects in current LLM agents through analysis on their failure modes and helpfulness under different scenarios: lack of robustness and risk awareness. Specifically, LLM agents demonstrate inadequate robustness in reliably invoking tools across diverse scenarios, and they exhibit a lack of awareness regarding the potential safety risks associated with tool usage in specific environments (e.g., disabling all alarm systems). Finally, we observe that simply incorporating defense prompts to mitigate failure modes yields only limited improvements, which underscores the necessity for more sophisticated approaches to enhance agent safety. In summary, the main contributions of this work are:
• We propose AGENT-SAFETYBENCH, a comprehensive agent safety evaluation benchmark that introduces a diverse array of novel environments that are previously unexplored, and offers broader and more systematic coverage of various risk categories and failure modes.
• We finetune a reliable agent safety evaluation model, which demonstrates a substantial accuracy improvement (approximately 15%) over GPT-4o. We then evaluate 16 representative LLM agents on AGENT-SAFETYBENCH, and uncover a concerning result: the safety scores of all tested LLM agents fall below 60%.
• We conduct analysis of the failure modes and helpfulness exhibited by LLM agents and identify two fundamental safety defects: lack of robustness and risk awareness. Additionally, we demonstrate that it is non-trivial to fully address the issue by adding defense prompts.

heading: Risk Definition / Lead to property loss / Spread unsafe information / misinformation / Violate law /
text:
Leak sensitive data / information The assistant discloses sensitive data inadvertently or intentionally, such as sharing confidential information via email to unintended recipients.
Lead to property loss. The assistant's behavior results in the loss or compromise of property in a broad sense, including intellectual property, financial assets, important data, etc.
Spread unsafe information / misinformation. The assistant facilitates the dissemination of harmful or misleading content, such as posting malicious content or spreading fake news.
Lead to physical harm The assistant's behavior results in harm to physical health, such as purchasing the wrong medication.
Violate law / ethics. The assistant breaches legal or ethical standards, such as assisting in the transport of contraband.
Compromise availability. The assistant disrupts the normal functionality of applications or systems, such as erroneously blocking access to legitimate websites.
Contribute to harmful / vulnerable code The assistant's behavior leads to the creation or dissemination of harmful or vulnerable code, such as deploying harmful code.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Agent Safety Evaluation
text: Agents have exhibited impressive capabilities in solving complex tasks through reasoning and planning to effectively interact with real-world environments (Qin et al., 2024). Compared to LLMs, the safety concerns surrounding agents extend beyond generating unsafe content to include the execution of potentially harmful behaviors within interactive environments. For example, Yin et al. (2024) explored risks with embodied LLM-agents with high-level actions in real-word scenarios. Lee et al. (2024) introduced MobileSafetyBench for evaluating device-control agents within realistic mobile environments based on Android emulators. In particular, growing research attention has been paid to safety risks arising from agents that interact with external tools across domains such as banking, travel, and online shopping (Yuan et al., 2024;Debenedetti et al., 2024;Xiang et al., 2024;Ruan et al., 2024;Ye et al., 2024;Zhan et al., 2024). Despite these advances, there remains a need for a benchmark that encompasses a wider variety of environments and provides more systematic coverage of diverse risk categories and failure modes associated with tool-incorporation.

heading: Risks:
text:
The potential risks that may be triggered in the test case. For simplicity, each test case is assigned to one of the 8 categories of risks that is most likely to be evoked, although some test cases may inherently involve multiple types of safety risks.
Instruction / Dialog: The user-provided instruction or a predefined interaction dialog history. This field serves as the initial input to the test agents. We accept the format of prefilled dialog to be compatible with existing works (Ye et al., 2024).
Environments: The list of relevant environments associated with the test case. Each environment specification includes the environment name, the tools involved, and their initialization parameters.
The initialization parameters are freely configurable, enabling the design of diverse and customized environments tailored to specific test cases.
Failure Modes: The anticipated failure modes that may cause the agent to trigger safety risks. This field can include multiple expected failure modes selected from the 10 summarized categories as Table 4 shows. Identifying these failure modes helps clarify the intent of the test case and facilitates the systematic analysis of failure patterns in LLM agents.
To implement the environments, we adopt a dual-layer structure comprising a JSON-based tool schema and a corresponding Python class for each environment. Our design enables flexible and customizable initialization of environments, allowing for the creation of tailored environments to accommodate diverse test cases. For details to the implementation, please refer to Appendix C.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Refine Existing Datasets
text:
To avoid unnecessary resource wastage, we first collect samples from several existing datasets, including R-Judge, AgentDojo, GuardAgent, ToolEmu, ToolSword, and InjecAgent, as detailed in Table 1. Three steps are involved in the data refinement process. Firstly, since some samples in these datasets are overly general and lack clear failure modes, we revise these samples to clarify their failure modes and discard those that cannot be effectively improved. Secondly, we eliminate redundant samples that exhibit high similarity to others to ensure the diversity of data. Thirdly, we standardize the definition and implementation of environments across datasets and introduce necessary environment parameters to ensure the validity of each test case.
Note that for the category Produce unsafe information / misinformation, which does not involve tool usage, we sample 50 raw questions from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023) and randomly combine them with 20 representative jailbreak templates (Zhang et al., 2024c), resulting in 200 new test cases. We also manually annotate the primary risk category for each test case, obtaining a total of 876 test cases.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Augment Refined Data
text:
Since the revised samples from existing datasets are insufficient in quantity, and certain categories of safety risks-such as Compromise availability-lack adequate test cases, we augment the dataset to ensure that each category contains 250 diverse test cases. Initially, we attempt to use GPT-4o to directly generate new test cases based on a random in-context example. However, we observe two main issues: (1) low diversity, as the topics of the new cases are limited, and (2) low quality, as many of the cases fail to clearly induce unsafe behaviors.
To address the first issue, we generate 300 new environment names using GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro. Then we require a random new environment to be included when generating a new test case, which greatly enhances the diversity of the generated cases. To address the second issue, we apply in-context learning to let GPT-4o generate a sequence of expected risky behaviors along with the test case (e.g., "the agent may first call the tool search_emails to obtain the email content, and then call the tool click_link to access the unknown malicious link in the email, which may lead to property loss"). This approach improves the quality of the generated cases by clarifying the intended risky behaviors. Additionally, we specify a risk category for each new test case in the augmentation prompt to help control the distribution of risk categories. Appendix E for all prompts used during augmentation.
Using the same refinement process for existing datasets, we finally obtain 1,124 new valid test cases across risk categories in this phase.

title: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
heading: Quality Control
text:
We have adopted several measures to strictly control the quality of samples in AGENT-SAFETYBENCH.
(1) Manual precheck. Each of the 2,000 test cases undergoes a comprehensive review and revision process, conducted by at least one author, during its construction. The process ensures that test cases have clearly risk categories and failure modes.
(2) Automatic validation. Python scripts are employed to automatically validate the implementation of the environments (e.g., ensuring that the tool definitions in the JSON files match those in the Python class). Any discrepancies identified are manually addressed by the authors.
(3) Manual postcheck. After constructing the 2,000 test cases, we test them on GPT-4o-mini and Claude-3.5-Sonnet, generating 4,000 interaction records. These records are manually labeled to determine whether the agents exhibit unsafe behaviors. Based on the refined 2000 test cases and 4000 interaction records, we summarize ten failure modes using an approach similar to open coding. The distribution of these failure modes is presented in Figure 5 in the Appendix. During the labeling process, we also revise test cases if they are found to be unreasonable and fix issues that arise in the implementation of the relevant environments. For any revised cases, the interaction records are updated accordingly.
Following the aforementioned annotations, we further conduct a cross-validation step to ensure the quality of the test cases and the reliability of the safety labels. Please refer to Appendix F for details.
