heading: Zigzag Development Trend in Optimizing Agentic ROI
text:
Building on these findings, we argue that the development and deployment of LLM agents should explicitly optimize for Agentic ROI. This leads us to the next critical question: how can Agentic ROI be effectively optimized?
We posit that the trajectory of LLM agent development is unlikely to follow a linear path. Instead, it may exhibit a zigzag pattern characterized by alternating phases of scaling up and scaling down. This insight is inspired by performance trends observed in the OpenAI model series (see Figure 3). Specifically, we identify a recurring cycle: new model families typically begin by scaling up to push the frontier of capabilities (e.g., the transition from o1-mini to o1). Subsequent iterations then tend to scale down, introducing smaller, more efficient variants (e.g., o3-mini, o4-mini) that retain comparable performance while significantly reducing inference costs (e.g., o3-mini vs. o1, o4-mini vs. o3).
In the context of LLM agents, we observe a similar optimization process in which each generation makes tradeoffs along different axes of the ROI surface: information gain, time savings, and cost-first scaling up to improve information gain and time savings, then scaling down to reduce cost. This zigzag development trend is not unique to LLM agents. Similar patterns have been observed in other areas of technological innovation, e.g., computer processors and smartphones (Lotfi-Kamran et al., 2012).
At present, the development of LLM agents remains in the "scaling up" phase. Large-scale models are being deployed to push the upper bounds of generalization, reasoning, and tool usage (Google DeepMind, 2025;OpenAI, 2025). The high information quality and time savings of LLM agents are achieved at the cost of increased computation and infrastructure demands. Looking ahead, we anticipate a "scaling down" phase in which advances in efficiency, specialization, and model architecture will lower the cost of deployment.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: AGENT QUALITY: SCALING SLEEP-TIME COMPUTE
text:
• Scaling user preference reasoning: Most current systems rely on surface-level cues, such as explicit queries, to infer user needs (Li et al., 2024). However, users' preferences, values, and goals are often implicit, buried within years of fragmented digital traces (Chai et al., 2025). In many cases, users themselves may struggle to articulate their underlying intents (Mohamed et al., 2019 reasoning, agents shift from passive responses to a deeper, contextualized understanding of the user.
• Scaling iterative simulation: Idle periods offer a critical window for agents to engage in extensive self-play and counterfactual simulation (Lin et al., 2025). By generating divergent future trajectories and validating them against live APIs or external data sources (Fang et al., 2025;Froger et al., 2025), agents can pre-compute optimal solutions and update their operational knowledge. Consequently, this "mental sandbox" enables the system to produce more robust, verified strategies.
• Scaling agent swarms: Sleep-time compute provides the ideal environment to deploy agent swarms (Kimi, 2026), collaborative networks of specialized sub-agents, without the bottleneck of real-time coordination latency. During idle periods, a primary agent can decompose complex, latent user goals into sub-problems and distribute them across a swarm. These sub-agents can asynchronously explore vast solution spaces, cross-verify information, and debate conflicting strategies.
Ultimately, scaling sleep-time compute redefines the lifecycle of LLM agents. Agents become persistent, selfimproving collaborators that continuously learn, adapt, and validate across both user and environment dimensions. Moreover, this approach aligns with cognitive models of human expertise: just as individuals consolidate memories and refine mental models during rest (Klinzing et al., 2019), agents can leverage downtime to refine policies and simulate future trajectories. In this sense, sleep-time scaling serves as the computational analog of cognitive rehearsal and long-term memory consolidation.

These sub-agents can asynchronously explore vast solution spaces, cross-verify information, and debate conflicting strategies.
Ultimately, scaling sleep-time compute redefines the lifecycle of LLM agents. Agents become persistent, selfimproving collaborators that continuously learn, adapt, and validate across both user and environment dimensions. Moreover, this approach aligns with cognitive models of human expertise: just as individuals consolidate memories and refine mental models during rest (Klinzing et al., 2019), agents can leverage downtime to refine policies and simulate future trajectories. In this sense, sleep-time scaling serves as the computational analog of cognitive rehearsal and long-term memory consolidation.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: HUMAN TIME: SCALING MULTI-STEP CAPABILITIES
text:
A key consideration in evaluating the deployment potential of LLM agents is the concept of baseline human time, denoted as T 0 . This represents the time required for a human to complete a given task. Understanding the characteristics of T 0 is crucial for identifying domains where LLM agents can provide meaningful time savings. The following properties of T 0 are particularly relevant:
• Context-Dependence: The value of T 0 is inherently sensitive to the context in which a task is performed. A task that is trivial in a static environment may become significantly more time-consuming when subjected to environmental constraints or divided attention. For instance, as discussed in Section 3.3, ordering a coffee via a mobile application may take mere seconds when a user is seated comfortably at home. However, performing the same action while driving drastically inflates T 0 due to safety constraints and limited interaction bandwidth.
• Personalization and Accessibility: The baseline human time T 0 varies widely across individuals. Expertise, prior knowledge, tool familiarity, and cognitive style all influence task duration. What is trivial for an expert may be slow and error-prone for a novice. This variability is particularly critical for elderly users or individuals with disabilities, who may require extended time to navigate standard digital interfaces due to motor or visual impairments. In this light, LLM agents offer a pathway to digital equity (Resta & Laferrière, 2008).

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: HUMAN TIME: SCALING MULTI-STEP CAPABILITIES
text:
• Non-Linearity of Task Composition: As tasks become more compound-involving multiple steps, interdependencies, and decision points-T 0 tends to rise superlinearly. This non-linearity arises from the cognitive switching penalty (Schmitz & Krämer, 2023): the mental effort required to maintain working memory of the overall goal while executing individual sub-steps. For humans, multi-step tasks necessitate sustained planning, state tracking, and context switching, all of which increase the probability of fatigue-induced errors.
Reflecting on the observations in Section 3.3, it is clear that LLM agents are most impactful in domains where the baseline human time T 0 is relatively high. These domains typically involve contextually demanding and multi-step tasks. To operate effectively in these high-T 0 scenarios, LLM agents must scale their multi-step capabilities. Key requirements include:
• Long-Horizon Reasoning: Maintaining coherence, consistency, and goal alignment across extended interactions and multi-turn reasoning sequences.
• State Persistence: Accurately retaining and transferring relevant information across steps without hallucination, drift, or data loss. This is essential for preserving task continuity and avoiding redundant sub-tasks.
• Self-Correction: As the probability of failure compounds in longer reasoning chains, agents must be able to detect, localize, and correct intermediate errors to avoid cascading failures and improve reliability.
The ability to handle such multi-step, stateful tasks will be a defining feature of next-generation LLM agents and a central driver of their economic value. Currently, however, agent capabilities degrade drastically as the number of steps increases (Lu et al., 2024a).

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: AGENT INTERACTION TIME: SCALING PROACTIVE INTERACTION
text:
Agent interaction time, denoted as T Agent , represents the total time a human user spends engaging with an agent to complete a task. Unlike agent latency, which refers to computational processing time, T Agent is a measure of human effort. This includes all phases of interaction: initial prompt formulation, intent clarification, iterative refinements (e.g., rephrasing, follow-up questions), and final result verification.
To reduce agent interaction time, systems must shift the burden of context acquisition from the user to the agent (Lu et al., 2024b). This requires a transition from reactive execution to proactive interaction, where the agent actively infers goals, anticipates needs, and automatically completes the task. This shift is tightly coupled with scaling sleep-time compute, allowing the agent to reason and prepare before user interactions occur. Reducing T Agent can be achieved through three key mechanisms:
• Intent Inference and Goal Prediction: Agents should be capable of inferring user intent from partial, implicit, or ambiguous inputs. Rather than relying on the user to fully articulate the task, agents can leverage interaction history and environmental cues to predict likely goals. Clarifying questions should be asked only when necessary, minimizing interaction turns. However, as shown in Lu et al. (2024b), current LLM agents still fall short in predictive capabilities and often fail to anticipate user goals effectively, highlighting a key area for improvement.
• Implicit Context Resolution: In traditional reactive paradigms, users are responsible for explicitly verbalizing the state of the world. Proactive agents can mitigate this by integrating multimodal inputs (e.g., voice, imagery, and structured UI elements) to automatically capture environmental and task-specific context (Durante et al., 2024).

text:
Moreover, agents can reduce input overhead by offering intelligent autocompletions, prefilled templates, and context-aware suggestions. These features lower interaction costs, especially in repetitive or structured tasks, and enable faster transitions from intent to execution.
• Proactive Verification and Trust: The time allocated to result verification is inversely proportional to user trust. When trust is low, users scrutinize every detail and mentally simulate the agent's steps, effectively duplicating the computational effort. To compress this verification phase, agents must proactively perform self-verification before presenting the final output. This includes running internal consistency checks and cross-referencing sources. By exposing a concise, human-readable reasoning trace, the agent transforms verification from a forensic audit into a lightweight sanity check.
The long-term goal of scaling proactive interaction is to drive T Agent toward zero for routine and well-understood tasks. In such cases, the user's role shifts from active instruction to strategic oversight and high-level delegation.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: Scaling Down for Cost Reduction
text:
While recent advances stem from scaling up for information gain, we argue that this expansion must be followed by a phase of scaling down to optimize unit utility. Once a capability threshold is met, the focus shifts from maximizing performance at any cost to minimizing the resources required to maintain it. We discuss critical strategies for lowering the operational burden of LLM agents without compromising output quality.
• From Real-time Thinking to Memory Retrieval: Agents relying solely on real-time inference incur high computational penalties, especially when regenerating reasoning chains for similar tasks (Wu et al., 2025). By integrating long-term memory systems, agents can bypass redundant computation through retrieval-based reasoning, transforming time complexity from expensive generation to efficient lookup. This mirrors human cognitive efficiency (Gabrieli, 1998;Evans, 2003): experts solve tasks rapidly not because they think faster, but because they remember better. Shifting from compute-bound inference to memory retrieval dramatically reduces latency and cost, particularly in repetitive or domain-specific applications.
• From Generalist Giants to Specialized Experts: While large generalist models define the state-of-the-art, they are often over-parameterized for routine sub-tasks. Scaling down involves compressing these capabilities into compact, specialized architectures through knowledge distillation (Xu et al., 2024). Techniques such as quantization, pruning, and speculative decoding allow these models to operate within tighter resource budgets, significantly lowering the barrier to deployment (Egashira et al., 2024).
• Hardware-Software Co-optimization: Infrastructure dictates the lower bound of operational cost. Advances in AI-specific hardware (e.g., Groq (Gwennap, 2020), Cerebras (Lie, 2022)) and inference-optimized software stacks (e.g., vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022)) directly alleviate bottlenecks. Improving agent efficiency at scale requires the co-evolution of software and hardware, moving beyond raw FLOPs to metrics that matter for interactive agents, such as cost per task.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: Call to Action
text:
To close the usability gap and unlock the next wave of adoption, we must reframe the development and deployment of LLM agents around maximizing Agentic ROI.
First, we call for a redesign of agents intended for the mass market, everyday applications. Today's LLM agents thrive in high-ROI domains such as coding and research, where expert users tolerate back-and-forth interactions in exchange for significant utility gains. However, to serve the broader public, agents must become more robust, proactive, and accessible. This means designing systems that reduce interaction friction and anticipate user intent. By shifting the focus from raw model capability to real-world usability, we can create agents that are not only powerful, but also intuitive and dependable.
Second, to make informed and scalable deployment decisions, we must adopt Agentic ROI as a first-class evaluation metric. Unlike traditional benchmarks, Agentic ROI captures the tangible value delivered to users by balancing improvements in information quality and time savings against the cost of agent usage. Its utility spans the ecosystem: for researchers, it offers a benchmark that aligns model progress with real-world human benefit; for developers, it guides optimization across quality, latency, and computational efficiency; for organizations, it provides a framework for assessing the economic viability and practical impact of agent integration; and for users, it ensures that systems are responsive to their time, expectations, and constraints.
We encourage the community to collaborate on shared datasets, benchmarks, and tools for estimating Agentic ROI across tasks, domains, and user populations. This shift from abstract performance scores to metrics grounded in lived experience is essential for meaningful progress.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: Alternative Views
text:
While we advocate for a framework grounded in Agentic ROI, we must address alternative perspectives shaping current deployment strategies. Below, we re-examine two common views through this lens.
• View 1: Repetitive tasks automatically warrant LLM agent deployment. This view rests on the intuition that automation is most valuable when tasks are repetitive, and thus, LLM agents should naturally be applied in such contexts.
Response: Repetition only increases ROI if it yields time savings and quality at a reasonable cost. Many repetitive tasks are better served by traditional rule-based automation or lightweight models. LLM agents here may be overengineered and expensive. Worse, if the agent introduces variability or errors in an otherwise deterministic process, the resulting verification costs can negate any time savings.
• View 2: Model capability and accuracy determine usability. This view assumes that higher raw model performance automatically translates to a more usable agent.
Response: Capability is merely one component of usability. A powerful model requiring complex prompting or heavy verification offers low practical usability. Conversely, a modest but responsive and intuitive agent may deliver higher net utility. Moreover, because accuracy gains often incur higher computational costs, Agentic ROI diminishes when marginal improvements fail to offset the expense, thereby reducing practical usability.

title: Position: The Real Barrier to LLM Agent Usability is Agentic ROI
heading: Conclusion
text: In this position paper, we argue that the key barrier to the practical usability of LLM agents lies not in model capability alone, but in the agent's ability to deliver utility relative to the costs incurred during real-world use. To formalize this tradeoff, we introduce and operationalize the concept of Agentic ROI. Agentic ROI quantifies the ratio of information gain and time savings to the cost. Applying this metric, we reveal a usability gap, noting that domains with the highest market demand show significantly lower Agentic ROI. We analyze development trends in optimizing Agentic ROI and outline future directions for bridging the usability gap, paving the way for LLM agents that are truly usable, scalable, and accessible in real-world applications.

title: Large Language Models as Urban Residents: An LLM Agent Framework for Personal Mobility Generation
heading: Abstract
text: This paper introduces a novel approach using Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated into an agent framework for flexible and effective personal mobility generation. LLMs overcome the limitations of previous models by effectively processing semantic data and offering versatility in modeling various tasks. Our approach addresses three research questions: aligning LLMs with real-world urban mobility data, developing reliable activity generation strategies, and exploring LLM applications in urban mobility. The key technical contribution is a novel LLM agent framework that accounts for individual activity patterns and motivations, including a self-consistency approach to align LLMs with real-world activity data and a retrieval-augmented strategy for interpretable activity generation. We evaluate our LLM agent framework and compare it with state-of-the-art personal mobility generation approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and its potential applications in urban mobility. Overall, this study marks the pioneering work of designing an LLM agent framework for activity generation based on realworld human activity data, offering a promising tool for urban mobility analysis. Source codes are available at https://github.com/Wangjw6/LLMob/ .

title: Large Language Models as Urban Residents: An LLM Agent Framework for Personal Mobility Generation
heading: Introduction
text:
• Semantic Interpretability. Unlike previous models, which have predominantly depended on structured data (e.g., GPS coordinates-based trajectory data) for both calibration and simulation [17,27,47], LLMs exhibit proficiency in interpreting semantic data (e.g., activity trajectory data). This advantage significantly broadens the scope for incorporating a diverse array of data sources into generation processes, thereby enhancing the models' ability to understand and interact with complex, real-world scenarios in a more nuanced and effective manner. • Model Versatility. Although other data-driven methods manage to learn such dynamic activity patterns for generation, their capacity is limited for generation under unseen scenarios. On the contrary, LLMs have shown remarkable versatility in dealing with unseen tasks, especially the ability to reason and decide based on available information [26]. This competence enables LLMs to offer a diverse and rational array of choices, making it a promising and flexible approach for modeling personal mobility patterns.
Despite these benefits, ensuring that LLMs align effectively with real-world situations continues to be a significant challenge [36]. This alignment is particularly crucial in the context of urban mobility, where the precision and dependability of LLM outputs are essential for the efficacy of any urban management derived from them. In this study, our aim is to address this challenge by investigating the following research questions: RQ 1: How can LLMs be effectively aligned with semantically rich data about daily individual activities? RQ 2: What are the effective strategies for achieving reliable and meaningful activity generation using LLM agents? RQ 3: What are the potential applications of LLM agents in enhancing urban mobility analysis?

Despite these benefits, ensuring that LLMs align effectively with real-world situations continues to be a significant challenge [36]. This alignment is particularly crucial in the context of urban mobility, where the precision and dependability of LLM outputs are essential for the efficacy of any urban management derived from them. In this study, our aim is to address this challenge by investigating the following research questions: RQ 1: How can LLMs be effectively aligned with semantically rich data about daily individual activities? RQ 2: What are the effective strategies for achieving reliable and meaningful activity generation using LLM agents? RQ 3: What are the potential applications of LLM agents in enhancing urban mobility analysis?

title: Large Language Models as Urban Residents: An LLM Agent Framework for Personal Mobility Generation
heading: Introduction
text:
To this end, our study employs LLM agents to infer activity patterns and motivation for personal activity generation tasks. While previous researches advocate habitual activity patterns and motivations as two critical elements for activity generation [17,43], our proposed framework introduces a more interpretable and effective solution. By leveraging the capabilities of LLMs to process semantically rich datasets (e.g., personal check-in data), we enable a nuanced and interpretable simulation of personal mobility. Our methodology revolves around two phases: (1) activity pattern identification and (2) motivation-driven activity generation. In Phase 1, we leverage the semantic awareness of LLM agents to extract and identify self-consistent, personalized habitual activity patterns from historical data. In Phase 2, we develop two interpretable retrieval-augmented strategies that utilize the patterns identified in Phase 1. These strategies guide LLM agents to infer underlying daily motivations, such as evolving interests or situational needs. Finally, we instruct LLM agents to act as urban residents according to the obtained patterns and motivations. In this way, we generate their daily activities in a specific reasoning logic.
We evaluate the proposed framework using GPT-3.5 APIs over a personal activity trajectory dataset of Tokyo. The results demonstrate the capability of our framework to align LLM agents with semantically rich data for generating individual daily activities. The comparison with baselines, such as attention-based methods [8,22], adversarial learning methods [6,42], and a diffusion model [46], underscores the advanced generative performance of our framework. The observation also suggests that our framework excels in reproducing temporal and spatio-temporal aspects of personal mobility generation and interpretable activity routines. Moreover, the application of the framework in simulating urban mobility under specific contexts, such as a pandemic scenario, reveals its potential to adapt to external factors and generate realistic activity patterns.

heading: Methodology / Activity Pattern Identification
text:
To construct a pipeline for activity trajectory generation, we design an LLM agent with action, memory, and planning [33,32]. Action specifies how an agent interacts with the environment and makes decisions. In LLMob, the environment contains the information collected from real-world data, and the agent acts by generating trajectories. Memory includes past actions that need to be prompted to the LLM to invoke the next action. In LLMob, memory refers to the patterns and motivations output by the agent. Planning formulates or refines a plan over past actions to handle complex tasks, with additional information optionally incorporated as feedback. In LLMob, we use planning to identify patterns and motivations, thereby handling the complex task of trajectory generation. Plan formulation, selection, reflection, and refinement [14] are employed in succession, and the agent keeps updating the action plan based on its observation [41]: The agent first formulates a set of activity plans by extracting candidate patterns from historical trajectories in the database. The agent then performs self-reflection through a self-consistency evaluation to pick the best pattern from the candidate patterns. With historical trajectories further retrieved from the database, the agent refines the identified pattern to a summarized motivation of daily activity, which is then jointly used with the identified pattern for trajectory generation. In addition to the above agentic components, we also suggest the personas of the agent, which can facilitate the LLM to simulate the diversity of real-world individuals [29].

text: This step derives activity patterns based on activity trajectory data (e.g., individual check-in data). As illustrated in the left panel of Figure 2, this scheme consists of the following aspects: For each person, we start by specifying a candidate personas to the LLM agent, providing the inspiring foundation for subsequent activity pattern generation. This approach also encourages the diversity of the generated activity patterns, as each candidate persona acts as a unique prior for the generation process (e.g., the significance of user clustering from activity trajectory data in producing meaningful distinctions has been demonstrated [24]). Meanwhile, we perform data preprocessing to extract key information from the extensive historical data. Moreover, we propose adding candidate personas to the prompt during candidate pattern generation to promote the diversity of the results. Without loss of generality, for each person, a set of C (C = 10) candidate patterns, denoted as CP, are generated according to the historical data and C candidate personas, respectively. We provide the details of these candidate personas in Appendix C.4.

text: Metrics. The following characteristics related to personal activity are used to examine the generation: (1) Step distance (SD) [42]: The travel distance between each consecutive decision step within a trajectory is collected. This metric evaluates the spatial pattern of an individual's activities by measuring the distance between two consecutive locations in a trajectory. (2) Step interval (SI) [42]: The time gap between each consecutive decision step within a trajectory is recorded. This metric evaluates the temporal pattern of an individual's activities by measuring the time interval between two successive locations on an individual's trajectory. (3) Daily activity routine distribution (DARD): For each decision step, a tuple (t, c) is created, where t represents the occurring time interval (e.g., from 0 to 144 in a day) and c identifies the activity category based on the location visited at that step. A histogram is then constructed to represent the distribution of the collected tuples. This feature presents the patterns of individual activities characterized by activity type and timing (e.g., activity type, time). It provides insight into how activities are distributed over space and time and reflects semantic information such as habitual behavior. (4) Spatial-temporal visits distribution (STVD): For each decision step, a tuple (t, latitude, longitude) is created, where t represents the occurring time interval (e.g., from 0 to 144 in a day) and latitude, longitude are the geographic coordinates of the location visited at that step. A histogram is subsequently built to represent the distribution of the collected tuples. This feature provides a granular perspective on the generated activities by assessing the spatial-temporal distribution of visited locations within each trajectory, including geographical coordinates and timestamps. It enables a detailed analysis of where and when activities occur.

This metric evaluates the spatial pattern of an individual's activities by measuring the distance between two consecutive locations in a trajectory. (2) Step interval (SI) [42]: The time gap between each consecutive decision step within a trajectory is recorded. This metric evaluates the temporal pattern of an individual's activities by measuring the time interval between two successive locations on an individual's trajectory. (3) Daily activity routine distribution (DARD): For each decision step, a tuple (t, c) is created, where t represents the occurring time interval (e.g., from 0 to 144 in a day) and c identifies the activity category based on the location visited at that step. A histogram is then constructed to represent the distribution of the collected tuples. This feature presents the patterns of individual activities characterized by activity type and timing (e.g., activity type, time). It provides insight into how activities are distributed over space and time and reflects semantic information such as habitual behavior. (4) Spatial-temporal visits distribution (STVD): For each decision step, a tuple (t, latitude, longitude) is created, where t represents the occurring time interval (e.g., from 0 to 144 in a day) and latitude, longitude are the geographic coordinates of the location visited at that step. A histogram is subsequently built to represent the distribution of the collected tuples. This feature provides a granular perspective on the generated activities by assessing the spatial-temporal distribution of visited locations within each trajectory, including geographical coordinates and timestamps. It enables a detailed analysis of where and when activities occur.

text:
After extracting the above characteristics from both the generated and real-world trajectory data, Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) is employed to quantify the discrepancy between them. Lower JSD is preferred.
Methods. LLMob is evaluated against: Markov-based mechanic model (MM) [27], an LSTM-based prediction model (LSTM) [12], two attention-based prediction models, including DeepMove [8] and STAN [22]. Within the domain of deep generative models, we select two adversarial learning frameworks, including TrajGAIL [6] and ActSTD [42], as well as a diffusion model, DiffTraj [46]. We use the source codes of the baselines provided by their respective authors and adapt them to our setting.
To achieve a balance between capability and cost efficiency, we employ GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 as the LLM core. We use "LLMob-E" to represent the proposal with the evolving-based motivation retrieval scheme, and "LLMob-L" to denote the framework that incorporates the learning-based motivation retrieval scheme (parameter settings in Appendix C.3). To validate the necessity of each module proposed, we conduct ablation studies with the following configurations: "LLMob w/o P" denotes the framework generating trajectories without using the pattern (i.e., directly summarizing motivations from past trajectories). "LLMob w/o M" denotes the framework without the motivation (i.e., directly generating trajectories with the identified pattern). "LLMob w/o SC" denotes the framework without the self-consistency evaluation (in this case, a candidate pattern is randomly picked as the identified pattern). Furthermore, "LLMob w/o P & M" represents the framework excluding both patterns and motivations.

heading: Main Results and Analysis
text:
Generative Performance Validation (RQ 1, RQ 2). The performance evaluation involves analyzing generation results in three distinct settings: (1) Generating normal trajectories based on normal historical trajectories in 2019, a period unaffected by the pandemic. (2) Generating abnormal trajectories based on abnormal historical trajectories in 2020, a year marked by the pandemic. (3) Generating abnormal trajectories in 2021 (pandemic) based on normal historical trajectories in 2019.
The results of these evaluations are detailed in the metrics reported in Table 2. Through the comparison, it can be observed that although LLMob may not excel in replicating spatial features (SD) precisely, it demonstrates superior performance in handling temporal aspects (DI). When considering spatial-temporal features (DARD and STVD), LLMob's performance is also competitive. In particular, LLMob achieves the best performance on DI and DARD for all three settings and is the runner-up on STVD. Baselines like DeepMove and TrajGAIL perform the best on SD and STVD, respectively, but become much less competitive when evaluated in other aspects. We suggest that the pronounced advantage of LLMob in terms of DARD (roughly 1/2 to 1/3 JSD compared to the best of baselines) can be attributed to the LLM agent's tendency to accurately replicate the motivation behind individual activity behaviors. For instance, an agent may recognize patterns like a person's habits to have breakfast in the morning, without being restricted to a specific restaurant. This phenomenon highlights the enhanced semantic understanding capabilities of the LLM agent.

heading: Main Results and Analysis
text: Exploring Utility in Real-World Applications (RQ 3). We are interested in how LLMob can elevate the social benefits, particularly in the context of urban mobility. To this end, we propose an example of leveraging the flexibility and intelligence of LLM agents in understanding semantic information and simulating an unseen scenario. In particular, we enhance the original setup by incorporating an additional prompt to provide a context for the LLM agent, enabling it to plan activities during specific circumstances. For example, a "pandemic" prompt is as follows: Now it is the pandemic period. The government has asked residents to postpone travel and events and to telecommute as much as possible. By integrating the above prompt, we can observe the impact of external elements, such as the pandemic and the government's measures, on urban mobility and related social dynamics. We use the activity trajectory data during the pandemic (2021) as ground truth and plot the daily activity frequency in 7 categories in Figure 4. TrajGAIL, despite delivering the best STVD in Table 2, displays very low frequencies for all the categories, and fails to reflect the tendency of each category. In contrast, a comparison between LLMob-L and the one augmented with the pandemic prompt demonstrates the impact of external factors: there is a significant decrease in activity frequency with the pandemic prompt, which semantically discourages activities likely to spread the disease (e.g., food).

text: Additionally, from a spatial-temporal perspective, two major activities (e.g., Arts & entertainment and Professional & other places) are selected to observe the behavior, as shown in Figures 5a and5b. These activities are particularly insightful as they encapsulate the impact of the pandemic on the work-life balance and daily routines of residents. Specifically, with the pandemic prompt, LLMob reproduces a more realistic spatial-temporal activity pattern. This enhanced realism in the generation is attributed to the integration of prior knowledge about the pandemic's effects and governmental responses, allowing the LLM agent to behave in a manner that aligns with actual behavioral adaptations. For instance, the reduction in Arts & entertainment activities reflects the closure of venues and social distancing guidelines, while changes in Professional & other places activities indicate shifts toward remote work and the transformation of professional environments. Intuitively, prompting the LLM agent to generate activities based on various priors shows great potential in real-world applications. The utility of such a conditioned generative approach, coupled with the reliable generated results, can significantly alleviate the workload of urban managers. We suggest that this kind of workflow can simplify the analysis of urban dynamics and aid in assessing the potential impact of urban policies.

Impact of Patterns. In Table 2, by comparing LLMob with and without using patterns ("w/o P"), we observe that the identified patterns consistently enhance the trajectory generation performance. The improvement on DARD is the most significant (reducing JSD by around 50%), showcasing the use of patterns is a key factor in capturing the semantics of daily activity. We provide example patterns in Appendix D.1 to show how the habitual behaviors of individuals are recognized by patterns.
Impact of Self-Consistency Evaluation. By comparing LLMob with and without self-consistency evaluation ("w/o SC") in Table 2, we find that self-consistency is useful in all aspects, and its impact is the most significant on DARD, especially when generating abnormal trajectories from normal data, showcasing its effectiveness in processing semantics. We also observe that "w/o SC" performs even worse than "w/o P" in many cases, because in "w/o SC", a candidate pattern is randomly picked for summarizing motivations, potentially introducing inconsistency to an individual's daily activity.
Impact of Motivations. We compare LLMob with and without motivations ("w/o M"). As can been seen in Table 2, the impact of motivations is similar to that of patterns. By comparing to LLMob with both patterns and motivations removed ("w/o P & M"), we observe that these two factors collectively lead to better performance. title: Large Language Models as Urban Residents: An LLM Agent Framework for Personal Mobility Generation
heading: Conclusion
text:
Contributions. This study is believed to be the first personal mobility simulation empowered by LLM agents on real-world data. Our innovative framework leverages activity patterns and motivations to direct LLM agents in emulating urban residents, facilitating the generation of interpretable and effective individual activity trajectories. Extensive experimental studies based on real-world data are conducted to validate the proposed framework and demonstrate the promising capabilities of LLM agents to improve urban mobility analysis. Social Impacts. Leveraging artificial intelligence to enhance societal benefits is increasingly promising, especially with the advent of high-capacity models such as LLMs. This study explores one of the potential avenues for applications using LLMs as reliable agents to simulate specific scenarios to assess the effects of external factors, such as pandemics and government policies. The introduced framework offers a flexible approach to enhance the reliability of LLMs in simulating urban mobility.
Limitations. In this study, we focused on modeling the activities of individual agents without considering interactions between them. As future work, we aim to extend this to a multi-agent scenario to capture interactions (e.g., where individuals may follow the activities of friends or family members). Given the challenges in collecting high-quality personal mobility data-many datasets lack completeness in capturing daily activities-we limited our comprehensive experimental evaluation to a single dataset. Furthermore, due to cost-efficiency considerations, only GPT-3.5 was fully evaluated. An additional analysis in a different city is provided in Appendix D.3, and Appendix D.4 includes supplementary evaluations using other LLMs. Student: typically travel to and from educational institutions at similar times.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: Abstract
text: Tool-using language-model agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because they must act on untrusted external content. Existing training-time defenses can reduce attack success rates, but often at the cost of general capabilities. We show that training-based defenses induce substantial drift in the model's output distribution, altering its behavior even in benign settings and providing a potential mechanism for utility degradation. We further identify a failure mode of these defenses: On benign tool-use tasks, the model refrains from a step needed to finish an authorized task, particularly when that step is indicated by a tool output. To address these limitations, we introduce RAISED (Robust Attack Invariance through SElf-Distillation), a training framework that combines self-generation and selfdistillation. The model first generates its own tool-use scenarios, with an emphasis on cases where task completion requires acting on legitimate guidance from tool outputs. Then, through self-distillation, the student is trained to match the teacher's clean-context behavior on both clean and injected variants of the same trajectory. RAISED substantially reduces the attack success rate of prompt injections in tool responses while, unlike prior training-based defenses, preserving utility on both agentic and general-purpose benchmarks.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
Tool-using LLM agents are deployed as browsing assistants, coding assistants, and enterprise copilots, connected to emails, documents, CRM systems, and other services through APIs or the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Yao et al. (2023); Schick et al. (2023); Qin et al. (2023); Zhou et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024a); Jimenez et al. (2024). Through these tools, agents process untrusted content from webpages, emails, documents and tool outputs. This exposes them to indirect prompt injection, where instructions hidden in that content hijack the agent away from its assigned task Greshake et al. (2023). Real-world attacks have already demonstrated this risk, including attacks that secretly extracted data from productivity tools Reddy & Gujral (2025) and manipulated MCP-based agents Beurer-Kellner & Fischer (2025); Wang et al. (2025). This growing threat has motivated a range of defenses, including prompting, filtering, and training-time alignment methods, all of which face a trade-off between robustness and utility Liu et al. (2024a): the model must resist adversarial instructions in untrusted tool outputs while still acting on the task-relevant guidance they may contain.
Training-based defenses aim to improve robustness while preserving benign behavior Chen et al. (2024;2025). However, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on targets drawn from an external source rather than the base model's own output distribution can shift the model away from its original behavior Yang et al. (2024). Preference-based defenses instead use direct preference optimization (DPO) to favor legitimate-task responses over responses to injected instructions Rafailov et al. (2024). Even when the preferred responses come from the original model, as in SecAlign++ (Chen et al., 2026), DPO optimizes them relative to rejected responses on contexts containing injections without directly matching the model's predictive distribution on clean contexts.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
Beyond general output-distribution drift, we identify a failure mode in training-based defenses: models execute benign tool-use tasks up to a point, then refrain from an authorized step that depends on guidance from a tool output. This leaves the task unfinished, even when the model is explicitly instructed to complete it end to end without further user involvement. The training objective creates an asymmetry: it consistently pushes the model away from responses that follow injected directions in tool outputs, while providing much less signal to follow legitimate actionable information from the same channel. The observed failures match a natural shortcut under this asymmetry: the model uses tool outputs as information but avoids acting on their guidance, even when doing so is necessary to complete the authorized task.
To address these limitations, we introduce RAISED, a framework combining self-generation and self-distillation. A frozen copy of the model being defended serves as both the data generator and the teacher, while a trainable copy serves as the student.
In the self-generation stage, the frozen model creates tool-use scenarios emphasizing cases where task completion requires acting on legitimate guidance from tool outputs. The same model generates both the clean task-solving trajectories and the injections for their tool outputs.
In the self-distillation stage, the student is trained on clean and injected contexts to match the teacher's next-token distribution on the corresponding clean context via KL divergence. On clean contexts, this limits output-distribution drift; on injected contexts, it trains the student to be insensitive to the injection while preserving legitimate tool-output guidance. Together, these target a model-relative robustness ideal: preserving the base model's behavior on clean contexts while recovering that behavior on their injected counterparts.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
We evaluate RAISED on general-knowledge, agentic-capability, and prompt-injection benchmarks across different models and compare against undefended agents, prompting, filtering, and alignmentbased defenses, measuring benign utility, utility under attack, and attack success rate (ASR). On AgentDojo with Gemma, RAISED reduces ASR from 39.5% to 1.0% and increases utility under attack from 64.0% to 80.5%, while losing only 1 point of benign utility. This matches the robustness of SecAlign++ without its 7-point drop.
Our contributions are threefold:
• We show that existing training-based defenses can induce output-distribution drift on benign settings and identify a behavioral failure mode in which defended models leave authorized tasks unfinished. • We introduce RAISED, a framework that combines self-generation and self-distillation to train models to resist prompt injections while preserving their behavior on benign tasks. • We show across three open-weight models and multiple general-knowledge, agenticcapability, and prompt-injection benchmarks that RAISED reduces attack success rates and improves utility under attack while preserving benign utility.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: RELATED WORK
text:
Indirect prompt injection. Instructions injected in content retrieved by an agent can be mistaken for legitimate user instructions (Greshake et al., 2023). This threat extends direct prompt injection (Perez & Ribeiro, 2022;Branch et al., 2022) to agents that retrieve untrusted content, including tool responses. Later work mapped this attack surface (Lee & Tiwari, 2024;Yu et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2025b;Wang et al., 2026) and developed benchmarks that plant injections in the tool outputs of interactive environments (Zhan et al., 2024;Debenedetti et al., 2024;Li et al., 2026).

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: Example
text:
Consistency training and self-distillation. Consistency training augments a prompt with irrelevant cues and trains the model to preserve its clean-prompt behavior; Chua et al. (2025) use it against biased chain-of-thought and Irpan et al. (2025) against sycophancy and jailbreaks, both on singleturn prompts. On-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024) provides dense per-token supervision along the student's own rollouts. Self-distillation uses a copy of the student as teacher, conditioned on privileged context: a document (Kujanpää et al., 2025), a verified reasoning trace (Zhao et al., 2026), a safety context (Fu et al., 2026), or a user's follow-up (Buening et al., 2026). Self-generated targets also limit fine-tuning forgetting (Yang et al., 2024). RAISED applies consistency training to multi-turn tool-use trajectories, where the injection sits inside a tool observation and legitimate guidance may share that channel. It distils off-policy from stored top-K teacher distributions along the clean continuation, and generates both its training scenarios and its attacks with the model being defended, including scenarios where completing the task requires acting on legitimate guidance returned through a tool.
Self-generated tool-use and adversarial data. Prior work has used language models to synthesize instruction data (Wang et al., 2023) and tool-use or function-calling data, including Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023), ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023), API-Gen (Liu et al., 2024b), and ToolACE (Liu et al., 2025a). APIGen and ToolACE additionally use execution-based checks to filter generated examples. RAISED applies model-based generation and execution-based validation to agent trajectories. Whereas prior injection-training pipelines rely on templated attacks (Chen et al., 2024;2025), RAISED has the defended model write its own injections, in an attacker role, after solving each scenario.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: AGENT SETTING
text:
A tool-using agent receives a system prompt, a user request u, and a menu of tools T . It acts in turns: at each turn it either calls a tool, which changes the environment state and returns an observation o j (a search result, an e-mail, an API response), or writes a final answer. The context c j seen by the model before turn j is the rendering of everything so far: system prompt, tool menu, user request, and the alternating actions and observations. The episode starts from an environment state s 0 , ends in a state s J , and succeeds if a success check G u (s J ) holds, i.e. if the request was actually fulfilled.
Observations are the only part of the context that comes from outside the agent's trust boundary. They may legitimately contain instructions ("to confirm, enter the code sent to your inbox"), so ignoring all instructions in tool outputs would amount to the tool-output distrust as a source of guidance failure mode described in Section 1. The formal definitions are given in Section A.

As discussed earlier, training-based prompt-injection defenses can alter benign behavior in two ways: by shifting the model's output distribution and by leaving tool-use tasks unfinished when completion depends on guidance from a tool output. We analyze these effects below.

heading: COST 1: OUTPUT-DISTRIBUTION DRIFT IN BENIGN SETTINGS
text:
To quantify the first utility cost, we conduct a controlled analysis on Gemma-4-12B-it using a heldout benign set of 500 standalone questions drawn from several general-purpose benchmarks. For each question, we generate the base model's answer and teacher-force that same answer through every trained checkpoint. We then compare the next-token distributions of the base model p θ0 and trained model p θ at each answer position. We report forward and reverse KL divergence,
(2) where H contains all evaluated answer prefixes. We also report top-1 agreement, the fraction of positions where the two models assign the highest probability to the same next token. The benignset construction and full measurement protocol are detailed in Section B.1.
To isolate the effect of the objective from that of the data, we evaluate SFT, DPO, and the selfdistillation objective used by RAISED under the same data and training setup, varying only the objective and its targets. All methods use 5K injection-augmented trajectories, rank-16 LoRA, and 313 training steps. Under this short, parameter-efficient training regime, SFT and DPO induce measurable output-distribution drift on the held-out benign set. As shown in Fig. 2, self-distillation yields forward and reverse KL of only 0.0010, respectively 44× and 55× lower than SFT and 29× and 30× lower than DPO, while reaching 0.993 top-1 agreement with the base model. Section B.1 provides the full controlled setup and shows that the drift increases with additional SFT and DPO training, while self-distillation remains close to the base distribution. While this analysis does not establish that output-distribution drift directly causes downstream utility loss, it shows that standard defensive training can substantially alter the model's behavior on benign inputs, identifying a potential contributor to utility degradation that self-distillation largely avoids.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: COST 2: BEHAVIORAL DRIFT IN BENIGN TOOL USE
text: Beyond output-distribution drift, defensive training can also change how the model acts on benign tool outputs. Figure 3 shows a representative example: the base model retrieves a verification code returned through the available tools and completes the authorized password change, whereas the defended model stops at that step and asks the user for the code despite being instructed to complete the task end to end. This behavior exposes a shortcut in defensive training: the optimization signal consistently pushes the model away from responses that follow injected directions in tool outputs, while providing much less signal for acting on legitimate guidance from the same channel. The observed failures follow this pattern: the model uses tool outputs as information while becoming reluctant to act on their guidance, leaving otherwise solvable tasks unfinished. Section B.2 provides additional examples across Gemma and Nemotron, including separate failures for SFT and SecAlign++, and shows that RAISED completes the corresponding tasks on which these defenses fail.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: RESULTS AND ANALYSIS / RAISED IMPROVES THE SECURITY-UTILITY TRADE-OFF
text:
We first evaluate RAISED on Gemma and Nemotron across prompt-injection robustness, benign agentic and general capabilities.
RAISED IMPROVES THE SECURITY-UTILITY TRADE-OFF. Table 1 reports results on InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and AgentDyn. We consider attack success together with clean utility (U ) and utility under attack (U atk ), since a defense can obtain a low ASR simply by making the agent less likely to act.
On Gemma, RAISED reduces AgentDojo ASR from 39.5% to 1.0 ± 0.3% while preserving clean utility (84.5% vs. 83.5 ± 0.8% for Vanilla). Compared with SecAlign++, RAISED achieves similar robustness while retaining substantially more utility, particularly on AgentDyn, where clean utility is 60.0 ± 2.4% versus 45.6 ± 0.8% for SecAlign++. RAISED also substantially improves U atk , reaching 80.5 ± 0.5% on AgentDojo compared with 64.0% for Vanilla. Nemotron shows a complementary pattern: RAISED improves robustness over SecAlign++, at matched or higher clean utility. AgentDojo ASR falls to 0.5 ± 0.1% versus 4.0 ± 0.7% for Se-cAlign++, while AgentDyn ASR falls to 1.9 ± 0.6% versus 7.8 ± 0.3%. Clean utility remains close to the Vanilla checkpoint, including 25.0% on AgentDyn.
For SecAlign++, we report the 313-step checkpoint, chosen to avoid substantial utility degradation.
Longer training can further reduce ASR, but at the cost of broader capability degradation, Appendix D.8 reports the training-step trade-off.
The filtering baseline further shows why ASR should not be interpreted in isolation. On Gemma AgentDojo, PromptGuard2 lowers ASR from 39.5% to 16.1%, but U atk falls from 64.0% to 42.9%. RAISED instead reduces ASR to about 1% while increasing U atk to 80.5 ± 0.5%.

heading: RAISED PRESERVES BENIGN AGENTIC CAPABILITIES
text:
Table 2 reports performance on five benign tool-use benchmarks.
On Gemma, RAISED preserves benign tool-use performance across all five benchmarks. The largest change is on WorkBench, where performance increases from 55.9 to 61.5 ± 0.7, while BFCL and MMT-Bench remain essentially unchanged. A plausible explanation is that RAISED repeatedly trains on verified multi-step trajectories that require maintaining state and completing sequences of interdependent actions, which closely matches the type of task evaluated by WorkBench. Although we do not isolate this effect causally, the result suggests that robustness training can reinforce some forms of multi-step tool use rather than merely preserve them.
Nemotron shows slightly more variation, but only modest overall changes: RAISED improves BFCL from 30.0 to 32.8 ± 0.2, remains close to Vanilla on WorkBench and MMT-Bench, and incurs only moderate decreases on ToolTalk and AsyncTool. This contrasts with some inference-time defenses. RAISED preserves general capabilities across all ten benchmarks for Gemma and Nemotron (Table 3), with scores close to the Vanilla checkpoints and no systematic degradation. Variations are small and mixed in sign, indicating that the gains in prompt-injection robustness do not come at the cost of general or benign agentic capabilities. title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: CONCLUSION
text: We introduced RAISED, a self-distillation defense that trains the model to be invariant to prompt injection. The model generates its own tool-use scenarios and injections, including cases where completing the task requires acting on legitimate guidance from a tool output, and learns to match its clean-context next-token distributions on injected contexts. RAISED matches or exceeds the robustness of SecAlign++ while better preserving benign utility, and induces far less distribution drift than SFT or DPO. More broadly, when the desired behavior already exists in the clean model, defensive training should preserve it under attack rather than learn a new defensive policy. Since RAISED preserves the base model's behavior rather than improving it, it also inherits its errors; we discuss this and other limitations in Section G, and broader impact in Section H.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: ETHICS STATEMENT
text: This work studies defenses against indirect prompt injection in tool-using language-model agents. Because the evaluation and training procedures include the generation and execution of adversarial prompt injections, the techniques described in this paper have potential dual-use implications. Our intent is to improve the robustness and reliability of language-model agents operating over untrusted external content. The attacks considered in this work are evaluated in controlled benchmark environments and are used to measure and strengthen defensive behavior. RAISED should be viewed as a defense-in-depth mechanism and not as a substitute for established safeguards such as access control, sandboxing, capability restriction, and least-privilege tool design.

Longer Scope of the evidence. These examples are intended to characterize the failure mode rather than estimate its prevalence. We include a broad set of standard agentic benchmarks to support comparable evaluation of benign tool-use utility across defenses, but those benchmarks are not constructed to isolate this particular behavior. The interaction pattern itself is important in realistic tool use: a tool output may surface a verification requirement, corrected retry target, prerequisite, or followup action that is necessary to complete the user's authorized task. AgentDojo contains such cases, and AgentDyn more directly includes helpful third-party guidance that the agent may need to act on. Our examples show that training-based defenses can fail on this class of interaction, but they do not establish how frequently such cases arise in deployed systems. Estimating their real-world prevalence would require deployment data beyond the scope of our evaluation. Nevertheless, these interactions represent plausible and operationally important workflows, since failing to act on the returned guidance can leave an authorized task incomplete. A broader quantitative evaluation of both the prevalence of these cases and defense behavior on them remains important future work.

heading: C.2 SPOTLIGHTING
text: Spotlighting is a family of prompt-engineering defenses that transforms untrusted text to help the model distinguish it from trusted instructions Hines et al. (2024). We use its delimiting variant, following the spotlighting_with_delimiting implementation evaluated in Agent-Dojo Debenedetti et al. (2024). We append an instruction to the system prompt explaining that tool outputs will appear between « and » and that instructions within these delimiters must not be followed. Every tool response is then wrapped with these markers, as illustrated in Figure 5. The transformation is applied independently to each new tool response and requires no fine-tuning or auxiliary model.

heading: C.3 PROMPTGUARD2
text:
Prompt Guard 2 is an 86M-parameter classifier developed by Meta to detect prompt injections and jailbreaks Chennabasappa et al. (2025). Following the implementation from AgentDyn Li et al.
(2026), we apply the classifier independently to every new tool response and classify it as an injection when its safety score is below 0.5. Responses classified as safe are left unchanged, while flagged responses are replaced in full by "<Data omitted because a prompt injection was detected>" before being passed to the agent, as illustrated in Figure 6. Unlike the previous prompting defenses, this method removes suspicious content from the model's context but requires running an auxiliary classifier after each tool call.
C.4 SECALIGN++ SecAlign++ (Chen et al., 2026) is the closest training-based baseline to RAISED. It refines SecAlign (Chen et al., 2025) with three changes. First, the chat template gains a dedicated role for untrusted content, so that the model can learn to follow instructions from the system and user roles while treating text in that role as data. Second, training-time injections are placed before or after the clean input at random, rather than always appended to it, which prevents the model from learning a positional shortcut. Third, the preferred response in each preference pair is the undefended model's own response to the clean instruction alone, so that the target is in-distribution for the model being trained, whereas the rejected response is the undefended model's own response to the injected instruction alone, both sampled independently rather than produced within a single shared context. The model is then trained with DPO on these pairs, using LoRA.

Third, the preferred response in each preference pair is the undefended model's own response to the clean instruction alone, so that the target is in-distribution for the model being trained, whereas the rejected response is the undefended model's own response to the injected instruction alone, both sampled independently rather than produced within a single shared context. The model is then trained with DPO on these pairs, using LoRA.

text:
Adaptation to tool use. The original recipe targets single-turn instruction following, with the untrusted content held in a single input message. We adapt it to the agentic setting at inference time by rendering tool-response messages with the input role of the SecAlign template, so that the model applies the learned trust boundary to real tool output.
The preference data follow the original SecAlign++ recipe: pairs are constructed from the Cleaned-Alpaca instruction set (Ruebsamen, 2023), and therefore contain no tool calls or tool responses. SecAlign++ is nevertheless evaluated by its authors on AgentDojo and other agentic benchmarks, relying on the learned trust boundary to transfer from single-turn untrusted inputs to tool outputs. We preserve this training setup for the method-level comparison. Our ablation in Section E separately evaluates the SecAlign++ DPO objective on agentic trajectories while controlling the training data and input representation.

text: Hyperparameters. We fine-tune with DPO (β = 0.1) and LoRA (rank 16, α = 32, applied to the query, key, value and output projections) for one epoch over 5,008 examples subsampled from Cleaned-Alpaca (313 steps at batch size 16), with a constant learning rate of 2 × 10 -5 and no warm-up, in bfloat16 on one GB200 GPU per run; training is repeated over three seeds. This is a considerably smaller budget than the original recipe, which trains for several epochs over the full 51K-example set, and matches the budget of the controlled comparison in Section 4.1; the 625-step checkpoint of Section D.8 uses the same 10K-example training budget as RAISED. We use the 313-step checkpoint in the main comparison as a common operating point on the robustness-utility trade-off. On Gemma, SecAlign++ already reaches near-zero ASR on InjecAgent and AgentDojo at this budget and further training primarily reduces utility without materially improving robustness. title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: C.5 RAISED -ROBUST ATTACK INVARIANCE THROUGH SELF-DISTILLATION C.5.1 SELF-GENERATION DETAILS
text:
Overview. Self-generation uses independent calls to the same frozen checkpoint p θ0 for scenario generation, task solving, and attack generation; no model state is carried between these calls. The scenario generator first creates an executable tool-use task. A separate call to the frozen model then solves and validates the task through its standard tool-use interface, after which additional calls generate prompt injections for selected tool outputs. Each model family generates and solves its own scenarios using the same generation procedure. Generation continues until 10,000 validated trajectories are retained for each model.
Executable scenario generation. The scenario generator produces a world state represented as JSON, a user request, an executable success check, and a menu of 3-6 tools. Each tool has a model-visible name, description, and argument schema, together with a deterministic Python implementation that reads or updates the shared world state. The implementation is executed in a sandbox and is never exposed to the agent. Generated tools and schemas are validated before rollout to ensure that they can be executed consistently.
The user request specifies an end goal rather than an explicit sequence of tool calls. The generator is prompted toward tasks requiring several dependent calls, typically 3-8, so that information obtained earlier in the trajectory is needed to make progress later. Tool menus similarly contain complementary capabilities rather than multiple near-duplicate operations.
Failure-focused structures. A central goal of self-generation is to increase the number of benign tasks in which legitimate guidance returned through a tool must determine what the agent does next. We therefore guide generation toward three high-level structures that directly target the behavioral drift identified in Section 4.2. These structures specify the dependency that should be present while leaving the domain, tools, entities, records, and concrete interaction to the generating model.

heading: Follow-through
text:
Derived-value scenarios require a later answer or tool argument to be computed from quantities returned by earlier tools rather than copied directly from an observation. For action tasks, the computed value must be used in a subsequent tool call; for read-only tasks, it must appear in the final answer. The expected value is recomputed independently during verification. Eligible scenarios can additionally span multiple interaction turns with a changing tool menu: an initial set of tools supports discovery or preparation, after which an additional capability becomes available while preserving the same world state and user goal.
Sampling and structural coverage. The structural requirements are sampled before scenario generation and determine which high-level constraints are included in the generation prompt. Compatible requirements can be active in the same scenario. Their sampling probabilities therefore control how often a structure is requested, not how often it appears in the final training corpus: after generation, the scenario must still be solved successfully and pass the common execution-based and structure-specific verification pipeline.
Different structures survive this pipeline at different rates. To calibrate the sampling probabilities, for each structure and each model family we run 50 pilot generations with that structure activated while the other compatible structures follow their normal sampling procedure, and measure the fraction ultimately retained after solving and verification. We use these empirical keep rates to choose one set of sampling probabilities, shared across model families, that gives the active structures a reasonably balanced presence in the retained corpora.
Surfaced guidance and recovery/completion are sampled with probability 0.40, follow-through with 0.35, read-and-report and clarification with 0.25 each, and derived-value tasks with 0.15.
The changing-tool-menu structure is applied whenever an eligible scenario is generated. Within surfaced-guidance cases, injection-like surface phrasing is sampled with probability 0.30.

Diversity across generated scenarios. The structural requirements specify properties of the interaction rather than complete task templates. To vary their concrete realization, the scenariogeneration prompt is additionally varied along several dimensions independently of the selected structures. We sample cues for the application domain, concrete entities and attributes, tool capabilities, and the dependency shape connecting successive operations. These cues guide generation but do not fix the resulting task: the model may replace, combine, or extend them while satisfying the requested structural constraints.
As a result, the same high-level structure can be instantiated with different domains, records and entities, tool menus, and patterns of dependency between calls. Scenario generation uses temperature 0.9.

heading: Solve and validate.
text:
A separate call to the same frozen model receives the generated user request and model-visible tool schemas and attempts to complete the task through its standard tool-use interface using greedy decoding. Each emitted tool call is executed against the shared world state, its actual output is returned to the model, and state mutations persist across subsequent calls. The rollout continues until the model produces a final answer or reaches the execution limit.
Generated scenarios are filtered before entering the training corpus. Tool implementations and schemas must be executable and internally consistent, and the resulting trajectory must satisfy its generated success criterion. For state-changing tasks, the success check evaluates the resulting world state and is required to fail on the initial state and pass on the final state, preventing already-satisfied tasks from being retained. For read-only tasks, completion is instead verified from the model's final answer. Scenarios that cannot be executed consistently or remain incomplete after rollout are discarded. Structure-specific checks additionally verify that the dependency requested during generation is actually realized in the resulting task.
Attack generation. Attack generation is performed only after a clean trajectory has been successfully solved and verified. For each retained scenario, a separate generation step produces a concrete adversarial objective appropriate to the scenario and, when needed, plausible in-domain attacker tools that make the objective executable. Any attacker tools are included in both the clean and injected contexts, so their presence alone does not distinguish the injected example.

For each selected output, the injection writer receives the clean tool output, the adversarial objective, the available tool schemas, any attacker tools, and any injections already placed earlier in the same trajectory. The writer generates the adversarial text and chooses its placement within the selected output, either embedding it in an existing string field or placing it before or after the original content. heading: Solve and validate.
text: Training configuration. The student is initialized from the same checkpoint as the frozen generator and teacher. We train it with LoRA applied to all linear layers, using a learning rate of 5 × 10 -5 and batch size 16 for one epoch on the 10, 000 generated cases, with an injection ratio of 0.5. Training uses the injection-augmented self-distillation objective described in Section 5. We deliberately selected models with substantially different architectures to test whether RAISED depends on a particular transformer design. Gemma-4-12B-it uses a dense architecture combining sliding-window and full-attention layers, whereas Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B uses a hybrid architecture that combines attention, Mamba-style state-space layers, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) blocks. Qwen3.8-27B provides a third configuration, interleaving linear-attention and full-attention layers. This diversity allows us to evaluate whether the proposed self-distillation objective transfers across different sequence-modeling mechanisms and parameter-routing strategies, rather than being specific to a single model architecture.

heading: D.3 GENERAL-KNOWLEDGE EVALUATION
text:
We evaluate general knowledge and related capabilities to measure whether the defense methods preserve broad knowledge and general problem-solving capabilities.
LM Evaluation Harness. We use the LM Evaluation Harness Gao et al. (2021) for all reported general-knowledge evaluations. For each benchmark, we report the group-level metric produced by LM Evaluation Harness. Group metrics are micro-averaged over evaluation samples, such that every question, prompt, or programming problem receives equal weight.
MMLU. MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2020) evaluates broad knowledge and reasoning through multiple-choice questions spanning 57 subjects across the humanities, social sciences, STEM, and professional domains. We report accuracy, where a response is correct when the answer option assigned the highest likelihood matches the reference option.
MMLU-Pro. MMLU-Pro Wang et al. (2024b) evaluates more challenging, reasoning-intensive multiple-choice questions organized into broad subject categories. We report exact-match accuracy after applying the benchmark's answer-extraction procedure to the generated response.
Multilingual MMLU. Multilingual MMLU (OpenAI, 2025) evaluates knowledge and reasoning across multiple languages and subject areas using multilingual versions of MMLU-style multiplechoice questions. We report accuracy, where a response is correct when the answer option assigned the highest likelihood matches the reference option.
GPQA Diamond. GPQA Diamond Rein et al. (2023) is a particularly challenging subset of GPQA consisting of expert-written questions in biology, physics, and chemistry that are designed to require domain expertise and resist superficial answer retrieval. We report exact-match accuracy using the benchmark's flexible answer-extraction procedure, which extracts the selected answer option from the generated response.
AGIEval English. AGIEval English Zhong et al. (2024) evaluates general and professional reasoning on English-language examination questions drawn from several standardized and professional examinations. We report accuracy, where a response is correct when the predicted answer matches the reference answer.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.4 AGENTIC-CAPABILITY EVALUATION
text:
We evaluate agentic capabilities to measure whether the defense methods preserve the models' ability to use tools and complete tasks in interactive environments. For each agentic-capability benchmark, we report the micro-averaged success rate over its elementary evaluation units, such that every conversation, multi-turn entry, workplace task, mission, or subtask receives equal weight.
ToolTalk. ToolTalk Farn & Shin (2023) evaluates an assistant's ability to use APIs correctly in multi-turn conversations. Conversations require the model to select appropriate tools, provide the required arguments, and execute sequences of tool calls as the interaction evolves; the benchmark includes 28 tools grouped into seven application domains. We report conversation success rate. A conversation is successful when the model recalls every reference tool call and makes no incorrect action-tool call over the complete conversation.
BFCL Multi-Turn. The Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) Patil et al. ( 2025) evaluates function-calling capabilities across a broad range of tool-use settings. We evaluate its multi_turn_base subset, in which each entry may require multiple turns and multiple tool calls against a stateful environment. We report entry-level accuracy: an entry is correct only if the model's tool calls across all turns satisfy BFCL's official multi-turn checker, including selection of the required functions and construction of valid arguments.
WorkBench. WorkBench Styles et al. (2024) evaluates whether language-model agents can complete realistic workplace tasks by interacting with software tools in a sandboxed environment. Tasks include activities such as sending emails and scheduling meetings and often require planning and executing multiple tool calls that modify the underlying environment state. We report task-completion accuracy. A task is successful when the model's executed actions leave the sandbox in the reference final state.
