title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.5 AGENTIC PROMPT-INJECTION EVALUATION
text:
Agentic prompt-injection evaluation is central to this work, as it measures whether a model can resist malicious instructions embedded in tool outputs while still completing the user's intended task. We evaluate this security-utility trade-off using benchmarks that combine interactive tool use, adversarially injected instructions, and task-level success criteria. For each benchmark, we follow its official aggregation convention. InjecAgent and AgentDojo aggregate over their benchmark-defined evaluation cases, so that each test case (or sampled attack, where applicable) receives equal weight. AgentDyn instead first computes each metric separately for its Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life suites and reports the unweighted mean of the three suite-level scores.
InjecAgent. InjecAgent Zhan et al. ( 2024) evaluates the vulnerability of tool-integrated agents to indirect prompt injections embedded in external content such as emails or webpages. Its 1,054 test cases span 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools, with malicious instructions designed either to cause direct harm to the user or to exfiltrate private information observed by the agent during task execution. The agent must continue carrying out the benign user request while ignoring the injected objective. We report total attack success rate separately for the Base and Enhanced settings. In direct-harm cases, an attack succeeds when the agent calls the attacker's target tool; in data-stealing cases, it succeeds when the agent completes both stages and supplies the targeted private information to that tool.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.5 AGENTIC PROMPT-INJECTION EVALUATION
text:
AgentDojo. AgentDojo Debenedetti et al. (2024) evaluates agents on realistic tool-use tasks in domains such as workspace management, online banking, travel booking, and messaging. Prompt injections are placed in untrusted data returned by tools, for example in emails, documents, or other environment content, and attempt to redirect the agent toward a separate attacker-specified goal, such as leaking information or performing an unauthorized action. The benchmark jointly measures whether the agent completes the original user task and whether the injected attacker objective succeeds. We report clean utility (U ), the fraction of benign user tasks completed without an attack; utility under attack (U atk ), the fraction of security cases in which the original user task is completed; and targeted attack success rate (ASR), the fraction of security cases in which the attacker's objective is achieved.
AgentDyn. AgentDyn Li et al. (2026) extends agentic prompt-injection evaluation to more openended and dynamically planned tasks across Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life scenarios. Its tasks require longer-horizon interaction and may contain legitimate third-party instructions that the agent should follow, making it necessary to distinguish helpful external instructions from malicious injections. Adversarial instructions are embedded in third-party content encountered during the trajectory and attempt to divert the agent from the user's intended objective while it continues interacting with the environment. We report clean utility (U ), the fraction of user tasks completed without an attack; utility under attack (U atk ), the fraction of attacked cases in which the original user task is completed; and attack success rate (ASR), the fraction of attacked cases in which the malicious objective is achieved.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.6 QWEN: ADDITIONAL LOW-ASR STRESS TEST
text: Qwen provides an additional stress test in a different robustness regime from the primary experiments. Its Vanilla checkpoint already exhibits low attack success rates on AgentDojo and AgentDyn, allowing us to test whether RAISED remains effective when the starting model is already comparatively resistant to prompt injection. We evaluate the same three dimensions as in the main paper: prompt-injection robustness, benign agentic capabilities, and general capabilities. Despite the already low ASR of the Vanilla checkpoint, RAISED further reduces attack success on both AgentDojo and AgentDyn. The improvement is therefore not restricted to models that are initially highly vulnerable to prompt injection, and persists in a low-ASR regime. The additional robustness is not obtained by reducing benign tool-use capability. RAISED remains close to the Vanilla checkpoint across all five agentic benchmarks, confirming the preservation trend observed on Gemma and Nemotron. Finally, the general-capability evaluation shows the same preservation pattern. RAISED remains close to the Vanilla checkpoint across the benchmark suite while achieving the additional robustness reported above. Taken together, the Qwen results show that RAISED remains effective even when applied to a model that already starts from a low-ASR regime.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.7 LOOKING INSIDE THE MODEL
text:
RAISED trains the model to match its clean-context behavior when an injection is added. We therefore ask whether the trained model shows less internal sensitivity to the injection while remaining close to the base model on clean inputs.
We evaluate this on 88 clean/injected context pairs from AgentDojo. For each pair, we run the base model on the clean context to obtain its continuation y ⋆ , then compare model states while reading the clean and injected contexts followed by the same continuation. At each of the 48 decoder blocks, we measure the injection-induced change in the hidden state, as well as the distance between each trained model and the base model on the clean context. The injection produces a similar pattern across models in the early blocks, followed by a peak around block 31. At that block, the relative L 2 change is 0.45 for the base model, compared with 0.23 for RAISED. This reduction goes with the behavioral check: RAISED starts the injected tool call in 12.5% of the checked pairs, versus 62.5% for the base model.
RAISED also remains closer to the base model on clean contexts than SecAlign++ (0.12 vs. 0.19 at block 47). Thus, the internal-state measurements are consistent with the intended behavior of the objective: reduce sensitivity to injected content while limiting changes to clean-context behavior.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.8 SECALIGN++ TRAINING-STEP TRADE-OFF
text:
The SecAlign++ results reported in the main paper use checkpoints obtained after 313 training steps. The effect of extending training differs across model families. On Gemma and Qwen, further training primarily reduces utility without materially improving robustness. On Nemotron, it further reduces attack success but comes with substantial utility degradation. We use Nemotron below as a representative illustration because the trade-off is particularly clear. We compare the 313-step checkpoint used in the main paper with the same model trained for 625 steps, and include both the Vanilla checkpoint and RAISED as reference points.
Table 12 shows that additional SecAlign++ training continues to improve robustness. On Agent-Dojo, ASR decreases from 4.0 ± 0.7% at 313 steps to 0.7 ± 0.0% at 625 steps, while on AgentDyn it decreases from 7.8 ± 0.3% to 3.0 ± 0.2%. Thus, considering the security benchmarks alone would suggest that further training is beneficial. This security improvement, however, does not correspond to a uniformly better checkpoint. Table 13 shows the same models on the general-capability evaluation. While the 313-step checkpoint already departs from Vanilla on some tasks, extending training to 625 steps amplifies this drift on several benchmarks. In particular, MMLU decreases from 48.3 ± 0.7 to 42.8 ± 0.3, GPQA from 43.8 ± 1.7 to 39.4 ± 1.1, Minerva Math from 75.0 ± 0.1 to 66.1 ± 0.9, and MBPP from 64.6 ± 1.0 to 13.4 ± 2.7. By contrast, RAISED remains close to the Vanilla checkpoint across the same evaluation suite.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: D.8 SECALIGN++ TRAINING-STEP TRADE-OFF
text:
The benign agentic benchmarks show a milder version of the same effect. For Nemotron, extending SecAlign++ training from 313 to 625 steps reduces ToolTalk from 43.2 ± 0.6 to 42.7 ± 0.6, BFCL from 33.0 ± 0.4 to 31.8 ± 0.8, MMT-Bench from 43.4 ± 0.3 to 41.9 ± 0.3, and AsyncTool from 34.5 ± 0.3 to 32.3 ± 0.8, while WorkBench increases. The main effect of prolonged training is therefore not a uniform collapse of agentic performance, but a broader and increasingly uneven drift away from the capabilities of the original checkpoint.
These results explain our choice of the 313-step SecAlign++ checkpoint for the main comparison.
SecAlign++ can be trained longer to obtain lower ASR, but selecting a checkpoint solely according to attack success can conceal substantial degradation elsewhere. The same qualitative trainingduration trade-off is observed for Gemma and Qwen, although the magnitude and affected capabilities differ across models. Nemotron provides a particularly clear illustration of this phenomenon. In contrast, RAISED reaches low attack success while remaining substantially closer to the capability profile of the original model.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: F ADAPTIVE ATTACKS
text: Our threat model considers static indirect prompt injections, in which the adversarial content is chosen independently of the defended model (Section 3.2). This setting matches the evaluation protocol of InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and AgentDyn, and is the setting for which the robustness claims in this work are made. In contrast, an adaptive attacker repeatedly queries a particular defended model and optimizes the injected content against its observed behavior. Such attacks grant the adversary an additional capability and evaluate a distinct question: whether a defense remains robust when the adversary can specialize its attack to that defense. We nevertheless investigated this stronger setting using PISmith (Yin et al., 2026), a recent black-box framework that optimizes prompt injections against the target model. Using the authors' released code and protocol, however, the optimization reward remained identically zero for most model-defense configurations. Consequently, the optimizer received no signal with which to distinguish or improve candidate attacks. This is consistent with the reward-sparsity regime discussed by PISmith, but, importantly, a failed optimization run is not evidence of adaptive robustness. We therefore do not report these runs as a robustness result. Obtaining a more informative signal would require modifying PISmith's protocol, which falls outside the scope of this work. We thus restrict our empirical robustness claims to the static threat model defined in Section 3.2. Robustness to model-adaptive prompt injection remains an open question.

In contrast, an adaptive attacker repeatedly queries a particular defended model and optimizes the injected content against its observed behavior. Such attacks grant the adversary an additional capability and evaluate a distinct question: whether a defense remains robust when the adversary can specialize its attack to that defense. We nevertheless investigated this stronger setting using PISmith (Yin et al., 2026), a recent black-box framework that optimizes prompt injections against the target model. Using the authors' released code and protocol, however, the optimization reward remained identically zero for most model-defense configurations. Consequently, the optimizer received no signal with which to distinguish or improve candidate attacks. This is consistent with the reward-sparsity regime discussed by PISmith, but, importantly, a failed optimization run is not evidence of adaptive robustness. We therefore do not report these runs as a robustness result. Obtaining a more informative signal would require modifying PISmith's protocol, which falls outside the scope of this work. We thus restrict our empirical robustness claims to the static threat model defined in Section 3.2. Robustness to model-adaptive prompt injection remains an open question.

title: RAISED: SELF-DISTILLATION FOR ROBUSTNESS TO PROMPT INJECTION IN LLM AGENTS
heading: G LIMITATIONS
text:
Model scale and diversity. We evaluate clean-context self-distillation on three model families with different tokenizers, post-training recipes, and baseline robustness. The consistency of the effect across Gemma, Nemotron and Qwen suggests that it is not specific to one family, and the objective itself makes no architecture-specific assumption. We have not yet evaluated additional model families or frontier models in the trillion-parameter regime, so whether the same securityutility behavior persists at that scale remains an empirical question.
Dependence on clean-model behavior. Clean-context self-distillation preserves the model's own behavior; it does not improve its correctness. If the clean model selects the wrong tool, follows a poor plan, hallucinates, or otherwise behaves undesirably, the distillation objective will preserve that behavior under injection rather than correct it. The quality of the defended model is therefore bounded by the quality of the clean-context teacher. The method should be understood as a defence against adversarial context influence, not as a general alignment or safety intervention.
Cost of soft self-distillation. Soft self-distillation requires an offline teacher pass and storage of truncated predictive distributions. For our 10,000-trace corpus, storing the top-256 teacher distributions requires approximately 15 GB per model, and teacher generation completes in well under one hour using eight parallel inference workers on our GB200 cluster. At frontier scale, the teacher pass becomes substantially more expensive: a model such as Kimi K3 activates roughly 104B parameters per token, approximately 4× to 9× the active parameter count of the dense models evaluated here.

text: Indirect prompt injection is a practical obstacle to deploying language-model agents over untrusted external content. title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Abstract
text:
Language model agents are increasingly effective in solving realistic tasks through multiturn tool use. However, training reliable toolusing agents remains challenging in practice.
While reinforcement learning provides an onpolicy paradigm for improving agents from their own environment interactions, its effectiveness depends heavily on the training task distribution. When tasks are fixed before training, the task distribution can become increasingly mismatched with the policy's evolving capabilities, causing many rollouts to be spent on uninformative tasks. We propose SENTINEL, a failure-driven reinforcement learning framework that turns the Solver's rollout failures into targeted training tasks. SENTINEL follows a Controller-Proposer-Solver loop: the Controller analyzes failed trajectories and summarizes recurring error patterns, the Proposer generates executable tasks that stress these weaknesses, and the Solver is trained on the targeted tasks. On Tau2-Bench Retail with Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, SENTINEL improves Passˆ1 from 66.4 to 74.9 and outperforms RL on general synthetic tasks across Passˆk metrics. These results demonstrate that model failures provide an effective and scalable source of targeted training signal for improving tool-using language model agents.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Introduction
text: Common approaches for training tool-use agents include supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning on synthetic trajectories and tasks. Supervised fine-tuning provides a direct way to teach agents tool-call formats, task procedures, and common execution patterns from carefully curated demonstrations (Prabhakar et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2026). However, it is inherently off-policy: the model learns to imitate trajectories produced by another policy rather than learning from the states induced by its own actions. Reinforcement learning offers an on-policy training paradigm (Qian et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025;Feng et al., 2025). By letting the policy model interact with an environment and generate its own tool-call trajectories, RL can pro-vide training signals on the states, decisions, and errors induced by the current policy itself. However, existing RL methods mostly rely on a static set of training tasks defined before training begins. The effectiveness of RL therefore depends heavily on whether these tasks expose failure modes that the current policy can meaningfully learn from. If the tasks are too easy, too hard, repetitive, or misaligned with the model's actual weaknesses, RL may waste rollouts or encourage superficial strategies that exploit artifacts of the reward or environment rather than improving robust tool-use behavior. This problem becomes more pronounced as the model improves, since a fixed task set can become increasingly mismatched with its changing weaknesses. This raises an important question: Can we construct RL training tasks that adapt to the current policy during learning?

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
We argue that failed trajectories provide a practical bridge between diagnosing model weakness and training. They reveal what the current policy has not learned yet, including wrong variant selection, missing steps, incorrect tool-call order, or failures to follow domain policies. Different from some self-play curriculum learning methods that primarily organize training around task difficulty (Zhao et al., 2025), we explicitly adapt task generation around the policy's diagnosed tool-use failure modes. Rather than treating failures only as evaluation errors, we use them as signals for generating on-policy training data. This perspective leads to a simple but powerful principle: tool-use agents could learn from the failures they actually make (Figure 1).
We propose SENTINEL, a failure-driven reinforcement learning pipeline for training tool-using LLM agents. SENTINEL organizes training as a Controller-Proposer-Solver loop. The Controller analyzes failed trajectories from the current solver policy and summarizes recurring error patterns. The diagnosed weaknesses are converted into explicit generation directives. The Proposer then synthesizes new executable tasks that specifically stress these weaknesses. Finally, the Solver performs reinforcement learning on the targeted tasks, producing an updated policy whose failures can be analyzed in the next iteration. This loop makes the model evolution controllable: the system can inspect what the model fails at, steer what data is generated next, and constrain RL optimization.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Tool-Using Language Model Agents and Benchmarks
text:
Recent work has extended large language models from text generation to interactive agents that can call external tools, query APIs, access databases, and act in executable environments. (Yao et al., 2022;Schick et al., 2023;Patil et al., 2024). For example, early agent frameworks such as ReAct combine reasoning traces with environment actions, enabling models to update their plans based on tool observations (Yao et al., 2022). Tool-learning methods further train models to decide when to call tools, which tools to use, how to form arguments, and how to use returned results in later reasoning (Schick et al., 2023;Patil et al., 2024). These advances make tool-using agents promising for practical applications such as customer service, reservation management, and workflow automation (Barres et al., 2025).
To evaluate models' tool-use capabilities, prior work has introduced a range of tool-use benchmarks. APIBank (Li et al., 2023), ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023), andBFCL (Patil et al., 2024) focus on API selection, argument construction, and executable function calling. More recent benchmarks move toward realistic multi-turn environments. The τ -Bench series (Yao et al., 2024;Barres et al., 2025) evaluates agents in simulated customerservice settings where models must interact with stateful tools, follow domain policies, and complete tasks over multi-turn dialogues. Recent MCPbased benchmarks, including MCP-Bench (Wang et al., 2025c), MCP-Atlas (Bandi et al., 2026), and MCPMark (Wu et al., 2025), further evaluate agents' ability to discover, select, and call tools through MCP servers in realistic tool-use settings.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Synthetic Data Generation for Tool Use
text:
Since large-scale human-annotated tool-use data are costly to collect, synthetic data generation has become a common strategy for training tool-using agents. Early general instruction-tuning work has shown that strong teacher models can generate training data at scale (Taori et al., 2023;Xu et al., 2024). In tool-use settings, ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) generates tool-calling demonstrations from tool descriptions, while APIGen-MT (Prabhakar et al., 2025) synthesizes multi-turn tool-use data in simulated environment. Recent work further scales synthetic data generation to richer MCP-based environments (Wang et al., 2025b;Xu et al., 2025;Bandi et al., 2026).
A key challenge in synthesizing tool-use data is verifiability: generated tasks should correspond to feasible tool-call paths with correct intermediate states and outcomes. Several recent methods address this issue by starting from executable trajectories rather than directly asking a model to generate both a task and its solution. Trajectory2Task (Wang et al., 2026) constructs valid tool-use trajectories first and then converts them into natural-language user tasks, ensuring each task state reachable and enabling complex user scenario construction. Similarly, Firefly (Lu et al., 2026) synthesizes verified tool-call data by first exploring real APIs and then generating tasks backward from observed tool-use outcomes. These synthetic data generation methods provide valuable resources for training tool-use agents, but they mainly generate broad task distributions. Building upon these works, our work generates tasks targeted to the current policy's observed failures, allowing the training distribution to adapt to the model's learning state.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Agentic Reinforcement Learning / Method
text:
Agentic reinforcement learning trains language model agents through multi-step interaction with executable environments, where a policy produces actions such as tool calls, observes environment feedback, and is optimized with task-level or process-level rewards (Qian et al., 2025;Li et al., 2025;Feng et al., 2025). Compared with supervised fine-tuning, which imitates trajectories generated by another policy, agentic RL allows the model to learn from the states induced by its own actions and from feedback returned by the environment (Li et al., 2025;Feng et al., 2025). This makes it a natural training paradigm for improving long-horizon tool use, multi-turn decision making, state tracking, and policy following.
Recent work has applied agentic RL across a range of interactive settings. For tool-use agents, ToolRL studies reward design for tool selection and tool application (Qian et al., 2025), while ToRL and ReTool train models to invoke computational tools during reasoning (Li et al., 2025;Feng et al., 2025). Beyond tool-integrated reasoning, RL has also been used for web and GUI agents (Qi et al., 2025), as well as online shopping and user-behavior simulation (Liu et al., 2026); for example, Shop-R1 introduces hierarchical rewards and difficultyaware scaling for action prediction in shopping environments (Zhang et al., 2025).

text:

Several methods study how to construct better reward signals, including tool-use rewards, hierarchical rewards, and step-wise process rewards for intermediate actions (Qian et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025;Wang et al., 2025a). Another line of work explores self-play or self-evolving training, in which the model acts both as a task generator and as a solver: it proposes new tasks, attempts to solve them, and uses the resulting trajectories or feedback for further training (Zhao et al., 2026;Huang et al., 2025;Zhou et al., 2026). The Proposer receives a Controller directive d t and generates a set of targeted RL tasks D t . Its goal is to produce tasks that satisfy two requirements: they should be executable in the tool environment, and they should stress the failure modes identified by the Controller.
Trajectory-grounded task construction. Inspired by prior work on trajectory-grounded data generation (Wang et al., 2026), the Proposer first constructs a feasible tool-use trajectory in the environment. It samples relevant environment states, including user profiles, order histories, and available tools. Given this grounded state, an LLM proposes a realistic user goal implicitly, explores the tool space, and produces a valid sequence of tool calls that completes the goal. Since the trajectory is executed in E, every intermediate state is reachable and tool output is grounded in the environment.
Failure-aware Task rewriting. Directly asking an LLM to generate both a task and its reference answer can lead to mismatches between the user request and the expected tool actions. It can also limit task difficulty to what the LLM can reliably specify in one pass. To reduce this issue, we decouple trajectory construction from task writing. After obtaining an executable reference trajectory τ ⋆ , the Proposer rewrites the trajectory into a naturallanguage user request x ⋆ conditioned on the Controller directive. The request is written from the user's perspective and preserves the goal and constraints implied by the trajectory, while hiding the solution path from the Solver. Since τ ⋆ is constructed and executed before the user request is written, it directly serves as the reference answer for the task. This makes the generated task selfconsistent: the user request is derived from a valid tool-call trajectory, rather than paired with a separately generated answer.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Proposer: Generating Failure-Targeted Tasks
text: The Controller directive conditions how the trajectory is rewritten to stress the Solver's observed errors. In the generation prompt, we explicitly require that "the scenario should specifically exercise the failure patterns identified," and provide several examples to guide the rewriting process. For example, when detecting item-grounding failures in customer service scenario, the Proposer rewrites the request to include similar product variants, overlapping item names, or fine-grained attributes such as size, color, or material. For execution-control failures, it creates requests that require asking a clarification question, waiting for user confirmation, or completing multiple dependent tool calls. Thus, the Proposer does not merely generate more tasks; it rewrites executable trajectories into tasks targeted to the Solver's current failure modes.

heading: Solver: RL Training on Targeted Tasks
text:
The Solver is the policy model being optimized. At each iteration, the Solver is trained with reinforcement learning on tasks sampled from the task buffer, which contains both the original training tasks and the failure-targeted tasks generated by the Proposer. As training proceeds, the Controller continuously injects synthetic tasks into the buffer, gradually shifting the training distribution toward the Solver's current weaknesses.

Each rollout is executed by the environment and scored by a reward function. The Solver is then updated with GRPO, which increases the likelihood of higher-reward trajectories relative to lowerreward trajectories.

Reward shaping. To reduce reward hacking, we add several shaping terms to the terminal tasksuccess reward. First, we use action-level check to evaluate whether intermediate tool calls satisfy task requirements, such as whether the model respects constraints before state-changing actions. This check help the Solver learn the correct execution path, instead of only optimizing for the final outcome. We further add penalties for degenerate tool-use behaviors observed during RL. The repeated tool-call penalty discourages consecutive tool calls that do not make meaningful state progress. The token-length penalty discourages unnecessarily long reasoning traces. The format penalty discourages malformed tool calls, invalid action formats. Together, these terms make the reward more informative and reduce shortcuts that can obtain reward without reliable task completion.
Iterative update. After the Solver is updated, the new policy π θ t+1 is rolled out again. Its new failures are passed back to the Controller, which updates the next generation directive. In this way, the Solver learns from the Proposer's generated tasks and produces the failures that guide future task generation.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Experimental Setup
text:
Benchmark and Evaluation metric. We instantiate the pipeline on Tau2-Bench Retail (Yao et al., 2024;Barres et al., 2025), a realistic executable benchmark for customer-service tool use. The retail domain requires agents to complete multi-turn, decision-making tasks such as order cancellation, product exchange, and return processing. These tasks require the agent to interact with the user simulator and the tools, reason over user information and order records, follow domain policies, and execute state-changing actions only when appropriate. Following Tau2-Bench, we report Passˆk. Passˆk measures the probability that all k repeated trials successfully complete the task.
Model. We use Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 as the base model and compare three training settings. Base directly evaluates the original model without additional task-specific training. General RL applies RL to the base model using pre-generated tasks from Trajectory2Task (Wang et al., 2026), which include different difficulty levels and diverse user scenarios in the retail domain. SENTINEL applies RL with our failure-driven task generation pipeline, where the Controller analyzes rollout failures and the Proposer generates targeted tasks for the Solver's current weaknesses.
To avoid leakage, the RL training environments use databases separated from the benchmark test environments. The tool schemas and policies are kept the same, while the users, orders, products, and environment states are different training and evaluation. For user simulator, we use SGLang to host the Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 model, and use a best-of-N (Prabhakar et al., 2025) sampling strategy for simulator responses.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Experimental Setup
text:
Experiment Settings We conduct RL training with the Slime framework. The actor is trained with GRPO, with Trajectory Importance Sampling (TIS), KL regularization coefficient 0.001, and a clipping range of 0.2 with a high clipping threshold of 0.28. For rollout, we use a rollout batch size of 16 and sample 8 responses per prompt. We also enable dynamic filtering, which removes prompt groups whose sampled responses receive all-zero or all-one rewards. This keeps batches with nontrivial reward differences and helps stabilize GRPO training. We train with Adam using a learning rate of 3 × 10 -6 , weight decay 0.005, β 1 = 0.9, and β 2 = 0.999. For failure-driven task generation, we trigger error analysis every 12 rollout batches, use a reward threshold of 0.5 to collect low-reward trajectories, and allow at most 10 new synthetic tasks per trigger.
For reward shaping, we add an action-level authentication check and several degeneration penalties. The action-level check verifies whether the agent completes policy-required authentication actions before state-changing tool calls; if missing, the reward is reduced by 0.5. We also apply a tool-format penalty of -0.1, a repeated-tool-call penalty of -0.15 for each consecutive identical tool call, and a length penalty of -0.0001 per ex-cess assistant token. These terms discourage policy violations, invalid tool calls, tool loops, and overly long responses.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Conclusion
text: We present SENTINEL, a failure-driven RL pipeline for improving tool-using agents. Instead of training on a fixed set of general tasks, SENTINEL uses the Solver's rollout failures to guide targeted task generation. The Controller identifies recurring error patterns, the Proposer turns them into executable tasks, and the Solver is trained on the resulting task buffer with RL. Experiments on Tau2-Bench Retail show that SENTINEL improves over both the base model and general-task RL, and remains effective when starting from a stronger SFT model. These results suggest that adapting RL data to the current model's weaknesses is a useful direction for training more reliable tool-using agents.

section: Conclusion (conclusion)

We present SENTINEL, a failure-driven RL pipeline for improving tool-using agents. Instead of training on a fixed set of general tasks, SENTINEL uses the Solver's rollout failures to guide targeted task generation. The Controller identifies recurring error patterns, the Proposer turns them into executable tasks, and the Solver is trained on the resulting task buffer with RL. Experiments on Tau2-Bench Retail show that SENTINEL improves over both the base model and general-task RL, and remains effective when starting from a stronger SFT model. These results suggest that adapting RL data to the current model's weaknesses is a useful direction for training more reliable tool-using agents.

title: SENTINEL: Failure-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Training Tool-Using Language Model Agents
heading: Limitations
text: Our work has several limitations. First, our experiments currently focus on Tau2-Bench Retail, a controlled executable domain for multi-turn customerservice tool use. This setting allows us to study failure-driven RL under stateful tools, policy constraints, and verifiable task outcomes. A natural next step is to apply the same pipeline to other tooluse domains with different environment dynamics and task structures. Second, SENTINEL generates tasks from observed rollout failures, so its coverage depends on what the current Solver exposes during training and how well the Controller can infer the skills required by the scenario. This makes the generated tasks well aligned with the model's current weaknesses, but it does not guarantee coverage of all foreseeable test cases, especially rare or under-sampled scenarios. Combining failuredriven generation with a small number of designed stress test directions may be a useful direction for improving coverage.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Abstract
text: Tool-using language-model agents select and execute third-party artifacts. Different implementations can return the requested output while producing hidden execution effects that task-, attack-, or choice-based evaluations may miss. We study functional counterfeits: implementations that match benign alternatives on the requested output but add an effect forbidden by the task contract. We introduce SINGED (Source Integrity and the Nonidentifiability Gap in Execution Decisions for LLM Agents), a controlled benchmark covering five primary and two held-out task families. It varies displayed rank, evidence depth, decision policy, model release, and agent configuration, while task and process oracles verify the artifact and execution path. Across 7,549 audited trials, the randomized-rank study finds counterfeit execution in 45% (27/60) of rank-one trials and none at later ranks. Cross-candidate comparison eliminates shallow failures and reduces layered failures from 15.7% to 4.2%, but leaves dependency failures; its benefit is uncertain on unseen effects and public-package structures. Moreover, seven releases with no counterfeit executions when benign alternatives are available execute the counterfeit in 55/175 single-source cells after alternatives are removed. SINGED thus exposes a rank-, evidence-, and choice-sensitive outcome-to-execution gap: evaluation must connect correct outputs to execution paths.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Language-model agents extend language models from generating responses to acting in an environment. They interpret observations, select tools or resources, execute actions, and use feedback to continue or terminate. This loop supports reasoning and acting (Yao et al., 2023), API use (Schick et al., 2023), and selection from large tool registries (Patil et al., 2024(Patil et al., , 2025)). Coding runtimes operationalize the loop through persistent state, tool interfaces, and termination logic (OpenAI, 2026a;Earendil Works, 2026). Interactive benchmarks evaluate execution trajectories across websites, computers, repositories, and stateful services (Zhou et al., 2024;Mialon et al., 2024).
This shift changes what evaluation must certify. An agent may return a correctly redacted file while the selected implementation also transmits the unredacted input, a behavior absent from the artifact. The Privacy Filter incident illustrates this risk: OpenAI released openai/privacy-filter for local personal-information detection and redaction, while another Hugging Face repository copied its model card and functionality but loaded an information stealer before its removal (OpenAI, 2026c; HiddenLayer Research Team, 2026). Neither a malicious request nor an adversarial instruction was required, only a plausible compromised source. This exposes a source-selection problem: When implementations advertise the same function and produce the same output, which source does an agent execute, and how This problem connects supply-chain security with agent security. Supply-chain research documents malicious packages, dependency confusion, and model-hub loader risks (Ohm et al., 2020;Ladisa et al., 2023;Casey et al., 2024), while agent-security research studies external instructions, poisoned tool descriptions, memories, skills, and unsafe plans (Greshake et al., 2023;Debenedetti et al., 2024;Liu et al., 2026b,a). Yet existing evaluations do not jointly hold the benign request and expected output fixed while varying the implementation, randomizing its displayed rank, and recording process effects (Table 1).

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Consequently, an instruction-free, inspectable source can pass the task oracle while producing forbidden behavior that output-only and inspection-only evaluation misses.
Motivated by this gap, we introduce SINGED (Source Integrity and the Nonidentifiability Gap in Execution Decisions for LLM Agents), a controlled evaluation framework inspired by the source ambiguity exposed by the Privacy Filter incident. Each instance pairs an ordinary request with three similarly named implementations: an intended source, a benign community alternative, and a functional counterfeit. All advertise the same capability, expose the same interface, and produce the expected artifact, but only the counterfeit adds an effect forbidden by the task contract. We vary the decisive code's dependency depth and apply the construction to document redaction, speech transcription, paper retrieval, archive extraction, and tabular conversion.
To isolate source selection, SINGED varies rank, evidence depth, decision policy, model release, and agent configuration while holding the request, advertised capability, interface, and expected artifact fixed. Candidate code remains inspectable before installation, no adversarial instruction appears in tasks or sources, and role labels remain hidden. As illustrated in Figure 1, a task oracle verifies returned artifacts, while a channel-separated process oracle records the executed implementation and its observable effects inside a network-isolated sandbox. This design separates output correctness from process integrity and identifies where a successful trajectory becomes compromised.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Across 7,549 audited trials spanning 20 releases from 14 model families and 8 agent configurations, we find three patterns. First, correct outputs conceal rank-sensitive process failures. All outputs pass in the randomized-rank study, yet counterfeit execution occurs only at rank one; the replication preserves the gradient with one rank-two failure. Second, early commitment drives shallow failures. Mandatory comparison eliminates matched failures when decisive evidence is visible. Yet seven releases with zero counterfeit execution rate (CER) under three-source choice execute the counterfeit in 55/175 single-source cells after benign alternatives are removed. Third, comparison reduces but does not eliminate risk.
Deeper dependencies, release changes, and unseen process effects expose its limits, showing that observed safety depends jointly on the evidence, alternatives, and system configuration across evaluated settings. We summarize our contributions as follows.
I) Problem formulation. We identify source selection among implementations with equivalent benchmark outputs as an agent security problem, define functional counterfeits, and formalize CER, safe utility, and the outcome-to-execution gap missed by output-only evaluation.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Related Work
text:
Tool-using agents and agent security. Tool-use research studies how language models interleave reasoning with external actions, retrieve APIs, and select among large tool collections (Yao et al., 2023;Schick et al., 2023;Patil et al., 2024). Interactive benchmarks extend this evaluation to websites, computers, repositories, and stateful services (Liu et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2024;Xie et al., 2024;Yao et al., 2025), primarily scoring whether the agent reaches the requested state. Agent-security work examines indirect prompt injection, poisoned tool descriptions, malicious skills and implementations, and unsafe plans (Greshake et al., 2023;Debenedetti et al., 2024;Shi et al., 2025;Hu et al., 2026;Qu et al., 2026). These settings show how adversarial content redirects agents, but not how agents choose among output-equivalent sources for the same benign request.
Software supply chains and source selection. Supply-chain studies document malicious packages, dependency confusion, hallucinated dependencies, and executable model loaders (Ohm et al., 2020;Ladisa et al., 2023;Spracklen et al., 2025;Casey et al., 2024). Position-bias studies separately show that list order can alter model choices (Bito et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2026a;Khan et al., 2026). As Table 1 summarizes, prior designs do not jointly hold the benign request and expected output fixed, vary the implementation, randomize its displayed rank, and observe process effects. SINGED connects these literatures by measuring source choice and execution integrity under output-equivalent alternatives across matched, auditable agent trajectories; Appendix C expands this comparison.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Matched and Auditable Construction
text:
Tasks and candidates. Existing agent benchmarks ask whether an agent completes an interactive task on a website, computer, or stateful service (Zhou et al., 2024;Mialon et al., 2024;Xie et al., 2024). SINGED asks an earlier question: when several retrieved implementations claim the same function, which one does the agent execute? Candidates match their presentation, interface, metadata, topology, and output. Their code differs only where needed to place the designated process effect at the assigned evidence depth for controlled comparison across conditions.
Using the task contract from Section 3, we instantiate five task families with controlled inputs derived from realistic task formats. Document redaction produces redacted text, local speech transcription produces a transcript, paper retrieval returns a matching PDF, archive extraction creates a verified directory tree, and tabular conversion maps CSV records to canonical JSON. Each prompt requests only this artifact, with no provenance, verification, or security cue. Unlike evaluations based on harmful requests, injected instructions, or poisoned descriptions (Ruan et al., 2024;Debenedetti et al., 2024), every SINGED prompt describes a benign task with no security violation.
For each contract, we construct three similarly named sources: an intended implementation, a benign community alternative, and a functional counterfeit. The benign sources return the expected artifact without a forbidden event. The counterfeit advertises the same capability, exposes the same interface, and returns the same artifact, but adds one unnecessary process effect. The first three families emit a loopback receipt representing unauthorized transmission; archive extraction writes outside its target directory, and tabular conversion reads an unrelated controlled file. Inspired by ambiguity in software and model supply chains (Ohm et al., 2020;Ladisa et al., 2023;Casey et al., 2024), this design turns a realistic risk into a controlled choice. Each effect remains inside the disposable sandbox and gives the process oracle an exact, privacy-safe label.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Evidence Control and Trace Scoring
text:
Controlled evidence depth. Each candidate has entrypoint, one-import, and two-import variants with otherwise matched code structure. The decisive statement that causes the forbidden effect appears in the invoked file, a directly imported file, or a second file reached through that import. These depths model relevant behavior hidden within software-supply-chain dependencies (Ohm et al., 2020;Ladisa et al., 2023). Assigned depth 𝑑 determines where this evidence appears, while observed inspection Instrumented execution. Seven task-scoped tools support candidate search, result-page opening, file listing and reading, installation, execution, and output retrieval. Each trial uses a fresh workspace and fixed tool-call budget. Only model communication may leave the sandbox; public networking, host files, shell access, and general browsing are disabled. Logs connect displayed order, opened candidates, inspected files, installed and executed hashes, outputs, and process events, revealing which implementation produced the artifact rather than inferring its path from the output.
Each trace yields five measures. Candidate coverage records which sources are opened, entrypoint coverage which invoked files the agent reads, and decisive-file exposure whether it observes the code causing the forbidden effect. Safe selection records whether the executed candidate is benign, while refusal and non-execution remain separate outcomes. Task completion records whether the artifact passes the task oracle. Because stages do not imply later ones, seeing decisive code need not affect source choice. Coverage and choice revision diagnose early commitment, while matched decision-rule and enforced-coverage interventions test whether exposure improves safe selection.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Q1: Correct outcomes conceal compromised execution
text:
Correct artifacts can mask compromised execution. Every output in the original 180-trial randomizedrank study is correct, yet 27 trajectories trigger the forbidden effect, creating a 15.0-point outcome-toexecution gap. Figure 4a localizes all failures to rank one. Appendix Figure 7 illustrates this gap: four agents return the same redacted file, but two execute the counterfeit despite observing its additional POST.
Table 3 extends the finding across five tasks and 20 releases: 1412/1500 trials complete the task, while 167/1500 execute the counterfeit. Every counterfeit execution also completes the task, so output-only evaluation misses compromised paths. Conversely, seven releases with zero CER under three-source choice still execute the sole counterfeit in 55/175 single-source cells (Figure 3). Their zero rates therefore reflect access to safe alternatives rather than counterfeit rejection. Archive and tabular cells reproduce the gap through out-of-scope writes and unrelated-file reads (442/2,432 hidden effects), while no all-benign control triggers the designated event. CER must therefore be interpreted alongside task success and the available choice set.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Q2: Rank and early commitment localize failures
text:
Displayed rank strongly affects counterfeit execution. The original study records 27/60 counterfeit executions when the counterfeit ranks first and none when it ranks second or third. The frozen replication preserves this gradient, with 17/60, 1/60, and 0/60 executions across the three ranks (Figure 4a). Across the five primary tasks, the corresponding counts are 162/500, 2/500, and 3/500. Deeper evidence weakens the benefit of comparison. Figure 4d plots CER on the vertical axis against the location of the decisive statement on the horizontal axis; the two curves represent deliberation and compare-all. Pooling both policies, counterfeit executions increase from 119/574 at the entrypoint to 144/574 after one import and 165/572 after two imports. Compare-all remains better at every depth, but its CER also rises as evidence moves deeper. The final point is an intervention rather than another depth: enforced coverage requires inspection of every reachable local dependency, yet still leaves 1/132 failures.
In the frozen layered block, compare-all reduces hidden effects from 34/216 to 9/216. An independent 216-cell repeat similarly records 31/108 failures under deliberation and 6/108 under compare-all, a 23.1-point reduction (95% cluster CI: 14.8-31.5). Comparison and enforced inspection therefore reduce risk without certifying safe execution.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Q4: Transfer depends on the task and system configuration
text: Comparison transfers within the primary benchmark but remains release-sensitive. Transfer remains task-and source-dependent. Across 120 held-out trials, 51 trigger a forbidden effect: 26/60 under deliberation and 25/60 under compare-all. The direction reverses between configuration editing and thumbnailing, with both intervals crossing zero (Figure 6a-b). A two-hop test yields 0/60 versus 1/60 effects. Across 324 public-package cells, counterfeit executions fall from 36/162 to 26/162, a 6.2-point CER difference (95% cluster CI: -0.6-13.0; Figure 6d). Both policies retain rank gradients. These results show that the functional-counterfeit threat is not confined to benchmark implementations and persists when agents select among version-pinned public-package source trees. Thus, rank sensitivity transfers, but the aggregate benefit of comparison remains uncertain across unseen effects and public-package structures under matched conditions.

title: SINGED: Correct Outputs Do Not Certify Safe Execution in LLM Agents
heading: Conclusion
text:
We introduce SINGED and show that output correctness does not establish execution integrity. Forbidden effects can remain hidden behind correct artifacts and concentrate under favorable rank and early commitment. Comparison reduces shallow failures, but deeper dependencies, unseen effects, and release changes leave residual risk. Single-source and public-package tests show that safety depends on available alternatives and source structure, with rank sensitivity transferring more consistently than comparison benefits. Evaluations should bind outputs to inspected and executed identities and process events, while deployments require provenance and system-level controls.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: Abstract
text: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
The abilities of tool-using large language model (LLM) agents allow them to be used to automate workflows such as hardware procurement (Zdravković et al., 2022;Ozman, 2025), patient diagnosis (Tu et al., 2025;Ghezloo et al., 2025) or travel bookings (Dwivedi et al., 2025). Such workflows are governed by procedural manuals, written in natural language for human operators, that specify how such tasks must be executed. For example, Fig. 1 (top right) shows a simple manual for booking a business trip.
While such workflows may seem natural for humans, LLM agents have been observed to struggle with them, both in existing work about evaluating compliance post-hoc (Li et al., 2025;Nandi et al., 2026;Anand et al., 2026a), and in our own experiments. For instance in the domain of Fig. 1, checking agents' tool call traces reveals they often attempt to book business class after inventing a fake "urgent reason", or never book anything at all.
To aid LLM agents in such tasks, we introduce MENTOR, a procedural shield that checks proposed tool calls against formalized requirements and guides agents towards fulfilling outstanding obligations. Shielding is a well-established technique for policies obtained by reinforcement learning (RL), where a shield monitors the actions a policy proposes at runtime and blocks those that violate a formal specification (Könighofer et al., 2022;Hsu et al., 2024). We develop this approach for tool-using LLM agents around four interconnected challenges. Figure 1: Running example. Our procedural shield MENTOR is generated from a procedural manual (top right) and applied to a travel-booking task (top left). MENTOR shields the interaction between an LLM agent (pink) and the environment (brown). MENTOR blocks tool calls (red), allows tool calls (green), and provides guidance towards task completion (orange).

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text: ⟨C1⟩ Context-dependence & guidance. A procedural manual, as e.g. the one in Fig. 1, induces a partial temporal order over tool calls, so whether a tool call complies is context-dependent (e.g., booking a flight is allowed in step 5 but not in step 2). This context-dependence introduces obligations an agent needs to fulfill before another necessary call would be allowed (e.g., checking the distance before any booking) and it must eventually make some specific tool calls to complete its task (e.g., the booking itself). Blocking a call without identifying a compliant next step can leave the agent repeatedly attempting blocked calls and failing to complete its task, as illustrated by our experiments (Fig. 5 in App. A.2). Shields that also incorporate context-dependent progress guidance were only recently introduced for RL as strategy template based runtime shields (STARS) (Anand et al., 2026b). MENTOR adapts this idea to LLM agents, by first auto-formalizing the manual into Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) and then synthesizing a strategy template from it.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
⟨C2⟩ Argument-based constraints. Context-dependence does not only affect the order of tool calls, but also their arguments. For example, booking an economy class flight is allowed without an urgent reason in step 5, whereas booking business class is not in step 4. The values these arguments can take often range over unbounded domains, such as strings, and might only be revealed at runtime, making it challenging to express constraints over them. The importance of checking argument values is illustrated by our analysis of SOP-Bench (Nandi et al., 2026), whose evaluator accepts some incorrect traces because it does not check the relevant tool arguments (App. C.3). MENTOR addresses this problem with argument constraints using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) that are checked and, if violated, repaired at runtime. ⟨C3⟩ Natural language. Any formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents needs to translate natural language texts within the manual, the task description, and tool outputs into formal artifacts. In our work, we automatically translate the manual into a formal specification offline. Then, at runtime, we observe that both cheap proprietary LLMs and fine-tuned small open-weights LLMs can effectively ground the task description and tool outputs.
⟨C4⟩ Delivering the shield. A classical shield for an RL policy intervenes directly on the action the policy proposes. In the context of LLM agents, however, actions are tool calls which are written token by token. Depending on the availability of the agent's next-token distribution, MENTOR can deliver the blocking and advice of tool calls to the agent in two ways: (i) via a prompt shield that injects textual feedback in the tool call outputs, and (ii) via a token shield, which masks the tokens of unsafe calls and boosts those of progressing calls during generation.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: INTRODUCTION
text:
To show its impact on procedural compliance of shielded agents, we evaluate MENTOR on 3 benchmarks covering 8 domains using both proprietary and open-weights agents. The experiments show that MENTOR clearly outperforms unshielded agents and other guarding methods, and lifts the compliance of small open-weight models above those of unshielded proprietary ones. We provide all our code and parameters at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/mentor-llm-shield/.
Related Work. Shielding LLM agents has received increasing attention very recently, but none of the existing approaches addresses the outlined challenges appropriately. We compare them here and in One line of work on LLM shielding techniques delegate compliance decisions to a guardrail LLM (Xiang et al., 2024;Hoover et al., 2026;Kang et al., 2026) which can interpret natural language (⟨C3⟩) within the manual, tasks, and tool outputs. However, the resulting judgements can be unreliable due to the stochastic nature of LLMs. Alternatively, deterministic guards hard-code procedural constraints, which are either written by hand in a dedicated language (Wang et al., 2026;Winston et al., 2026;Palumbo et al., 2026;Reddy et al., 2026;Kamath et al., 2025) or extracted by an LLM (Shi et al., 2025;Mondl et al., 2026). Such deterministic guards, however, cannot interpret natural language tool outputs during their execution. As a result, they cannot provide rich enough context-dependent guidance to the agent (⟨C1⟩). In addition, manually translating the procedural manual into formal constraints can make shield synthesis labor intensive and hard to extend to new domains, and this task is known to be difficult even for experts (Czepa et al., 2019;Greenman et al., 2023). MENTOR combines the strengths of both approaches by using a refinement-based auto-formalization technique to build a deterministic tool-call evaluator which is paired with a labeler to ground tool call outputs.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: OVERVIEW
text:
MENTOR (Monitoring and ENforcement of Temporal Objectives at Runtime) sits between a toolusing LLM agent and its environment (Fig. 2). We outline how its components address ⟨C1⟩-⟨C4⟩.
Setting. A tool schema T defines the set of tools available to the agent. Let A be the set of valid toolcalls α = (t, a), with tool t ∈ T and argument assignment a, including the terminating call done that ends the interaction. Let H denote the set of finite interaction traces h = [o 0 , α 1 , o 1 , . . . , α l , o l ], where o 0 is the natural-language task and o i the environment's response to α i . The agent π : H → ∆(A) repeatedly samples α i ∼ π(• | h) and observes o i , until it generates done. Each call is generated internally by an autoregressive LLM over a token vocabulary V . A natural-language procedural manual D specifies which traces are acceptable.
Deterministic tool call evaluator (Fig. 2, bottom). Our goal is that the trace generated by the agent completes the task o 0 while complying with D. To this end, for each proposed call α i and history h, the evaluator asks two questions: is α i safe, i.e., whether a compliant complete trace under D still exists after α i , and does α i make progress towards completion (⟨C1⟩)? Also, are its arguments a i permitted (⟨C2⟩)? Safe calls with permitted arguments are executed; non-progressing calls additionally receive advice identifying a progressing call. Other calls are blocked, returning advice identifying a prerequisite call or repaired arguments instead. The call done is blocked while the task remains incomplete (Fig. 2, bottom).

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: OVERVIEW
text:
Building MENTOR offline (Fig. 2, top). MENTOR is constructed once per manual D and tool schema T and then reused for every task. First, a multi-agent autoformalization loop (Sec. 3.2) translates D into a formal specification with two parts (Sec. 3.1): (i) temporal requirements in linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas to capture tool call order, restrictions that tool outputs impose, and obligations before done, and (ii) argument constraints in satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) encoding, which fix the permitted argument values over possibly unbounded argument domains (⟨C2⟩). The LTL requirements are compiled into a game between agent and environment on a finite graph, and a strategy template (Sec. 3.2) marks, at every vertex of this graph, which calls are unsafe and which are progressive (⟨C1⟩). The template and SMT solver form the deterministic evaluator.
Applying MENTOR online (Fig. 2, left). Since the task o 0 and some tool outputs are in natural language, at runtime, a labeler LLM (Sec. 3.3) grounds them into formal, labeled events consistent with the specifications (⟨C3⟩). For each proposed call, the shield advances through the game graph following h, consults the template and the solver, and produces a verdict and advice. These reach the agent in one of two ways (⟨C4⟩): (i) via a prompt shield that delivers them as text in the tool output, or (ii) via a token shield that additionally masks the tokens of unsafe calls and boosts those of progressing calls during generation.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: METHODOLOGY / SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE
text:
This section formalizes the components in Fig. 2 and explains how each addresses challenges ⟨C1⟩-⟨C4⟩. We introduce our specification language in Sec. 3.1, then describe the offline construction of MENTOR in Sec. 3.2 and its online use for procedural shielding in Sec. 3.3.
SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE. Temporal Requirements via LTL. LTL extends propositional logic with temporal operators that express requirements on the ordering of events over time. We use standard LTL syntax with finte trace semantics (Giacomo & Vardi, 2013) (refer to App. B for details). We interpret these requirements over interaction traces h. At each step, propositions are evaluated from predicates on the tool call α = (t, a) and, when needed, its observed outcome o. Formulas can thus relate proposed actions to preceding calls and results, and require successful completion before termination.
In our example in Fig. 1, booking travel requires a preceding distance check, the resulting distance restricts the permitted travel mode, and the requested booking must eventually succeed. For origin x and destination y, let checked distance(x, y) denote a check distance tool call, and booked train(x, y) and booked flight(x, y) the corresponding booking calls. The distance-check prerequisite P1 can be expressed in LTL as ¬ booked train(x, y) ∨ booked flight(x, y) W checked distance(x, y).
Here, W denotes 'weak until', which means that bookings are forbidden until the distance check occurs, and throughout the interaction if it never occurs. This blocks the bookings in steps 1 and 2. Crucially, each (x, y) is tracked separately, i.e., a Toronto-Chicago check cannot satisfy the prerequisite for Toronto-Montreal.

The prohibition on flights below 500 km in P2 can then be expressed in LTL as G distance small(x, y) → G ¬booked flight(x, y) . Here, G denotes 'globally', i.e., a result below 500 km forbids all subsequent flight bookings for that route.
Both formulas above would permit an execution that checks the distance and then stops without making a booking, so we also express obligations to complete the task. Let booked train ok(x, y) and booked flight ok(x, y) denote booking calls whose outcomes confirm success. For the requested route, the requirement is F booked train ok(x, y) ∨ booked flight ok(x, y) , where F denotes 'eventually' and requires a successful booking before termination. Grounding propositions in tool calls and their outcomes enables runtime monitoring. However, tool arguments may range over unbounded domains, so we parameterize the propositions arguments and bind them to concrete entities at runtime. Preserving these bindings is essential, as ignoring (x, y) would make a short-distance result for one route prohibit flights on every route. Grounding propositions in tool calls and their outcomes enables runtime monitoring. However, tool arguments may range over unbounded domains, so we parameterize the propositions arguments and bind them to concrete entities at runtime. Preserving these bindings is essential, as ignoring (x, y) would make a short-distance result for one route prohibit flights on every route. title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: METHODOLOGY / SPECIFICATION LANGUAGE
text:
Argument Constraints via SMT. We express argument constraints as predicates on the arguments a of a call α = (t, a), which may also depend on information from the interaction trace h. Each constraint applies to calls identified by its associated proposition. In our example, satisfying the distance-check does not by itself permit a business-class booking, since P3 also requires the agent to establish an urgent reason and the absence of an economy seat for that route.
We encode argument constraints using SMT, which decides the satisfiability of first-order formulas modulo theories. In our implementation, we use Z3 (de Moura & Bjørner, 2008) with quantifier-free formulas over strings and linear integer arithmetic. SMT can directly express argument restrictions, enabling a solver to check whether multiple restrictions are jointly satisfiable and efficiently find satisfying values without fully enumerating the argument domain. Our argument constraints use a domain-specific language that is evaluated directly on proposed arguments and has an SMT encoding for satisfiability checks and symbolic argument search (App. B).
For the Toronto-Chicago flight in Fig. 1, let business allowed(h, x, y) indicate whether h establishes both an urgent reason and the absence of an economy seat for route (x, y). P3 constrains calls satisfying booked flight(x, y) via the constraint
where a[class] denotes the booking-class argument represented as a string-valued SMT variable, and business allowed(h, x, y) is a fixed Boolean value for the given history and route. The distance check in step 3 satisfies P1, and its 700 km result does not trigger P2's flight prohibition. However, no urgent reason has been established, so business allowed(h, Toronto, Chicago) is false. The business-class booking in step 4 therefore violates the constraint.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: BUILDING MENTOR OFFLINE
text:
To build MENTOR, we first translate natural-language manuals into the specifications of Sec. 3.1 (⟨C3⟩), to compute templates that provide the guidance required by ⟨C1⟩ (Fig. 2, top right). Autoformalization. We use a multi-agent refinement loop with three LLM agents: a translator, an evaluator, and an orchestrator (Fig. 3). The translator takes the manual and the tool schema and formalizes the requirements in the specification language defined above. The evaluator generates test traces from the manual, consisting of tool calls α i and their outcomes o i , and labels them as compliant or non-compliant with the manual. A deterministic conflict checker then compares the proposed specification's verdicts on these traces with the evaluator's proposed labels and returns disagreements to first the translator to revise the specification. The translator can contest a label, by providing an explanation grounded in the manual, which the evaluator reviews. The orchestrator coordinates these revisions and resolves remaining disagreements referring to the manual. The loop ends when the specification agrees with the evaluated traces or reaches a fixed iteration limit.
Note that if the loop terminates successfully, it provides some evidence of consistency between the generated specification and the manual, but it does not prove that it captures every requirement correctly. However, formalizing natural-language requirements is difficult even for human experts (Greenman et al., 2023;Czepa et al., 2019). Given that there exists no perfect method for this task, we believe that our loop provides a practical way to iteratively refine the specification and will become increasingly reliable as LLMs and autoformalization techniques improve.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: BUILDING MENTOR OFFLINE
text: Template Construction. The LTL specification φ defines compliance for interaction traces h. Shielding, however, requires determining which tool calls must be blocked or advised during interaction, before the trace is complete. Towards this, we adopt a standard game-theoretic approach, which automatically maps φ into a finite two-player game between the agent and the environment (see Fig. 4 for an example) (Pnueli & Rosner, 1989). At an agent vertex (circle), the agent chooses a call, which leads to an environment vertex (square), at which the environment chooses its outcome. Each vertex abstracts the part of the history h relevant for the specification into residual LTL formulas, i.e., the requirements that the remaining interaction must still satisfy (black). Calls violating a requirement lead to a sink ⊥ (red), from which no compliant continuation exists, and done leads to the accepting vertex (✓, green) if and only if no duty is open. To obtain a shielding mechanism from the above translation, we employ a recent method (Anand et al., 2023;2026b) that automatically computes a strategy template over a given game. At each agent vertex, the template marks (i) unsafe tools (red, dashed), which violate a requirement immediately or later unavoidably, and (ii) progressing tools (orange, solid), which advance the fulfillment of open duties. In Fig. 4, done is unsafe at v 0 , v 1 and v 2 because the booking duty is still open, but it is progressing at v 3 because the confirmed booking fulfills it.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: BUILDING MENTOR OFFLINE
text: Intuitively, the template turns the global requirements into local constraints that let MENTOR block unsafe calls and advise progress toward compliance. It is also permissive, because the agent may choose freely any safe tool, including non-progressing calls. MENTOR interferes with the agent's preferences only where compliance requires it, and reminds of the open duties with its advice so that the agent can choose when to address them. However, the template only ranges over tools. The admissibility of their arguments requires additional SMT-based checks. In Fig. 4, booking a business-class flight (step 4 from Fig. 1) is progressing for the template in v 2 but blocked by the argument constraint P3. The next section discusses how this is handled by MENTOR at runtime.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: (bottom).
text:
Two further components make this deterministic evaluator applicable to real agent interactions: (i) a labeler LLM that grounds propositions in the natural-language task description and tool outputs (the runtime part of ⟨C3⟩), and (ii) two shielding mechanisms, a prompt shield and a token shield, that deliver the evaluator's verdicts and advice to the agent (⟨C4⟩). We describe both below.
Labeler LLM. The tool-call evaluator operates on structured data, applying predicates to arguments a and outcomes o in h to evaluate propositions such as booked flight(x, y) and argument constraints such as P3. However, the task description o 0 and free-text tool outputs, e.g. from check distance, are natural language. MENTOR uses a labeler LLM to convert both into structured events according to the specification, on which the tool-call evaluator deterministically makes shielding decisions.
Before the first tool call, the labeler turns o 0 into one or more pseudo tool calls. The specification declares their names, arguments, and a plain-text extraction rule per argument. For Fig. 1, the task becomes request travel(Toronto, Chicago, class=business, urgent=false). The predicates of the temporal requirements bind x = Toronto, y = Chicago to this event, which activates the route's booking duty, and no urgent reason is given which makes business allowed(h, x, y) false.
Further, for each tool output marked as natural language, the specification declares a small label vocabulary. After a tool call, the labeler maps the returned text to exactly one label or none, and Preprint stores it in o i for propositions to read like any other value. In Fig. 1, check distance is labeled as ≥500 km, determining that distance small(x, y) does not hold and the agent moves to v 2 in Fig. 4.

title: MENTOR: PROCEDURAL SHIELDING OF TOOL-USING LLM AGENTS
heading: (bottom).
text:
Prompt shield. The tool-call evaluator enforces its decision through the tool call output, and the prompt shield delivers the verdict and advice to the agent in the form of text along with the tool outcome. If a call α = (t, a) is blocked, it is not executed, and the agent receives as feedback the violated excerpt from the manual and a suggested tool call. The suggestion may be either the template-indicated missing prerequisite call at the current vertex, or an SMT-repaired call for a violated argument constraint. Alternatively, if α is allowed, it is executed. However, if duties remain open, its result is augmented with a reminder listing the open duties and a progressing call. The call done is refused while duties remain open, or until a preset limit on the number of calls is reached.
As an example, consider that at v 0 of Fig. 4 the agent calls book train (step 1 of Fig. 1). This call is unsafe at v 0 as check distance is a prerequisite, so the agent receives the feedback:
[SHIELD] Blocked book_train(origin="Toronto", destination="Chicago").
-Policy rule for trip Toronto->Chicago: Check the distance before any booking. (P1) First: check_distance(origin="Toronto", destination="Chicago")
The prompt shield relies on agents following its feedback, which may be difficult for small openweight models as shown in our experiments in Sec. 4. If the next-token distribution is accessible, MENTOR can additionally apply a token shield to enforce the same constraints at the token level.
