Our ablation study results confirm that each block of our framework is essential. Removing any part will significantly decrease performance across various metrics. These parts are vital for managing information and enhancing plan quality, ensuring a robust and efficient planning process.

title: A Human-Like Reasoning Framework for Multi-Phases Planning Task with Large Language Models
heading: Conclusion and Future Work
text:
In this paper, we presented a novel human-like reasoning framework for travel planning using LLM Agents. Our approach integrates several key components: Outline Generation, Information Collection with blocks, and Plan Search. These components synergistically mimic human problem-solving strategies, enabling LLM agents to handle multi-phase tasks more effectively. Extensive experiments on the TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrated significant improvements across multiple models with our framework.
Future work can focus on applying our planning framework to real-world planning problems in practical environments. Additionally, the current tools within our framework are limited. Enhancing the framework by incorporating more advanced tools, such as those with additional parameters and capabilities, could further improve its planning and problem-solving effectiveness. This expansion could enable more sophisticated and adaptable solutions, making our framework even more robust in addressing complex, real-world challenges.
A Appendix / supplemental material A.1 Limitation
Although our framework has significantly improved performance compared to previous studies, achieving a Final Pass Rate of 100% akin to human performance remains elusive. One limitation we observed is that even when provided with detailed information, LLM Agents still tend to overlook certain key points. Addressing this challenge may require the integration of alternative planning strategies. Additionally, effectively utilizing extensive accommodation-related information to generate reasonable plans remains a significant challenge, even for advanced models like GPT-4-Turbo. Furthermore, the occurrence of hallucinations during the planning process presents another obstacle that requires attention.

title: ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset
heading: Abstract
text: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have developed rapidly in recent years to solve complex real-world problems using external tools. However, the scarcity of high-quality trajectories still hinders the development of stronger LLM agents. Most existing works on multi-turn dialogue synthesis validate correctness only at the trajectory level, which may overlook turn-level errors that can propagate during training and degrade model performance. title: ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset
heading: Introduction
text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have adopted Function Calling (FC) paradigm to interact with external environments, significantly expanding their capacity to solve complex real-world tasks [23,14]. This capability hinges on the model's proficiency in tool use, which requires reliable interpretation of user instructions, appropriate function selection, and precise parameter generation. A data-centric approach has proven effective in enhancing such capabilities, typically requiring large-scale, highquality datasets with diverse and accurate function-call demonstrations.
Recent studies have actively synthesized data for various function calling scenarios [8,17], spanning diverse application domains and interaction modalities such as selection from large toolsets, parallel function calls, and rejection of unspecified requests [10,12,18]. However, existing datasets have several critical limitations: limited scale, the absence of explicit reasoning traces, a lack of multi-turn interactions, and insufficient query diversity. These issues highlights the importance of high-quality, large-scale datasets to develop robust and generalizable tool-use models and agents.
A key challenge in constructing high-quality datasets lies in capturing the dynamic nature of realworld user-assistant interactions. First, user requests are often under-specified, lacking sufficient parameters for task completion (e.g., a query like "What's the weather in Beijing?" does not specify a time frame). Second, effective interaction requires an ongoing clarification process, in which the assistant can proactively request missing information from the user. Current open-source synthetic datasets rarely capture these dynamics, leading to models struggling with such scenarios.

title: ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset
heading: Introduction
text:
In this work, we introduce ToolMind, a reasoning-enhanced tool-use dataset comprising 360k samples. It integrates 160k assistant response turns synthesized through multi-agent simulations and 200k augmented turns adapted from open-source data. To ensure diversity, we collect 20k functions from open-source datasets and construct a function graph that captures inter-parameter correlations. Function chains are then sampled via random walks on this graph to synthesize user intents. Then, we employ a multi-agent framework for dialogue generation, orchestrating three dedicated roles-user, agent, and tool-each instantiated by a language model to capture the dynamics and complexities of real-world tool-use interactions. Finally, we apply a rigorous two-stage filtering process, comprising both trajectory-level and turn-level quality checks, to ensure that all training samples contain only valid conversation turns.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ToolMind dataset in enhancing the tool-use capabilities of LLMs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT), models of various scales show significant improvements over baselines across multiple benchmarks, including BFCL-v4 [11], τ -bench [20], and τ 2 -bench [1]. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
• High-Quality Tool-Use Dataset. We introduce ToolMind, a large-scale, high-quality tooluse dataset comprising 360k samples that effectively addresses the key limitations of existing datasets-namely in scale, reasoning traces, multi-turn interactions, and query diversity.
• Data Synthesis and Quality Filtering Pipeline. We develop a novel data synthesis pipeline that constructs a function graph based on parameter correlations and employs multi-agent simulations with three dedicated roles (a user, an assistant, and a tool), which better capture the dynamic nature of real-world tool-use interactions. A rigorous two-stage filtering process is further applied to ensure high data quality.
• Effectiveness of Large-Scale Simulation. We show that ToolMind delivers significant and consistent performance improvements across models of various scales. These results empirically validate that large-scale synthetic data generated from simulated environments can serve as an effective alternative to real-world data for achieving substantial gains in model performance.

heading: Background
text:
Function Calling. The integration of external tools and functions into language model workflows marks a major step toward extending model capabilities beyond text generation. Function calling refers to the structured mechanism through which language models invoke predefined functions or APIs to access real-time data or interact with external systems [14]. An early paradigm for using external tools is React [21], where models generate both reasoning traces and corresponding (2) Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Trajectory Synthesis, using language models to simulate multiple roles and generate interactive trajectories; and
(3) Quality Filtering, applying both trajectory-level and turn-level filtering to ensure data quality.
function calls in an interleaved manner. This paradigm was later refined and integrated into thinking models as a native capability (e.g., supporting function calling in chat templates) for training and inference [19,22], also known as the model's function call pattern. Our synthetic data aims to enhance the model's native function calling capabilities.
Benchmarks. Several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the tool-use ability of language models, i.e., their capacity to call appropriate functions for task completion [9,13,5,11,20,1,24]. These benchmarks have evolved from basic tool-use evaluations to assessing agent behavior in more realistic, interactive scenarios. BFCL-v4 [11] comprises four distinct versions that systematically progress from single-turn interactions to multi-turn dialogues, and from simple, static tool-use cases to complex tasks involving search and memory capabilities. Concurrently, τ -bench [20] focuses on sustained dialogue and function-calling tasks and τ 2 -bench [1] further enriches this scenario by extending function access to the user side. Together, these advances demonstrate a clear shift toward more dynamic and complex evaluation frameworks that better reflect real-world conditions. In this work, we evaluate models across the three benchmarks mentioned above to systematically assess the effectiveness of our synthesized data.

heading: Random Walk with Function Graph
text:
With the parameter embeddings in place, we proceed to build a function graph that captures relationships between functions. In this graph, each function is a node, and edges are established based on the semantic fit between outputs and inputs. Concretely, let G = (V, E) be a directed graph with V = F. For two distinct functions f i and f j , we measure how well an output of f i can serve as an input to f j by the maximum cosine similarity over their parameter embeddings:
where sim denotes cosine similarity. An edge i → j is created when this similarity exceeds a fixed threshold τ > 0, indicating that an output parameter of f i is semantically similar to an input parameter of f j . To ensure the reliability of these connections, we further employ a language model as a validator and keep only the accepted links.
We also introduce randomness into edge construction. This yields a more diverse connectivity pattern that better reflects the real-world function composition. With the constructed graph, we sample function chains via random walks that traverse existing edges:

title: ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset
heading: Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Trajectory Synthesis / Quality Filtering
text:
Based on the sampled function chains, we synthesize user intents to represent realistic user goals. A user intent represents the underlying goal that a user aims to achieve, rather than the exact query they pose. This distinction provides greater flexibility in modeling user behavior, as users often express the same intent in diverse ways. Since the tools are not executable in our setup, we employ a simulation framework to generate responses. The trajectories are created through a multi-agent simulation that involves three distinct agents:
• User Agent: Initiates the interaction by asking questions based on synthesized intent and drives the conversation forward.
• Assistant Agent: Responds to the user's queries, provides guidance, asks for clarification, or calls external functions when needed.
• Tool Agent: Simulates the execution of a function invoked by the assistant, returning tool responses based on simulated outputs.
These three agents operate in an iterative loop: the user agent poses a query, the assistant agent responds, and the tool agent simulates feedback when required. The process continues until a predefined turn limit or stopping condition is reached. This simulation produces a diverse set of interaction trajectories that serve as training data for modeling rich user-assistant-tool dynamics.
Empirical results demonstrate that even without real-world interaction, the large-scale synthetic data generated from these simulations significantly improves model performance. The flexibility and diversity of the simulated conversations provide valuable insights for training models in complex, multi-agent systems. For a detailed example of the generated data, see Appendix B.
Quality Filtering. To ensure that the synthesized interactions provide reliable learning signals, we apply a two-stage quality filtering process: trajectory-level filtering that maintains goal alignment and coherence, followed by turn-level filtering that removes erroneous or misaligned steps.

title: ToolMind Technical Report: A Large-Scale, Reasoning-Enhanced Tool-Use Dataset
heading: Turn-Level Filtering
text: Since trajectory-level filtering operates at a coarse granularity, it cannot effectively isolate erroneous turns within otherwise coherent trajectories. Trajectories may still contain erroneous or misaligned turns-such as failed intermediate attempts, tool calls based on incorrect assumptions, or role drift in user/tool messages. To further improve data quality, we address these remaining issues by applying a separate LLM-based judge to each turn. The model then masks invalid or role-inconsistent steps and retains only correct procedural actions, ensuring the final training data targets effective problem solving and precise tool use. We split each trajectory into multiple samples using the turns that passed the turn-level quality filter and analyze both trajectories (orange) and post-split samples (blue). See the distribution analysis in Figure 3. From a trajectory-level perspective, the overall distribution of data lengths is relatively uniform, and users show strong participation throughout the dialogues. After the conversations are segmented into turns and filters are applied, the distribution skews toward shorter instances, which is expected. We further analyze the distribution of step counts for consecutive tool calls. A sizable fraction of turns proceed without any tool calls, likely because the synthetic user is prompted to mimic natural dialogue-holding back some constraints so that the model must ask follow-up questions and confirm details. Taken together, these findings indicate that current tasks leave room for greater complexity, motivating future work on more demanding tool-use scenarios.

heading: Experiments / Experimental Setup
text:
This section presents the performance of models of varying sizes after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on our dataset. We first present the fine-tuning setup and then evaluate the resulting models against the baselines on widely-used tool-calling benchmarks.
Experimental Setup. Model and Fine-tuning Setup. We perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B [19]. The training is conducted using OpenRLHF [6] framework with a sequence length of 64k, a global batch size of 64, a learning rate of 5e-6, and a warmup ratio of 0.03.
Benchmarks. We evaluate our models on three widely used tool-calling benchmarks: BFCL-v4 [11], τ -Bench [20], and τ 2 -bench [1]. For BFCL-v4, we use the official evaluation setup for Qwen3 and benchmark our model against larger-scale models on the official leaderboards as of October 2025. For a comprehensive comparison, we incorporat results from both open-source models DeepSeek-V3 [7], DeepSeek-R1-0528 [4], Qwen3-235-instruct [19], Kimi-K2-Instruct [16] and closed-source models GPT-4o-2024-11-20, GPT5-2025-0807, and Gemini2.5-Pro [3]. For τ -Bench and τ 2 -Bench, we used GPT-4o as a user simulator and evaluate performance by directly comparing the model before and after fine-tuning.

We incorporat the following open-source datasets: xlam-function-calling-60k [10], When2Call [15], glaive-function-calling-v2 5 , ToolACE [8], BUTTONInstruct [2], APIGen-MT-5k [12], and the Tau-bench training set [20]. All open-source multi-turn datasets are subjected to the same split and quality-filtering procedures as the synthesised data. The statistics of the datasets can be found in Table 4.1. After preprocessing, each multi-turn conversation is split at each assistant message into multiple samples. For each splitted sample, we retain the full prior context up to (and including) the anchor assistant message and discard all subsequent turns. Each asisstant response is structured into three parts: think, content, and tool calls. During training, we compute loss only on the tokens of the anchored assistant response.

heading: Experimental Results
text: Overall Performance. The performance of our SFT models on τ -Bench [20], and τ 2 -bench [1], BFCL-v4 [11] is summarized in Table 2 and Table 3. On BFCL-v4, we observe notable improvements in both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B after training. Although their single-turn evaluation scores show modest fluctuations, they remain above most baseline models. Performance gains are most pronounced in multi-turn and agentic evaluations. Notably, after training on ToolMind, Qwen3-14B surpasses several larger-scale open-source and closed-source models. Similarly, on the τ -bench and τ 2 -bench benchmarks, both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B achieve substantial improvements in their average score after training on ToolMind. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the ToolMind dataset in improving model tool-use capabilities. Ablation Study. To evaluate the effectiveness of each component in ToolMind, we conduct an ablation study on Qwen3-8B. The study comprises the following configurations: (a) using only synthesized data, (b) using synthesized data without turn-level quality filtering, and (c) using only data augmented from open-source datasets. The experimental results, shown in Table 4, demonstrate that the open-source augmented data contribute to significant performance improvements on τ -bench and τ 2 -bench, while the graph sampling-based synthetic data lead to major gains on BFCL-v4, and the turn-level quality filtering significantly enhances the model performance. Moreover, the model trained on the combined dataset achieves the best results across nearly all evaluation metrics, demonstrating that each component of ToolMind is integral and effective.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Abstract
text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI research and enabled exciting agent systems. To build a complex LLM agent system, most existing research relies on insights from other domains or heuristics to manually build the agent system. However, this approach often requires heavy hand-engineering and fails to fully optimize for the downstream task of interest. Inspired by the tremendous success of deep learning, we propose to construct LLM agent systems in a modular manner, similar to building a deep neural network. Our key insight is to make analogies between LLM building blocks, such as retrievals, memories, and prompting strategies, and the successful deep learning modules, such as MLPs, attention, and recurrent modules. We further design forward inference and feedback mechanisms for LLMs, where prompts in LLMs are considered as the weights in deep models, and the prompt optimization from feedback is analogous to the back-propagation algorithm. We additionally leverage a search algorithm to search for the best configuration of LLM agent systems, similar to the neural architecture search (NAS) in deep learning research. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning recipe for LLM agent systems is highly effective, in particular: (1) Organizing LLM modules into deep-learning-style architectures yields noticeable performance gain; (2) Automatic prompt optimization, equivalent to backpropagation, is efficient in incorporating feedback from the task of interest and achieves at least 5% performance improvement; (3) NAS equivalent algorithm works well for further optimizing the LLM agent system architecture with 11% performance gain compared with randomly designed architectures. Overall, our research demonstrates the exciting opportunity of transferring the success of deep learning to building LLM agent systems.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Introduction
text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in achieving Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) due to their impressive planning and reasoning abilities (Wu et al., 2023b;Ge et al., 2023), which has sparked an upsurge in studies investigating sophisticated LLM agent systems (Zhao et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2023;Peng et al., 2023). LLM agent systems usually involve various LLM building blocks (Packer et al., 2023;Yao et al., 2023;Topsakal & Akinci, 2023;Pandya & Holia, 2023;Jeong, 2023), such as retrieval (Robertson et al., 2009;Izacard et al., 2022;Lin et al., 2023), memory modules (Zhao et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2023), and prompting strategies (Yao et al., 2024). We argue that the success of LLM agent systems relies on the integration of multiple LLM modules (Zhao et al., 2023;Talebirad & Nadiri, 2023;Wu et al., 2023a), which still receives limited attention from the community. Therefore, our paper aims to raise attention to the pressing research question: how to effectively and automatically construct LLM agent systems based on basic building blocks.
Constructing effective LLM agent systems often involves leveraging insights from various disciplines, such as neuroscience (Yao et al., 2022;Shinn et al., 2023;Kwon et al., 2023) and computer architecture Preprint (Packer et al., 2023;Talebirad & Nadiri, 2023). For example, MEMGPT (Packer et al., 2023) draws inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems to construct an LLM agent system with several manually designed LLM building blocks. However, applying such interdisciplinary insights to LLM agent system construction has the following shortcomings: (1) The approach is often domain-specific and not generic, requiring heavy manual designs; (2) Designing the LLM agent system necessitates extensive trial and error, making the process both costly and inflexible.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Introduction
text:
Inspired by the success of DL, we propose to design LLM agent systems with a Deep Learning recipe. Our approach involves defining building blocks of LLMs analogous to the DL modules, constructing LLM agent systems similar to defining NN architectures, and developing the prompt optimization algorithm of LLMs similar to the backpropagation algorithm. Specifically, we explore LLM modules including: (1) vanilla LLM as a single layer MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP) (Popescu et al., 2009); (2) Memory processer (Zhang et al., 2023;Packer et al., 2023) as an RNN; (3) Retrieval (Robertson et al., 2009;Izacard et al., 2022;Lin et al., 2023) as an attention network (Wang et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2019;Hou et al., 2019); (4) prompting strategies (Besta et al., 2023;Yao et al., 2024) as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) (Zhang et al., 2021;Shi et al., 2019;Kenning et al., 2022). Based on the defined LLM modules, we could construct more complex LLM agent systems by referencing successful DL architectures, notably, Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017a). Furthermore, we design a meta prompt module similar to the training parameters in DL to guide the forward inference, and a feedback-propagation module that incorporates the external feedback and iteratively updates the meta prompt similar to the backpropagation algorithm. We additionally leverage a search algorithm to search for the best configuration of LLM agent systems, similar to the neural architecture search (NAS) (Liu et al., 2018) in DL research. In summary, our main contributions are as follows:
• The first work to investigate constructing LLM agent systems from the DL perspective and recipe, extending the science and engineering of LLM agent systems.
• Proposing DL-style building blocks for LLMs and constructing a "Transformer" architecture for LLM agent systems. Observing at least 5% performance gain by "backpropagating" through the LLM agent system via a novel feedback-propagation algorithm.
• An automatic search algorithm for the best configuration of LLM agent systems, similar to NAS in DL, brings an 11% performance gain compared to prior practice.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Modules of Deep Learning.
text: In the area of DL, researchers have designed various basic modules to tackle different tasks. In the early period of DL design, researchers proposed MLP (Popescu et al., 2009) to solve tasks such as classification, prediction, and regression. However, this basic architecture is less effective for complex input data. Consequently, researchers have developed specialized modules with various functionalities. RNNs (Li et al., 2019;Selvin et al., 2017;Jordan, 1997) are tailored for sequential data, maintaining a hidden state to capture information across time steps. CNNs (Kiranyaz et al., 2015;2019) excel at capturing local patterns within images. Additionally, Attention mechanism (Wang et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2019;Hou et al., 2019) further refines model focus by emphasizing the most salient segments within the data. By combining and arranging these specialized modules, researchers have developed numerous powerful architectures. For instance, the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017b;Han et al., 2021), one of the most popular architectures today, relies on the attention mechanism and simple feed-forward layers. It has demonstrated surprising results in generative AI. Additionally, some researchers have integrated the attention mechanism into RNNs, yielding very promising outcomes (Wang & Tax, 2016;Merity, 2019). Researchers have further developed automated architecture engineering, such as Neural Architecture Search (NAS) (Liu et al., 2018;Zoph & Le, 2016;Pham et al., 2018), aiming to find the optimized design of our machine learning model.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Modules of Deep Learning.
text: Construction of LLM Agent Systems. Much of the current research on LLM agent systems relies on the insights and observations from other domains (Yao et al., 2022;Shinn et al., 2023;Kwon et al., 2023;Chen et al., 2023). However, these designs are often problem-specific and do not offer a systematic approach to defining a good LLM agent system architecture. Recent efforts, like Langchainfoot_0 and LlamaIndexfoot_1 , aim to offer standardized building blocks and modules for LLM agent systems. However, they still lack a systematic approach to designing different LLM agent systems for various tasks, providing limited guidance on their integration for sophisticated and meaningful architectural compositions. In response, we propose the development of standardized modules for LLM agent system design, inspired by the proven methodologies within the DL domain. In this work, we show that these basic building blocks can be synthesized into a coherent framework, offering a novel, modular approach to architectures in LLMs that builds a bridge between LLMs and DL.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Deep-Learning-Style Building Blocks of LLM Agent Systems / Forward Inference and Feedback Propagatio
text:
To introduce the basic building blocks of LLMs and the relationship between DL and LLMs, we "translate" the modules of LLMs into modules of DL as shown in Figure 1.
Vanilla LLM as Single Layer MLP. As a basic component when constructing an LLM agent system, an LLM receives a query q and outputs a response r. It can be translated as a single layer MLP, as shown in Figure 1(a), which also plays a fundamental role in DL (Popescu et al., 2009).
Memory Processor as Recurrent Neural Network. During the interaction process of the LLM, it will store the knowledge obtained by the interaction as memories {m 0 , m 1 , ...m n , q} and utilize these memories for future responses (Shinn et al., 2023;Kwon et al., 2023) as shown in Figure 1(b). Similarly, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) excels at processing sequential data due to its inherent structure that allows for the storage and utilization of previous information (Li et al., 2019;Selvin et al., 2017;Jordan, 1997). It achieves this by maintaining hidden states h t that are updated at each time step t, effectively encoding the history of the sequence {m 0 , m 1 , ...m n , q} up to that point. Therefore, we regard the memory processor as RNN.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Deep-Learning-Style Building Blocks of LLM Agent Systems / Forward Inference and Feedback Propagatio
text:
Retrieval as Attention Network. When LLMs interact with factual knowledge stored in the corpus context C, they utilize retrieval (Robertson et al., 2009;Izacard et al., 2022;Lin et al., 2023) to efficiently retrieve accurate context for future responses. As shown in the left part of Figure 1(c), to retrieve the accurate context, retrieval exploits the embedding similarity between query q and corpus context C and obtains the retrieved context C r of the top K similarity ranking. This process is similar to the attention network shown in the right part of Figure 1(c). They both utilize the embedding similarity between query q and corpus context C to obtain an importance score f , which determines the importance weights of each context. From this perspective, we translate the retrieval as an attention network. To be specific, single-query retrieval can be interpreted as single-head attention and multi-query retrieval can be regarded as multi-head attention (Wang et al., 2017;Fu et al., 2019;Hou et al., 2019).
Prompting Strategies as Graph Neural Network. As shown in Figure 1(d), common prompting strategies, such as Tree of Thoughts (ToT) (Yao et al., 2024) and Graph of Thoughts (GoT) (Besta et al., 2023) both decompose query q into interconnected thoughts, which are connected and related to each other. These query and thought nodes and their relationships can be abstracted into nodes and edges of Graph Neural Networks, respectively. Since a tree is a special case of a graph, we treat both ToT and GoT as instances of the GNN analogy in the subsequent introduction, denoting the corresponding architectures as Tree and GNN, respectively.

text:
Climate change is primarily caused by human activities.
Climate change is mainly due to natural factors.
Reflection:. This response overlooks the significant impact of human activities. In this process, meta prompt is regarded as trainable parameters in DL. For the forward inference, the input query goes through the composition of LLM building blocks to obtain the response, which is guided through the meta prompt. For the feedback propagation, the feedback from the self-reflection updates the parameters (meta prompt) of LLM.
Parameters of the LLM agent system. The parameters can be divided into two categories: training parameters and hyperparameters. Here, the meta prompt in Figure 2 is equivalent to training parameters in deep learning, since it guides forward inference and can be updated through feedback propagation. Moreover, hyperparameters in LLM agent systems include max tokens of each LLM (size of MLP); number of retrievals (head number of attention network); retrieve number of each retrieval (mask); node number or depth of tree/graph of thoughts (node number or layer number of GNN); etc. These are predefined before using the LLM agent systems.
Forward Inference. In the forward inference process of DL, the input data passes through each block of the neural network to obtain the final output (Buscema, 1998;Prabhushankar & AlRegib, 2022). Similar to this, in the forward inference process of LLM, the input query goes through the composition of LLM building blocks to obtain the response as shown in Figure 2. Here we set up a meta prompt to guide the forward inference of LLM, which contains the input query, previous responses, and reflection returned by the self-reflection module.

title: Building LLM Agent Systems the Deep Learning Way: From Modular Design to Architecture Search
heading: Composition of LLM Blocks Previous Responses: / Reflection:
text: Feedback Propagation. Many researchers attribute the success of DL to the feedback propagation process of DL (Buscema, 1998;Luft, 2014), which updates the parameters of DL through feedback of losses between outputs and ground truths. Inspired by this, as illustrated in Figure 2, we regard the meta prompt as parameters of LLM and design a self-reflection module as the loss function to evaluate the effect of response on input query and update the parameters of LLM. Specifically, the self-reflection contains LLM Evaluation and Metric Calculation. For some queries whose response quality has clear metrics, we will choose Metric Calculation. Otherwise, we utilize LLM Evaluation to make LLM judge the quality of the response. The generated reflections and responses will be used to update the meta prompt to guide the LLM response in the next round.

heading: Case study: Building a "Transformer" with LLM Building Blocks
text: In this section, we introduce how to build a (cross-attention) Transformer with LLM building blocks. As illustrated in Figure 3, we show the correspondence between the main modules of the cross-attention transformer and LLM building blocks to illustrate how to utilize LLM building blocks to build a transformer. For the cross-attention transformer, the two different features of data will first go through a cross-attention network, and the output will be obtained through an MLP layer. To avoid the vanishing gradient problem or gradient explosion, researchers will also add the residual module to improve the training performance The multi-query retrieval is equivalent to the cross-attention network, and the LLM is translated to MLP in DL. Additionally, the process of appending the raw query to the generated multiple queries is equivalent to the residual.

section: Models: Various Architectures for LLM Agent Systems (method)

We delve into the detailed descriptions of the architectures we explored, with a particular emphasis on their implementations and the methods employed for backward propagation across various modules. For the two LLM datasets without external knowledge, we design the following four basic architectures: (1) MLP: a single LLM;
(2) RNN-MLP: previous responses are appended to the meta prompt to guide the generation of response; (3) Tree-MLP: utilizes ToT to generate multiple thoughts for response generation;
(4) GNN-MLP: GoT is exploited to develop various thoughts for response generation.
We also develop four basic architectures for LLM agent systems with external knowledge. In order to interact with external knowledge, the four architectures are supplemented with the attention to retrieve relevant information based on the above architectures: (1) Att-MLP: a single retrieval to retrieve relevant information for LLM; (2) RNN-Att-MLP: previous responses are appended into the meta prompt to change the query for retrieval; (3) Tree-Att-MLP: utilize ToT to generate new query for retrieval; (4) GNN-Att-MLP:
GoT is exploited to develop new query to retrieve. More details about the basic architectures of LLM agent systems are introduced in Appendix C. Additionally, we have shown an example of the meta prompt used for RNN-MLP on the GSM8K dataset in Figure 4. Other meta prompts are also summarized in Appendix B.

As shown in Figure 5, we optimize the hyperparameters of each module using Optuna. To be specific, we first conclude the hyperparameters and define their optimization range in Table 5 of Appendix D: Output size m 1 (max tokens) for LLM prompting, head num h and retrieve num n of each head for multi-retrieval, output size m 2 for output LLM, and output size m 3 for self-reflection. We utilize 30% of the dataset (training set) for searching for an optimization architecture and 70% for testing (testing set) and further define F1 as the optimization goal. For each set of hyperparameters pr i = (m 1 , m 2 , m 3 , h, n), we calculate its F1 performance on training set. As illustrated in Figure 16 of Appendix D, we can obtain {pr i , F 1 i } k via k trials (120 trials in our experiment) and optimize the architecture by maximizing F1. title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Abstract
text: Large language model agents interleave reasoning, action selection, and observation to solve sequential decision-making tasks. In deployed settings where agents repeatedly handle related multi-step tasks, small actionselection errors can accumulate into wasted tool calls, latency, and reduced reliability. Despite this need for deployment-time improvement, however, existing inference-time adaptation methods for LLM agents mainly rely on prompting or retrieval, which influence behavior indirectly through context manipulation. For ReAct-style agents, such approaches do not expose an explicit decision layer that can score candidate actions, represent uncertainty, or be updated online from action-level feedback. As a result, they provide limited support for trackable, fine-grained, and uncertainty-aware adaptation during deployment. We propose OLIVIA, an inference-time action adaptation framework for ReAct-style agents. OLIVIA models the LLM's final action-selection layer as a contextual linear bandit over candidate actions, with frozen hidden states as decision contexts. This choice is particularly suitable for deployment because it adapts behavior directly at the action-selection interface, preserves the underlying reasoning process, and provides explicit uncertainty estimates and lightweight online updates from action-level feedback. With upper-confidence-bound exploration, OLIVIA improves the policy sample-efficiently with minimal computational overhead. We instantiate OLIVIA on four benchmarks and show that it consistently improves task performance over static ReAct and prompt-based inference-time baselines. Our results suggest that explicit online decision layers provide an effective alternative to purely prompt or retrieval-based adaptation for LLM agents during deployment.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Introduction
text: LLM agents increasingly operate as sequential decision makers in deployed settings such as tool-using assistants, API orchestration systems, and enterprise workflow agents. In these applications, the agent must interleave natural-language reasoning, action selection, and environment feedback through a sequence of thoughts, actions, and observations in order to complete multi-step tasks. ReAct-style prompting has emerged as a practical template for such agents because it exposes intermediate decisions, supports multi-step interaction, and can be deployed without parameter updates (Wu et al., 2025b;Nguyen et al., 2025;Xia et al., 2025). However, despite this sequential structure, agent behavior is typically static at inference time: the model follows a fixed prompt-guided policy, while feedback gathered during deployment is not used to systematically improve future decisions. In repeated or streaming deployments, this limitation can be costly. Agents may revisit similar decision states, repeat the same local mistakes, and waste interaction budget when an early error leads to an unproductive trajectory. A growing body of work seeks to improve inferencetime behavior through prompt engineering (Yao et al., 2023b), reflection (Shinn et al., 2023), or memory augmentation (Majumder et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2025a;b). These approaches can change what the model generates, but they typically do not provide an explicit online optimization mechanism for sequential decision making (Huang et al., 2025a). In particular, they offer limited support for adapting action-selection behavior from observed feedback over a stream of related tasks. As a result, improvements often remain indirect, heuristic, or tied to prompt design rather than to an explicit decision layer that can learn during deployment.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Online optimization of sequential decisions.
text: A complementary line of work treats inference itself as an online optimization problem over a sequence of intermediate decisions. In reasoning, this appears as explicit search or planning over thought states (Yao et al., 2023a;Hao et al., 2023); in agent settings, as treesearch-based interaction and planning with environment feedback (Zhou et al., 2024;Koh et al., 2026;Mundada et al., 2026); and in test-time compute scaling, as adaptive allocation of inference resources such as branching depth or search breadth (Inoue et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2024;Kveton et al., 2025). Related uncertainty-aware methods also use posterior sampling or contextual Thompson sampling to guide sequential choice under partial feedback (Cai et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2025;Xia et al., 2023). Together, these works motivate viewing inference as online optimization over reasoning, acting, and compute allocation. Our method is closest to this perspective: we study online adaptation for sequential LLM decision making using frozen-model contextual representations and lightweight online updates from observed step-level feedback. Closely related online-RL formulations adapt action policies under simulator-to-deployment dynamics shift (Wu et al., 2022), while pluralistic off-policy evaluation extends this view to multi-stakeholder alignment (Huang et al., 2025b;Xie et al., 2025).

heading: ReAct-Style Sequential Agents
text: We consider an LLM agent that interacts with an environment over multiple decision steps following the ReAct paradigm (Yao et al., 2023b;Zhou et al., 2024;Koh et al., 2026). In episode e, the agent receives a task input q e and a candidate action set A e . Let h e,t-1 denote the interaction history before step t, comprising prior reasoning traces, selected actions, and environment observations. At step t the agent selects an action a e,t ∈ A e,t , receives an observation o e,t , and updates the history: h e,t = h e,t-1 ⊕ (a e,t , o e,t ), where ⊕ denotes concatenation. The episode terminates when the agent issues a stop action or reaches a step budget. Because the history grows with each step, every action decision is conditioned on a distinct, trajectory-dependent context x e,t = (q e , h e,t-1 ).

heading: Problem Formulation
text: We study online inference-time action adaptation for sequential LLM agents. Our goal is to enable a frozen language model to improve its action choices over a stream of related episodes by updating only a lightweight decision layer from interaction feedback, without fine-tuning the backbone. This section develops the conceptual foundation in three steps: we first show that ReAct-style action selection naturally maps to a contextual bandit problem, then identify a linear decision interface inside the frozen LLM that can serve as the bandit's scoring mechanism, and finally argue that this structure enables principled online adaptation with exploration.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Online Adaptation and Exploration
text:
Replacing the frozen scoring weights with learnable parameters creates an online learning problem: the agent must estimate which actions yield high reward in each context from a growing stream of partial-feedback interactions. A critical challenge is that feedback is observed only for the selected action. If the learner always picks the action that currently looks best, it may never discover that an under-explored action is superior in a given context.
Existing inference-time adaptation methods do not address this challenge directly. Promptbased approaches such as reflection (Shinn et al., 2023) and memory augmentation (Majumder et al., 2023) influence behavior indirectly through context manipulation, but they have no mechanism to systematically explore uncertain actions or to quantify how confident the agent is about each candidate.
The linear bandit structure identified in Section 4.2 provides a principled solution. Because the learner maintains an explicit parametric model of action quality, it can estimate not only the expected reward of each action but also the uncertainty of that estimate. An optimistic selection rule can then add an exploration bonus proportional to the current uncertainty, favoring actions whose reward is still poorly characterized. As more feedback is collected, the uncertainty shrinks and the learner concentrates on high-reward actions-balancing exploration and exploitation automatically.

text:
The partial-feedback nature of the problem (Section 4.3) demands a selection rule that actively explores uncertain actions. We adopt the LinUCB strategy (Li et al., 2010), which augments the predicted reward with an exploration bonus that reflects the learner's uncertainty about each action in the current context.

The exploration bonus has two desirable properties. First, it is context-dependent: the bonus for a given action varies with the decision state, so the controller explores actions that are uncertain in the current context rather than exploring uniformly at random. Second, it shrinks automatically as data accumulates: each observation tightens the confidence ellipsoid, reducing the bonus for well-characterized actions and concentrating selection on those that remain uncertain. These properties distinguish UCB from simpler alternatives. ε-greedy exploration selects randomly and ignores the structure of the context space; Thompson sampling introduces stochastic noise that can be harder to diagnose in deployment; promptbased adaptation methods have no explicit exploration mechanism at all.

The partial-feedback nature of the problem (Section 4.3) demands a selection rule that actively explores uncertain actions. We adopt the LinUCB strategy (Li et al., 2010), which augments the predicted reward with an exploration bonus that reflects the learner's uncertainty about each action in the current context.

where α > 0 is the exploration coefficient. The first term is the current reward estimate; the second term is the exploration bonus, proportional to the width of the confidence interval for action a in the direction of the current context. The selected action is a e,t ∈ arg max

The exploration bonus has two desirable properties. First, it is context-dependent: the bonus for a given action varies with the decision state, so the controller explores actions that are uncertain in the current context rather than exploring uniformly at random. Second, it shrinks automatically as data accumulates: each observation tightens the confidence ellipsoid, reducing the bonus for well-characterized actions and concentrating selection on those that remain uncertain. These properties distinguish UCB from simpler alternatives. ε-greedy exploration selects randomly and ignores the structure of the context space; Thompson sampling introduces stochastic noise that can be harder to diagnose in deployment; promptbased adaptation methods have no explicit exploration mechanism at all.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Backbone models.
text:
We use Qwen/Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) and mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1 (Jiang et al., 2023) as base language models, chosen as representative open-weight backbones that support ReAct-style tool use while remaining practical for repeated online evaluation. We keep the backbone, system prompt, and few-shot demonstrations fixed across all methods so that performance differences can be attributed to the decision policy alone.
Baselines. We compare against both non-learning and inference-time adaptation baselines. CoT (Wei et al., 2023) uses chain-of-thought prompting for free-form reasoning and tool selection without online adaptation. BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) ranks candidate tools by lexical similarity to the task description. ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) performs iterative reasoning and tool selection but does not adapt across episodes. CLIN (Majumder et al., 2023) is a memory-based continual-adaptation method that updates a persistent textual memory after each episode to improve future decisions.
Online protocol. Each dataset is treated as a stream of episodes. For every seed, we randomly shuffle the episode order and run each method sequentially over that stream, reporting mean and standard deviation over three random seeds. All methods use the same per-episode step budget B = |G| + s, where |G| is the ground-truth tool-multiset size and s is a small fixed allowance for recovery from early mistakes, and each tool is capped at m selections per episode to prevent degenerate repetition.
Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate tool-selection quality using multiset-matching precision, recall, and F1 (Patil et al., 2023), reporting macro-averaged scores over episodes with F1 as the primary metric. For the synthetic experiments described in Section 6.3, we additionally report cumulative regret and parameter estimation error ∥ θtθ ⋆ ∥ 2 2 . OLIVIA converges faster and recovers the true reward parameter more accurately.

title: OLIVIA: Online Learning via Inference-time Action Adaptation for Decision Making in LLM ReAct Agents
heading: Conclusion
text:
We presented OLIVIA, an inference-time action adaptation framework for ReAct-style agents. By placing an explicit online decision layer at the action-selection interface of a frozen language model, OLIVIA adapts behavior directly from action-level feedback while preserving the underlying reasoning process. Instantiated as a contextual linear bandit over hidden decision states, the method provides lightweight online updates, explicit uncertainty estimates, and sample-efficient exploration through UCB. Across four benchmarks, OLIVIA consistently improves task performance over static ReAct and prompt-based inference-time baselines, showing that deployment-time adaptation can be achieved without model finetuning. More broadly, our results suggest that explicit online decision layers are a promising alternative to purely prompt-or retrieval-based adaptation for sequential decision making in LLM agents.
LLM usage: AI writing tools were used to assist with drafting and the icons in Figure1 are generated by AI drawing tool.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Abstract
text: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate Federated Agent Optimization (FAO), which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

heading: Introduction
text:
In recent years, large language model (LLM)-driven agents [60,130,182] have gradually evolved from general-purpose conversational systems [5] toward executing complex tasks in real-world environments, becoming an important paradigm for enterprise AI systems [207]. An increasing number of organizations are deploying agents in applications such as customer service [178,58,66], software development [146,19], data analysis [72,155], knowledge management [177,197,160], office automation [191], financial services [158], healthcare assistance [142,125,79,97], and business process execution [101,81,65,40]. Unlike traditional language models that primarily focus on content generation [102], enterprise agents [135] typically need to integrate internal knowledge [78], business data, proprietary tools, and operational workflows to autonomously privacy, and communication cost. Second, we organize existing and emerging approaches according to the agent capability being federated, including policies, memory, tool use, rewards, and structured knowledge and skills. Third, we characterize how private local experience can be transformed into transferable capabilities through abstraction, protection, aggregation, and local adaptation, and further examine when such transfer leads to mutual improvement across agents. Building on this framework, we identify key challenges in balancing performance, privacy, and communication, ensuring fair contribution and benefit allocation, and reliably evaluating federation gains. Finally, we highlight several open research directions toward trustworthy, efficient, and continuously improving federated agent systems.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Related Work
text: Federated Learning and Federated Large Models Federated learning [196,103,226] enables multiple clients [55] to collaboratively train models while keeping raw data local, providing a general paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed learning [80]. Early studies [145] mainly focused on model aggregation under heterogeneous data distributions, while subsequent work further explored communication efficiency [33], personalization [173], robustness [76,107], and privacy protection [195,106]. With the emergence of foundation models and large language models [241,126], federated learning has been extended to large-scale model adaptation [93], where parameter-efficient techniques such as federated fine-tuning [193,198], LoRA [171,14], prompt tuning [239,27], and knowledge distillation [162] are increasingly adopted to reduce computation and communication costs. Despite these advances, existing federated large-model methods still primarily treat model parameters or representations as the main optimization objects. In contrast, an agent [60] typically involves not only an underlying model, but also memory, tool use, rewards, skills, and external knowledge. Therefore, federating a large model is not equivalent to federating an agent, motivating a broader optimization paradigm that considers the complete capabilities of agents.

With the emergence of foundation models and large language models [241,126], federated learning has been extended to large-scale model adaptation [93], where parameter-efficient techniques such as federated fine-tuning [193,198], LoRA [171,14], prompt tuning [239,27], and knowledge distillation [162] are increasingly adopted to reduce computation and communication costs. Despite these advances, existing federated large-model methods still primarily treat model parameters or representations as the main optimization objects. In contrast, an agent [60] typically involves not only an underlying model, but also memory, tool use, rewards, skills, and external knowledge. Therefore, federating a large model is not equivalent to federating an agent, motivating a broader optimization paradigm that considers the complete capabilities of agents.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Related Work
text:
Multi-Agent Systems and Agent Reinforcement learning Multi-agent systems [69,221,98] study how multiple agents coordinate, communicate, divide tasks, and make joint decisions in shared or interacting environments. With the rise of large language models, recent LLM-based multi-agent systems [69,210,34] have further explored role specialization, discussion, negotiation, and mutual feedback to improve performance on complex tasks. In parallel, agent learning focuses on continuously improving agent capabilities through execution trajectories [176], environmental feedback [219], reinforcement learning [245,227], self-reflection [17], and teacher-agent guidance [215]. Despite this progress, most existing multi-agent and agent-learning methods assume that agents can directly exchange messages, trajectories, or feedback during collaboration, while privacy constraints and data isolation across organizations or private environments are rarely considered. This differs fundamentally from federated agent optimization, where agents are expected to benefit from each other while keeping local data, execution experience, and private knowledge decentralized.
Privacy-Preserving AI Privacy-preserving AI [131] aims to reduce the risk of sensitive information leakage while enabling effective model training and inference. Common techniques include differential privacy [6], secure aggregation [118], homomorphic encryption [87], secure multi-party computation [161], and access control [83]. These techniques have been widely adopted in distributed learning [32,22], cloud-based inference [62], and cross-organization collaboration [26,132] to protect training data, model updates, and intermediate representations. However, existing privacy-preserving methods mainly focus on data, model parameters, or inference processes. In agent systems, sensitive information may also be embedded in execution trajectories, memories, tool interactions, business rules, and skill representations, which calls for new protection mechanisms tailored to collaborative agent optimization.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Key Challenges
text: The mechanisms above illustrate how local experience can be transformed into transferable capabilities and ultimately improve other agents. However, they also expose three fundamental challenges that distinguish FAO from conventional federated learning. First, performance, privacy, and communication are inherently coupled rather than independently optimizable objectives. Second, heterogeneous participants may contribute and benefit unevenly, making fairness central to sustained collaboration. Third, the gains of federation are difficult to verify because agent outcomes are long-horizon, environmentdependent, and not yet supported by dedicated evaluation protocols. These challenges extend the statistical and system heterogeneity already studied in federated learning [86,96] from model optimization to the broader problem of collaborative agent improvement.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Performance, Privacy and Communication Trade-offs
text: The three objectives of FAO-task performance, privacy protection, and communication efficiency-form a tightly coupled trade-off. Improving performance generally requires sharing information that preserves sufficient detail about local experience, yet richer updates can increase both privacy exposure and communication overhead. Data locality alone does not eliminate this risk: gradients and model updates can reveal information about local training examples [54,129], while memories, skill descriptions, tool-use knowledge, and structured artifacts may disclose sensitive content more directly. Stronger protection, such as differential privacy, reduces disclosure but can also degrade the information available for optimization [1]. Conversely, aggressive compression can substantially reduce communication traffic [112], but may remove information that is important for capability transfer. Secure aggregation protects individual updates from direct inspection [18], yet this can further constrain validation of what is being shared. Client heterogeneity additionally changes the utility of the same update across participants and can induce objective inconsistency in global optimization [181]. The central challenge is therefore not to minimize any single cost in isolation, but to identify operating points at which useful capability transfer remains possible under explicit privacy and communication budgets. This makes the Pareto trade-off defined in Section 3 a central systems question for practical FAO.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: How to Ensure Fairness in Federated Agent Systems?
text: A second challenge is ensuring that the benefits and burdens of federation are distributed fairly across heterogeneous participants. Improvements in federation-wide utility may coexist with substantially different outcomes for individual clients [108,127]. Some agents may contribute highly valuable experience but receive limited benefit in return, whereas others may benefit primarily from knowledge produced elsewhere. At the same time, globally shared capabilities can induce negative transfer when local objectives, task distributions, tools, or operating constraints differ. Personalized federated learning provides mechanisms for retaining local specialization under shared optimization [107,172], but FAO requires a broader notion of fairness that also accounts for non-parametric artifacts such as memories, skills, rewards, and structured knowledge. Contribution estimation is itself difficult because task outcomes result from long sequences of decisions and feedback may be sparse or delayed [9]; attributing recipient-side gains to particular shared contributions introduces an additional layer of credit assignment [68]. The collaboration gain and pairwise contribution defined in Section 5 therefore provide important starting points, but a complete fairness framework must jointly consider what each participant contributes, what benefit it receives, and what privacy, computation, and communication costs it bears. Trustworthy participation ultimately requires that clients retain the ability to personalize, selectively adopt, or reject shared capabilities whose local value does not justify their associated cost or risk.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: How to Evaluate Federated Agent Systems?
text: A third challenge is establishing credible evidence that federated collaboration actually improves agent capability. Agent performance is inherently difficult to verify because success depends on interactions among reasoning, memory retrieval, tool execution, and environmental conditions. Tool-use research shows that apparently similar tools and interfaces can require substantially different execution behavior, while reasoning and environment-facing actions are tightly coupled in interactive agents [214]. Consequently, a shared artifact that appears semantically valid may still fail after transfer to a recipient environment. Verification becomes even harder over time: continual optimization can introduce stale capabilities, distribution drift, and interference with previously acquired knowledge [218,233]. Erroneous or adversarial contributions further complicate the distinction between genuine capability improvement and harmful shared updates [217]. Existing benchmarks evaluate general agent competence, web and desktop interaction, or tool-user workflows [114,244,205,213], while federated benchmarks such as FedScale primarily characterize model and system heterogeneity [95]. FAO requires evaluation protocols that combine these perspectives: controlled client heterogeneity, explicit information-sharing boundaries, repeated collaborative optimization, and credible local baselines. Beyond federation-wide task utility, evaluation should report privacy leakage, communication and system costs, client-level collaboration gains, contribution fairness, negative-transfer rates, and robustness under task or participant drift. Without such benchmarks and metrics, it remains difficult to determine when federation truly creates transferable intelligence rather than merely improving an aggregate score.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Future Works
text:
A central direction for future FAO research is to build trustworthy federated agent systems, where trustworthiness is treated as an end-to-end property of collaborative optimization rather than a single notion of model accuracy or privacy. We highlight several important research questions.
❶ How can transferred capabilities remain reliable and executable across heterogeneous agent environments? A capability that is effective for one agent may rely on specific tools, interfaces, permissions, task distributions, or workflow contexts that do not hold for another agent. Prior work on grounded planning, tool use, and multi-agent workflows highlights the importance of environment-aware execution and capability composition [77,67,104,73]. Future FAO systems should therefore explicitly model the applicability conditions, dependencies, and execution constraints of transferred capabilities, rather than assuming that capabilities remain valid after cross-agent transfer.
❷ How can federated agent systems protect privacy while remaining secure against unreliable or malicious contributions? Keeping raw data local does not eliminate leakage from model parameters, memories, textual abstractions, tool knowledge, or structured representations. Differential privacy and secure aggregation provide useful foundations for limiting such leakage [1,18], while robust aggregation is necessary to tolerate faulty or adversarial participants [15,21]. Future research should jointly consider confidentiality, update integrity, and the tension between protecting shared information and validating its quality.
❸ How can fair contribution and benefit allocation be achieved among heterogeneous agents? Different agents may contribute unequal amounts of useful experience, receive different levels of benefit, or even suffer negative transfer. Personalized and fairnessaware federated learning provide useful foundations for preserving local specialization and participant-level utility [49,82,156,111]. Future FAO research should further quantify contribution, collaboration gain, and participation cost, and ensure that agents receive benefits commensurate with the information, privacy, and resources they contribute.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Future Works
text:
❹ How should federated agent systems be evaluated? Reliable evaluation should verify whether collaboration genuinely improves local agents compared with credible local baselines, rather than relying only on shared evaluators or aggregate performance. This is particularly challenging when feedback is sparse, trajectories are long, and environments are stochastic [39,133,154,120]. Existing agent and federated benchmarks provide useful starting points [114,244,205,213,95], but FAO additionally requires explicit information-sharing boundaries, heterogeneous participants, repeated collaboration, and longitudinal evaluation of recipient-level gains, negative transfer, and robustness under drift.
❺ How should the full lifecycle cost of federated agent collaboration be measured and optimized? Communication volume alone is insufficient to characterize the cost of FAO. Collaboration may also incur substantial costs for local adaptation, privacy protection, validation, inference, tool execution, storage, synchronization, and continual maintenance, especially under heterogeneous computation and model capacities [4,123,43]. Future work should therefore develop lifecycle-level cost models that jointly account for the resources required to produce, protect, aggregate, validate, deploy, and maintain shared capabilities.
Taken together, these questions suggest that trustworthy FAO should jointly consider execution reliability, privacy and security, fairness, credible evaluation, and lifecycle cost, providing a principled basis for collaborative learning among autonomous agents across organizations.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: Conclusion
text: This paper formulates Federated Agent Optimization (FAO) as a general framework for collaborative improvement across policies, memories, tool use, rewards, and structured knowledge under distributed data and local constraints. By extending federated optimization beyond model parameters, we establish a multi-objective problem formulation, a taxonomy of federated agent components, and an improvement framework that connects local experience to transferable capabilities and recipient-side gains. Our analysis highlights three central challenges-balancing performance, privacy, and communication cost, ensuring fair contribution and benefit allocation, and reliably verifying the gains of federation-which together motivate the broader goal of building trustworthy FAO systems with reliable execution, privacy and security protection, credible evaluation, and principled cost accounting. We envision FAO as a foundation for scalable, trustworthy, and continuously evolving enterprise AI systems that benefit from collective experience while preserving local specialization and organizational control.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.1 Federated Policy Optimization
text:
The policy block ∆ π k carries parameters of the policy. Its form depends on how much access the clients have to the backbone.
Weights. When the backbone is open, clients fine-tune it on local data with parameterefficient methods and the coordinator aggregates the updates [229,216,235,203]. Later work addresses clients with different adapter ranks [193,38,11] and the instability of adapters under differential privacy noise [171]. Personalized variants keep part of the adapter local [211,116,59]. At the other extreme of communication cost, zeroth-order optimization lets clients and server exchange only random seeds and scalar gradients [151].
The same recipe has been applied to agents. GUI agents based on vision-language models are trained on decentralized user data [186,187,185]. Fed-SE fine-tunes adapters on the successful trajectories of each client [35]. FedAgent trains the policy by reinforcement learning on local trajectories and averages the parameters [29]. It finds the result robust to heterogeneity of tasks but not to heterogeneity of environment dynamics. This agrees with the theory of federated reinforcement learning [144,50,89], in which the suboptimality of the learned policy grows with the heterogeneity of the environments [84]. FedWave federates the role-specific adapters of a workflow whose stages belong to different organizations [240]. Frameworks that separate the execution of an agent from its training make such methods applicable to existing agents [117].

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.1 Federated Policy Optimization
text: Prompts. When the backbone is a frozen model behind an API, the policy is optimized through its prompts. Clients can share continuous prompts [61], optimize prompts without gradients by querying the model [170,113], or share textual prompts that the coordinator merges by summarization [30]. The last option connects FAO to the optimization of prompts and agentic workflows [208,88,222,3], where the variables are text and the optimizer is often itself a language model. Trade-offs. Weight sharing is the most mature form and the most expensive in communication: Fed-SE reports 76.3 MB per round for adapters of rank 8 [35]. Its leakage is well studied. Gradients can be inverted to recover training text, for recent attacks exactly and for large batches [246,64,139], and restricting the update to adapters does not remove the risk [163]. Secure aggregation and differentially private training are the standard defenses [18,1]. Prompt sharing has a small payload and works with closed backbones, but a textual prompt is readable by anyone who receives it and may quote the examples from which it was derived.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.2 Federated Memory Optimization
text:
The memory block ∆ M k carries experience in abstracted form. Raw trajectories are the most informative content of memory and the most sensitive, so they stay local. What can be shared are the products that agents already derive from trajectories for their own use: reflections on failures [167], insights extracted from successes and failures [237], workflows induced from repeated tasks [194], and reasoning strategies [134].
Several systems let agents share such items through a common store: a pool of prompt-answer pairs [53], a hierarchical memory for the agents of one system [228], and a knowledge base of workflows and fixes built from the trajectories of different agent frameworks [174]. Access control over memory that is shared among users has also been studied [157]. These systems assume that the store is trusted.
Federated methods avoid centralizing raw trajectories in such a store. In FoT, each client uploads summaries of its reasoning traces, without the problem instances or task instructions, and the server distills them into a library of insights that all clients can use [212]. FedAgentKE exchanges knowledge units that contain reusable workflows and corrections together with a utility score, and each client retrieves the units relevant to its task [109]. For document collections, federated retrieval-augmented generation [24] answers queries over the collections of several providers without centralizing the documents, protected by confidential computing [2] or homomorphic encryption [238], and it trains the retrievers of the clients by federated learning [121].
Aggregation. Memory items are text, so they cannot be averaged. The coordinator clusters the items, removes duplicates, merges items that express the same pattern, and ranks the result by utility or by the number of clients that support it. A language model performs these operations, which makes the coordinator an agent in its own right.

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.3 Federated Tool-Use Optimization
text:
The tool block ∆ T k carries knowledge about how to use tools. In the horizontal setting the clients use tools of the same kind, such as customer databases, payment interfaces, or document recognition, and standard interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol [8] make the descriptions of tools comparable across clients.
Research on single agents shows what this knowledge consists of [149,153]. Models learn to call tools from examples of correct calls [165,137,150]. Concise and consistent descriptions improve the use of a tool [220], and a description can be refined from the experience of calling the tool [152]. Agents can also create new tools [20,147,189].
Two methods federate such knowledge. In FICAL, each client writes a compendium that describes its tools, the scenarios in which to use them, precautions, and the coordination of several tools; the server concatenates the compendiums, and the agents retrieve from the result [200]. Typed federated artifacts replace free text by schema-validated objects with separate fields for privacy handling, conflict resolution, and transfer across models, and they are designed for frozen models of different vendors [25]. Usage statistics, such as the success rate of a tool for a given intent, are a third kind of tool knowledge. Only their sum is needed, so they can be protected by secure aggregation.

section: B.3 Federated Tool-Use Optimization (other)

The tool block ∆ T k carries knowledge about how to use tools. In the horizontal setting the clients use tools of the same kind, such as customer databases, payment interfaces, or document recognition, and standard interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol [8] make the descriptions of tools comparable across clients.
Research on single agents shows what this knowledge consists of [149,153]. Models learn to call tools from examples of correct calls [165,137,150]. Concise and consistent descriptions improve the use of a tool [220], and a description can be refined from the experience of calling the tool [152]. Agents can also create new tools [20,147,189].

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.3 Federated Tool-Use Optimization
text: Trade-offs. Tool knowledge in text is small compared with model weights: FICAL reports 0.078 MB against 26,000 MB for baselines that exchange parameters [200]. It is not small by nature, however, and a compendium of tool-routing experience can reach 20 MB per client and round [25]. The leakage concerns the systems of the client more than its data: tool schemas disclose the structure of internal systems, and the arguments of recorded calls may contain customer records. Shared tool knowledge is also an attack surface. A tool description is an instruction to the agent that reads it, and threats from malicious tool providers are documented for the Model Context Protocol [74]. Aggregation of tool knowledge therefore needs robustness against malicious contributions in addition to privacy. Evaluation is a further open issue: the study of typed artifacts reports that a simple retrieval baseline outperforms all of its routing variants based on language models, and concludes that the benchmark cannot measure the benefit of shared routing knowledge [25].

title: Federated Agent Optimization
heading: B.4 Federated Reward Optimization
text:
The reward block ∆ R k carries knowledge about how to judge a trajectory. The problem has a natural division of labor. Clients observe real outcomes and human judgments, but each client has few of them. The coordinator can run a strong evaluator, but language models used as judges show systematic biases [243], and on the trajectories of web agents no single judge is reliable across benchmarks [115].
Federated preference and reward models. Existing methods address the alignment of language models with human preferences [39]. In FedRLHF, the feedback and the reward function stay with the client, and the policies are federated [51]. FedBis and FedBiscuit federate the preference model itself: each client encodes its preferences in a binary selector, and the selectors are aggregated [199]. Reward models and preference predictors are also trained by federated averaging and then personalized by local finetuning [168,90], and a federation of client models can serve as a panel of referees [70]. To our knowledge, no method yet federates an evaluator of agent trajectories.
Building blocks for agents. Three lines of work on single agents provide the pieces. Evaluators can be trained or prompted to judge the success of web navigation and device control [136]. Since feedback arrives at the end of a trajectory, credit must be assigned to individual steps [140]; process reward models, which score each step, serve this purpose [110,23]. Language models can write reward functions from a description of the task [94,119,206]. The last line suggests a form of federation with very low cost: a language model at the coordinator proposes a reward function or a rubric, each client scores the proposal against its private outcomes, and only the scores return to the coordinator.
