title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Design Motivation and Principle
text:
As mentioned in Section 1, most LLM-based agents rely on a static toolset F composed of granular atomic actions. While recent studies have explored expanding the toolset through dynamic code generation (Wang et al., 2025;Yuan et al., 2024), they typically treat tool addition as a one-time event and lack a long-term management mechanism, leading to several critical limitations:
(i) Unreliable Tool Executability: Although LLMs can generate syntactically correct code, synthesized tools often fail in complex environments due to various engineering reasons. Without a systematic evaluation and refinement, tools remain fragile and cannot be trusted for long-term tasks.
(ii) Limited Generalization and Reusability: Tools derived from narrow scenarios often encode context-dependent logic that lacks broader applicability. Without a mechanism to iteratively abstract actions into reusable SOPs, the agent reinvents lowlevel logic, failing to achieve the hierarchical reasoning efficiency seen in human problem-solving.
(iii) Redundancy: In the absence of a lifecycle management (e.g., merging and pruning), continuous tool creation leads to a bloated toolset and brings noise to the agent's context. Increasing reasoning overhead complicates the LLM's decisionmaking, ultimately degrading the success rate.
To address these challenges, EVOSOP moves beyond simple tool creation by establishing a continuous and iterative tool optimization process.

As mentioned in Section 1, most LLM-based agents rely on a static toolset F composed of granular atomic actions. While recent studies have explored expanding the toolset through dynamic code generation (Wang et al., 2025;Yuan et al., 2024), they typically treat tool addition as a one-time event and lack a long-term management mechanism, leading to several critical limitations:
(i) Unreliable Tool Executability: Although LLMs can generate syntactically correct code, synthesized tools often fail in complex environments due to various engineering reasons. Without a systematic evaluation and refinement, tools remain fragile and cannot be trusted for long-term tasks.
(ii) Limited Generalization and Reusability: Tools derived from narrow scenarios often encode context-dependent logic that lacks broader applicability. Without a mechanism to iteratively abstract actions into reusable SOPs, the agent reinvents lowlevel logic, failing to achieve the hierarchical reasoning efficiency seen in human problem-solving.
(iii) Redundancy: In the absence of a lifecycle management (e.g., merging and pruning), continuous tool creation leads to a bloated toolset and brings noise to the agent's context. Increasing reasoning overhead complicates the LLM's decisionmaking, ultimately degrading the success rate.
To address these challenges, EVOSOP moves beyond simple tool creation by establishing a continuous and iterative tool optimization process.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Overview
text: As illustrated in Figure 1, EVOSOP consists of four collaborative modules that govern the optimization of the toolset, including: (i) CONSTRUCTOR: This module identifies recurring action sequences within execution trajectories ξ, which extracts logical segments of atomic actions that frequently co-occur and synthesizes them into callable SOPs, complete with executable code and semantic schemas; (ii) MERGER: To maintain a lean toolset, this module inspects newly generated SOPs for functional redundancy, merging overlapping routines into generalized and higher-order tools to prevent the bloating of the context C; (iii) EVALUATOR: The agent is equipped with the updated toolset F ′ and reexecutes tasks. This module produces new trajectories that reflect the actual utility and reliability of the evolved SOPs in environments; (iv) REVIEWER: This module acts as a critic by analyzing the performance metrics of synthesized tools, which prunes SOPs that exhibit high error rates or significant redundancy compared to existing tools. Agent Self-Evolution by Non-Parametric Learning. Although EVOSOP does not modify the learnable parameters of the underlying LLM, its iterative structure constitutes a form of nonparametric structural optimization. We formalize this by drawing a conceptual parallel between EVOSOP and the machine learning pipeline. First, the agent's interaction with training tasks represents the data acquisition stage, while the execution of tasks using the current toolset F corresponds to forward propagation. The resulting execution trajectories ξ serve as observable behavioral outputs, capturing the agent's reasoning process and tool-use patterns. Improvement is then achieved through a backward propagation, where EVOSOP analyzes reasoning inefficiencies or execution failures within the trajectories. Instead of updating model weights via gradients, the framework performs "symbolic" backpropagation by extracting and synthesizing reusable SOPs that encapsulate multi-step logic into cohesive routines.

The optimization lifecycle begins with the CONSTRUCTOR, an LLM-based module designed to distill reusable functional abstractions from historical execution trajectories ξ. As established in Section 2, raw trajectories record sequences of atomic actions and environment responses in strict temporal order. title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Tool Optimization Lifecycle in EVOSOP
text:
MERGER: Structural Optimization. As the agent accumulates experience across task domains, functional overlap and redundancy among synthesized SOPs become inevitable, often manifesting as noise within the context C t . Such noise complicates the LLM's decision-making and may lead to the selection of suboptimal or conflicting tools.
To address this, we design the MERGER, a module dedicated to simplifying the toolset and enhancing its overall quality through structural optimization.
The MERGER analyzes the candidate SOP set within a training batch to identify functional overlaps based on shared objectives or highly similar logic. When candidates with convergent functionalities are identified, the module integrates them into a single, more expressive SOP that preserves the constituent capabilities of its predecessors while maintaining a high degree of generality. We formalize this batch-based merging process as follows:
where b denotes the set of task indices, S b is the union of newly constructed SOPs, and S ′ represents the consolidated set generated by the merger.
EVOSOP adopts a non-destructive consolidation strategy during this stage. While newly merged, composite SOPs are added to the toolset, the original constituent SOPs are not immediately removed. This design choice is motivated by two critical observations regarding agent self-evolution. Firstly, even when two SOPs possess nominally identical functionality, they may differ significantly in implementation quality, including robustness, coding style, and the clarity of their docstrings, all of which affect the LLM's ability to invoke them correctly. Secondly, a larger composite SOP is not inherently superior to its more granular components; it may introduce implicit technical defects or reduce execution reliability in specific contexts. By deferring the removal of tools until the verification phase, EVOSOP ensures that the final toolset is refined based on empirical performance rather than static heuristics, adhering to the principle of hierarchical efficiency without sacrificing reliability.

text:
EVALUATOR: Execution-based Validation. As synthesized SOPs are inherently prone to fragility when deployed in complex and stateful environments, they cannot be immediately integrated into the agent's core capabilities without rigorous validation. Specifically, all constructed SOPs within the sets S b and S ′ are loaded into the execution environment. Since these SOPs are instantiated as callable functions, the framework must first bridge the gap between executable code and the LLM's reasoning interface. We accomplish this by extracting the functional schema for each SOP (i.e., comprising its name, semantic description, and parameter specifications) and updating the toolset F as:
This expanded toolset F ′ provides the agent with a hierarchical choice. It can either continue using granular atomic actions or invoke the newly synthesized SOPs to bypass multi-step reasoning.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Tool Optimization Lifecycle in EVOSOP
text:
REVIEWER: Quality Control and Simplification. The final stage of the EVOSOP lifecycle is a rigorous quality control procedure designed to ensure the reliability and effectiveness of the toolset. As SOPs are synthesized independently across varied trajectories, several systematic issues typically arise: (i) functional redundancy among overlapping tools; (ii) semantic misalignment, where misleading tool names or docstrings trigger retrieval errors; (iii) limited utility of tools that are rarely invoked; and (iv) latent technical defects that manifest only in specific stateful contexts. Addressing these challenges is essential to prevent the accumulation of technical debt and the resulting performance degradation caused by bloated toolsets.
Within the reasoning-acting loop, an agent's understanding of an SOP is governed by its docstring. Since these SOPs are automatically generated from historical logs, any discrepancy between the tool's implementation and its semantic description can lead to inappropriate invocations or reasoning failures. To operationalize the assessment of such risks, we introduce REVIEWER, an LLM-based module that functions as a critic. The REVIEWER analyzes the verification trajectories ξ and categorizes each SOP invocation into the following states:
• Optimal Execution: The SOP successfully completes its intended functionality as defined in its docstring without any technical exceptions.
• Partial Utility: The tool executes without technical error but achieves its intended goals partially with complicated reasons.
• Neutrality: The SOP returns successfully but produces no significant change in the environmental state, indicating low practical relevance.
• Negative Interference: The tool negatively impacts task progress or compromises the environmental state, leading to unacceptable outcomes.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Training Workflow
text:
As formally specified in Section 3.3, each component of EVOSOP is designed to support a parameter-free training paradigm. Unlike prior studies that predominantly rely on parametric finetuning, EVOSOP realizes the "training" process through iterative optimization of the toolset. The complete training workflow is presented in Algorithm 1 in Appendix A.
Mini-batching. At the beginning of the training process, we partition the initial execution trajectories ξ into discrete mini-batches. In those batches, the CONSTRUCTOR identifies tool-use patterns and proposes new functional abstractions. Notably, this is the exclusive stage for introducing new SOPs, ensuring the growth of toolset is strictly grounded in observed execution experience.
In every iteration, the MERGER first consolidates overlapping functionalities into generalized procedures to maintain a compact toolset. Subsequently, the system enters an evaluation phase where the agent re-executes all training tasks with the updated SOPs. Using the resulting rollouts, the RE-VIEWER assesses each tool's empirical contribution and prunes those that exhibit implementation defects or redundant reasoning.
Checkpointing. A critical challenge in LLMbased optimization is the potential stochasticity of model behavior, where aggressive pruning might inadvertently remove genuinely beneficial SOPs. To mitigate this risk, EVOSOP avoids a strictly linear update; instead, it adopts a checkpointing mechanism. At the end of each iteration, the full evaluation logs and the current SOP toolset are archived. Since task feedback is obtained directly from the environment in a self-supervised manner, we do not require a separate validation set. We select the iteration that yields the highest training success rate as the final epoch, ensuring that the output toolset S * represents the optimal balance between expressivity and reliability.

heading: Setup
text:
Our evaluation compares several distinct tool configurations: (i) ReAct and DFSDT, which use the original atomic actions; (ii) ASI (Wang et al., 2025), whose toolset is augmented with SOPs, referred to as skills in the original paper, induced through a one-time process; (iii) DRAFT (Qu , 2025), which equips tools with rewritten descriptions and usage guidance; and (iv) EvoSOP, our proposed method that performs iterative SOP optimization. The evaluation is conducted on ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025) and Tau2Bench (Barres et al., 2025). For ACEBench, we use the agent subset, while for Tau2Bench, we use the solo mode of the Telecom subset.
Throughout the experiments, GPT-4o serves as the backbone LLM for all evaluation agents. During the toolset construction phase, we adopt GPT-4o, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, and Qwen-Max to assess cross-model robustness. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix B.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Performance Comparisons
text:
The main experimental results are summarized in Table 1. In general, EVOSOP outperforms both the base agent and other selected tool-related baselines. On both subset of ACEBench, EVOSOP achieves a significant improvement over the base method, yielding gains ranging from 2.5% to 13.4% depending on the backbone model. This performance surge indicates that the evolved SOPs effectively address recurring reasoning bottlenecks by providing the agent with robust and reliable logic blocks.
In the challenging Tau2Bench-Telecom, which is characterized by a larger tool space and intricate stateful transitions, EVOSOP maintains a steady performance lead. Although the margin of improvement is more concentrated compared to ACEBench due to the inherent complexity of the domain, the results show that EVOSOP can navigate and optimize tools even in high-entropy scenarios where static or one-shot toolsets typically struggle.
From the experiments, we also observe that EVOSOP produces reliable SOPs. Our analysis of the trajectories reveals that GPT-4o often encounters reasoning failures as the context window grows or when tasks require precise temporal tracking. For example, in text message management scenario (e.g., deleting the earliest message), agents using atomic actions often become indecisive after multiple turns, frequently returning control to the user for clarification, or deleting the wrong target.

heading: Performance Comparisons
text:
While ASI can induce SOPs for such workflows, its one-shot nature often leads to brittle logic that may delete the latest message instead of the earliest, causing cascading errors in similar but slightly different contexts. In contrast, the behavior of DRAFT becomes more stable as it does not make substantial changes to the tools. EVOSOP employs its REVIEWER and MERGER to evaluate execution feedback. It identifies these subtle logic flaws, merges redundant tools, and prunes SOPs that exhibit high error rates. This iterative self-correction and complete lifecycle management ensure that the resulting toolset is not just larger, but fundamentally more reliable and useful. Reasoning Compression. A core hypothesis in this study is that SOPs should reduce the cognitive load on the agent by encapsulating multi-step workflows. In Figure 2, we illustrate the average number of reasoning rounds per task across the epochs.

In the initial phases, the toolset may contain experimental or unstable SOPs, occasionally leading to redundant trial-and-error reasoning. However, as the iterative cycle progresses, EVOSOP filters out low-utility tools and consolidates overlapping routines. By the final several epochs, the number of interaction rounds stabilizes at a significantly lower level than that of baselines. Such reasoning compression not only reduces API latency and cost but also minimizes the risk of the agent losing focus within long-horizon trajectories, which is a primary driver of the observed increase in success rates.

Specifically, the experimental results reveal that the iterative reviewing and pruning procedure, driven by the REVIEWER, has the most profound impact on final performance. When the pruning mechanism is disabled, the success rate of the agent significantly declines on both datasets. These results confirm that, while the CONSTRUCTOR introduces beneficial SOPs, it also inevitably generates low-quality or context-sensitive tools that can introduce noise. heading: Case Study
text:
To better understand the optimization process, we analyze a representative execution of EVOSOP on ACEBench. We track the utilization and performance metrics of selected SOPs to illustrate how EVOSOP distinguishes between high-utility, highrisk, and redundant tools. As shown in Figure 4, we observe some distinct lifetime patterns: (i) Fundamental SOPs: Tools like fetch_ message exhibit high invocation frequency and near-zero error propensity. These represent stable logic that the framework identifies early and retains as core components of agents.
(ii) Transient SOPs: manage_and_send_message is synthesized during Epoch 1 but immediately evicted by the REVIEWER due to a critical failure rate. This demonstrates the framework's ability to prevent unreliable code from polluting the toolset. Similarly, retrieve_flight_details is pruned after several epochs because its marginal utility is low, it is rarely invoked, and introduces non-negligible reasoning overhead without a pro-portional increase in success rate.
(iii) Merged SOPs: Initially, the CON-STRUCTOR generated two task-specific tools, i.e., order_food_online and order_food_from_ merchant. Later the MERGER identified their functional overlap and synthesized a generalized SOP, enhanced_manage_food_order. Consequently, the original specific tools are pruned to maintain toolset leanness, while the new SOP continued to perform reliably across diverse contexts.
This case clearly demonstrates how the designed components cooperate to produce a compact SOP toolset with high-quality SOPs. In general, the size of the SOP set remains consistently low, even as new SOPs are continually generated. We summarize the macro-level evolution of the toolset composition in Appendix C, showing that EVOSOP maintains the toolset at a compact scale.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
heading: Related Works
text: Early research primarily focuses on enhancing tool mastery through parametric updates, employing supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning to improve tool retrieval and invocation accuracy (Bai et al., 2025;Qin et al., 2024;Li et al., 2025). In contrast, non-parametric methods optimize tool use without modifying the underlying model. For example, DRAFT (Qu et al., 2025) and Easy-Tool (Yuan et al., 2025) refine tool documentation and retrieval strategies through trial feedback. Moving toward self-evolution, several studies empower agents to synthesize new tools via code generation, such as Voyager (Wang et al., 2023), CRAFT (Yuan et al., 2024), and Alita (Qiu et al., 2025), while ASI (Wang et al., 2025) introduces a mechanism to induce high-level skills from successful action trajectories. However, these works typically treat tool creation as a one-off event and lack a long-term management mechanism, often leading to toolkit bloating and reasoning redundancy, which motivates the development of EVOSOP in this study.

heading: Conclusions
text: In this study, we propose EVOSOP, a novel framework designed to empower LLM-based agents to self-evolve through iterative tool optimization. By synthesizing granular atomic actions into highlevel and reusable SOPs, EVOSOP boosts task success rates and addresses the reasoning overhead inherent in static toolsets. heading: Data preparation for EvoSOP and baselines.
text:
For each dataset, we first run the base methods, namely ReAct and DFSDT, to collect an initial set of trajectories, regardless of whether the trajectories are successful. During the training process of EvoSOP, we feed 5 randomly sampled trajectories in each of the first 5 iterations, exposing our method to 25 trajectories and tasks in total. In the last 5 iterations, EvoSOP only performs merging, evaluation, and review, meaning that no new SOPs are generated from trajectories.
To ensure a fair comparison, we expose the same number of trajectories to the ASI baseline for agentic skill induction. The reported results include performance on both exposed and unseen tasks.
Baselines. In addition to the ReAct agentic system described earlier, we reproduce another wellknown method, DFSDT (Qin et al., 2024), which implements a DFS-based algorithm to explore potentially promising choices and backtrack from failed branches.
DFSDT allows the agent to give up and backtrack to a previous state when encountering obstacles during task solving. Typically, when max_beam_size is set to 1, DFSDT effectively degenerates into a ReAct agent with the additional option of giving up. DFSDT dumps and restores the current states of both the agent and the environment before each reasoning step. When DFSDT gives up on a search branch, it restores the working state from the previously saved backup and performs a re-reasoning step, providing information about the failed branches in the prompt so that the agent can avoid repeating the same mistakes. For both ReAct and DFSDT, we set max_steps to 100, and we set max_beam_size of DFSDT to 3.

heading: C Toolset Maintenance and Convergence.
text: In this section, we supplement the description that EvoSOP maintains a condense but effective tool set at a low scale. Figure 5 summarizes the macro evolution of the toolset's composition. During the initial phase (Epochs 1 to 5), the toolset size undergoes rapid expansion as the CONSTRUCTOR explores various action patterns from the training trajectories. However, as the optimization loop proceeds, the growth curve flattens and eventually enters a dynamic equilibrium where new merged SOPs are only added if they offer significant utility gains over existing ones. Notably, EVOSOP maintains the toolset on a compact scale (typically fewer than 10 SOPs) while achieving a task success rate of approximately 80%. Such stabilization mirrors the behavior of a decaying learning rate in traditional optimization, where the system converges to a minimal yet powerful set of SOPs.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Abstract
text: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3×-194.9× more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that execute multi-step workflows rather than produce isolated responses. Each step appends system instructions, skills, earlier decisions, tool interactions, code, and environmental feedback to the next model call. The resulting context connects decisions across time, so losing an early constraint or observation can trigger an inconsistent action whose effects propagate through the remaining trajectory. Preserving the full context, however, increases prefill and attention computation, enlarges the key-value (KV) cache, and forces relevant evidence to compete with stale or redundant information. Long-horizon agents therefore face the central challenge of controlling this growing cost without disrupting the cross-step information flow required for coherent decisions.
Reducing context under this constraint is not an ordinary summarization problem. Agent context mixes semantic content with exact values. Explanations, code, and repeated observations can become redundant once the acting LLM has integrated their information, whereas identifiers, API arguments, and numerical values may determine later actions and must remain exact. Information that has little effect on the current action may also become decisive several steps later. Such delayed relevance makes one-shot importance estimates unreliable. Compressibility therefore cannot be inferred from length, repetition, or semantic similarity alone. It depends on what the acting LLM has already absorbed, what the current decision requires, and what a future step may need to recover. Because compression recurs as the trajectory grows, each operation must save more computation than it consumes. Effective context compression must therefore compact information already absorbed by the acting LLM, preserve exact or potentially useful evidence as the task evolves, and deliver savings across subsequent decoding and agent steps.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text: Existing context-compression methods typically rely on training, using either hard-token or soft-token compression. Hard-token methods prune or rewrite text, risking irreversible loss of exact values (Jiang et al., 2023;Pan et al., 2024;Xu et al., 2024a;Kang et al., 2026;Liu et al., 2026). Soft-token methods preserve continuous representations but require separately trained encoders or compressors (Mu et al., 2023;Chevalier et al., 2023;Ge et al., 2024;Li et al., 2026). More fundamentally, separately trained compressors create a model-taste gap. The information they learn to preserve may not match what the acting LLM has already absorbed or will need later. This motivates an in-model approach that uses the acting LLM's recurrent state to determine compressibility and carries absorbed information forward as agentic soft tokens.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text: In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free approach that uses the acting LLM's own computation to decide what its growing context must retain. The early layers have read the full context and the later layers would otherwise continue to process every original token. Figure 1 places this boundary within a continuing agent workflow and shows how the choice of compression stage changes task accuracy and workload. In hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention models (Yang et al., 2025), ASTC uses the native recurrent state as a memory of the context already processed. If a token's contribution is largely predictable from the preceding state, ASTC further checks whether it remains recoverable after the full observation has been processed. This guards against treating information overwritten by later updates as redundant. For content passing both checks, ASTC pools eligible hidden states into agentic soft tokens for later layers, while retaining protected exact values, such as identifiers and numbers, as explicit hard tokens. The shorter sequence reduces attention work for the current prediction and creates smaller KV caches that remain reusable as the agent continues. Each compression decision is therefore informed by what the model has already absorbed, and its benefit extends across the trajectory.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Across diverse long-horizon tasks, ASTC maintains task quality close to or above the uncompressed model while reducing end-to-end Attention Pairs by up to 59.84%. Preserving exact values avoids the sharp accuracy loss seen when protection is removed, while the compact cache continues to save attention work over later decisions with only small changes in action distributions. The same training-free criterion extends beyond tool observations, matching uncompressed accuracy with 19.48% fewer Decode KV interactions under full-history compression and reducing workload in additional long-context and code-repair tasks. ASTC combines the highest task accuracy with the lowest Attention Pairs per successful task, a 12.3×-194.9× advantage over trained compressors.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We identify the core challenge of long-horizon compression as reducing context cost without losing future-relevant evidence or diverging from the acting LLM's task representation.
• We introduce ASTC, a training-free method that uses native recurrent dynamics to retain exact values as hard tokens and carry absorbed content forward as soft tokens with reusable compact KV caches across subsequent agent steps.
• We bound trained-compressor objective mismatch, establish conditions under which ASTC has lower next-token distortion than equal-length hard-token representations, and quantify attention savings from cache reuse.
• Across long-horizon tasks, ASTC achieves comparable or better accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs and a 12. 3×-194.9× advantage in end-to-end Attention Pairs per successful task over trained compressors.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: In-Model Soft Tokens
text:
Context compression determines both how many tokens remain and which evidence reaches the acting LLM.
Existing methods make this decision before the model processes the compressed context, either pruning tokens or rewriting earlier interactions as shorter text (Jiang et al., 2023;Pan et al., 2024;Kang et al., 2026;Liu et al., 2026).
This ordering creates a selection mismatch because the value of a context span is not intrinsic to its text.
It depends on how the acting LLM represents the current task, what it has already absorbed, and which action it is about to take; the same observation can be redundant at one step and decisive at another.
An external compressor must approximate this model-dependent boundary from text alone.
In a long-horizon trajectory, a mistaken deletion can propagate because later decisions are made from the retained context.Hard-token output adds a second bottleneck because retained information must be serialized as a shorter sequence of vocabulary tokens, so exact structure or features distributed across positions must be reconstructed as short text.
Even a correctly selected span can therefore lose task-relevant information when forced into a short textual rewrite.
Moving compression inside the model lets the acting LLM judge compressibility where task information is represented, while soft tokens retain information in continuous contextual representations.
In-model selection and soft-token representation are therefore complementary, letting the acting LLM judge what matters and preserve that information in its own representation space, thereby avoiding both external selection mismatch and discrete textual reconstruction.
We analyze agent trajectories from real-world user interactions across systems such as Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.2 (Anthropic, 2026;OpenAI, 2026;Moonshot AI, 2026;Z.AI, 2026).
As Figure 3 shows, a consistent pattern emerges across these trajectories.
Tool observations occupy the largest share of the accumulated context and continue to grow as the agent interacts with its environment.
In our experiments, tool observations are the primary compression target.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Tool Observations
text: Tool observations are difficult to compress because they mix compressible natural-language and code spans with exact values, such as paths, identifiers, and checksums, that later actions may consume verbatim. Our preliminary experiments show that the former tolerates aggressive compression, whereas changing a single character in the latter can invalidate a later action. This heterogeneity makes tool observations a demanding but informative testbed. Effective agent compression must therefore compact semantic information distributed across many tokens without altering the exact values on which future actions depend.

heading: Model-Native Selection
text:
Hybrid GDN-attention models already compute a signal closely aligned with this decision during their normal forward pass. A GDN recurrent state acts as an online associative memory. Its gated delta update can be written as (Yang et al., 2025)
where α t controls how much previous memory survives, β t controls the write strength, and r t is the part of the incoming value that cannot be recovered from the retained state. Information already represented by the state produces a small correction, whereas novel or conflicting information changes the memory more strongly. The update therefore measures information relative to what the acting LLM currently remembers, not importance inferred from surface form alone. Moreover, the gate and delta update are optimized jointly with the LLM's predictions, so this distinction shares the representation space and task state used by downstream layers. Reusing GDN dynamics avoids teaching an auxiliary compressor to approximate the acting LLM's own notion of novelty. heading: Related Work
text: Discrete context compression shortens the sequence before it reaches the acting LLM. Selective Context (Li et al., 2023) prunes redundant spans; LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023) and LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) rank tokens for prompt pruning; LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) learns selection from distilled labels; and RECOMP (Xu et al., 2024a) trains compressors for retrieved evidence. For extended agent workflows, ACON (Kang et al., 2026) optimizes textual compression guidelines from task failures, while Context as a Tool (CAT) (Liu et al., 2026) trains SWE-Compressor to invoke context management during execution. MEM1 (Zhou et al., 2026) instead trains a compact memory jointly with agent reasoning. While these lines reduce accumulated context, text-level selection can discard exact evidence or diverge from the acting LLM's evolving task representation, and learned memory policies require additional training.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Related Work
text:
Soft-token methods retain information in continuous states. Gist Tokens (Mu et al., 2023) learns compressed prompt activations, AutoCompressors (Chevalier et al., 2023) produce recursive summary vectors, and ICAE (Ge et al., 2024) trains compact memory slots. Sentinel Tokens (Ren et al., 2023) and Activation Beacon (Zhang et al., 2025) compress intermediate activations for later processing. DAST (Chen et al., 2025) allocates soft tokens according to contextual information density, while Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs) (Li et al., 2026) train dedicated encoder-decoder models for large-scale compression. For tool-using LMs, Xu et al. (2024b) combine compressed representations with raw tokens for exact tool interfaces. These studies show that continuous memory can support incremental reuse and coexist with exact-token retention. Their compression behavior is nevertheless learned through model adaptation or auxiliary components, and their primary settings differ from a growing history of agent actions and observations. ASTC brings the continuous memory studied in soft-token compression to the growing histories addressed by agent context-management work. By operating within the acting LLM without a separately trained compressor, it keeps compression tied to the model's evolving task representation.
To the best of our knowledge, ASTC is among the first training-free, in-model soft-token methods for context compression in long-horizon LLM agents.

text:
We evaluate ASTC with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B acting model on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), OfficeBench (Wang et al., 2024), and 8-Objective QA (Zhou et al., 2026;Kang et al., 2026). We report two configurations that differ in compression scope: ASTC (Tools) compresses eligible tool observations, while ASTC (Context) extends compression to eligible spans across the full context. Both configurations use the same training-free compression mechanism with identical hyperparameter settings and preserve protected exact values as hard tokens. Unless otherwise stated, subsequent analyses use ASTC (Tools). We measure task quality and end-to-end Decode KV, Attention Pairs, and Generated Tokens. Decode KV counts decoding query-cache interactions; Attention Pairs counts causal query-key pairs across prefill, decoding, and auxiliary calls. Detailed setups and additional experiments are in Appendices L-M.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Persistence After One Commit
text: Compression helps a long-horizon agent only if its shorter KV cache remains useful when later steps revisit it, without substantially changing the agent's decisions. To isolate this mechanism, we branch from archived Base trajectories, allow at most one ASTC commit in one branch, and replay identical subsequent action tokens and tool results in both. This fixed continuation separates the effect of persistent cache compression from changes caused by diverging actions or observations. With no further commits allowed, savings at later horizons reflect reuse of the initial cache update rather than repeated compression. At successive action horizons during the shared continuation, we measure KL divergence between conditional action-token distributions and cumulative Attention Pairs saved since the commit. Figure 6 shows that the distributions remain close while savings recur at later actions, supporting the proposed amortization across the trajectory. A separate autonomous one-commit run probes whether this local stability carries through to task outcomes; its success is somewhat lower than archived Base and full ASTC, and differing archive versions make the comparison descriptive.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: Conclusion
text: Long-horizon agents must retain evidence for future decisions as context grows, while separately trained compressors may drift from the acting LLM's evolving task representation. ASTC uses native recurrent dynamics after early layers have read the full sequence, carrying absorbed content as agentic soft tokens and keeping exact values as hard tokens. The shorter sequence cuts later-layer computation and creates a compact KV cache whose savings persist across subsequent decisions. Without compressor training, ASTC keeps accuracy close to or above the uncompressed agent with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs; in the controlled comparison, it attains the highest accuracy and lowest Attention Pairs per successful task. Ablations and fixed-continuation analysis link these gains to exact-value protection, model-native selection, and persistent cache reuse. These results show how the acting LLM can compact absorbed context into reusable state without losing exact evidence for later decisions.

heading: E Cross-Model Transfer
text:
For the Qwen3.5-9B and Kimi-Linear comparisons in Section 6.5, we use the following model-specific configurations. Each frozen model uses a reader calibrated for its own internal state and a matching uncompressed Base run. ASTC compresses eligible tool observations while keeping API contracts and authentication content explicit. Qwen3.5-9B uses Stage 3, while Kimi-Linear uses Stage 5. Within each model, Base and ASTC share task IDs and decoding settings; these settings need not match across models. Kimi-Linear covers the first 68 Test-Normal tasks in official order; Qwen3.5-9B covers all 168.
On Kimi-Linear, ASTC reduces Decode KV, Attention Pairs, and generated tokens. Successes rise from one to three on its 68-task subset. These Kimi-Linear results do not establish a general accuracy gain across backbones.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: F Soft Aggregation and Subsequent Attention Reads
text: We test the value of soft aggregation and whether later attention uses the resulting representatives on all 168 AppWorld Test-Normal tasks, with Qwen3.5-9B, Stage 3, and Tool compression. The equal-length hard control uses the same groups, representative counts, and representative positions as ASTC on a common input prefix, but keeps the hidden state of each group's last original token instead of aggregating its member states. This isolates the representation choice at a fixed length budget. In a second control, read-masked soft representatives become inaccessible to attention starting from the next forward pass after their creation. Their physical KV entries and logical positions remain in place, and GDN updates follow the original rule. This control tests subsequent attention access while retaining the recurrent-state path.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: G Measured Runtime and Memory
text: We supplement the analytical workload counts with measured task latency, throughput, and peak GPU memory for Qwen3.5-9B on AppWorld and 8-Objective QA (Tables 6 and7). Mean task latency falls by approximately 3.7% on AppWorld and 13.45% on QA, and QA's P95 latency falls by 19.31%. AppWorld successes increase from 54 to 56, while QA EM/F1 increases from 28.91/37.51 to 30.81/39.18. Thus the task-level latency reductions accompany the reported task-quality results. The compression-entry host timer accounts for approximately 0.065% and 0.40% of ASTC's mean task latency on AppWorld and QA, respectively. AppWorld queue completion time decreases by 8.67% and queue token throughput increases by 3.64%. These queue statistics include startup, model loading, and warmup, and also depend on task scheduling. Per-GPU token throughput is slightly lower for ASTC on both datasets. Peak GPU memory is slightly lower on AppWorld and higher on QA; NVML sampling includes model weights, workspaces, and caches. The measured gains therefore concern task latency and the reported queue run, with distinct behavior in per-GPU throughput and memory.

heading: H Paired Uncertainty on OfficeBench and QA
text:
We follow ACON's official task selection and subtask expansion: OfficeBench contains 95 evaluation subtasks from 46 parent task groups, and accuracy is successful subtasks divided by 95. The 8-Objective QA set contains 99 tasks and 792 objectives. We use 10,000 paired bootstrap replicates, resampling the same task records for Base and ASTC in each replicate and recomputing quality differences and ratios of cumulative resource totals. The OfficeBench intervals use the 95 subtasks as sampling units.
QA uses the 99 tasks as units, sampling all eight objectives of each task together to preserve their dependence. All quality-difference intervals in Table 8 include zero. The OfficeBench workload intervals and the QA Tools workload intervals lie below 100%, whereas the QA Context workload intervals include the Base level. Thus the positive quality point estimates have uncertainty, while the evidence for resource reduction varies by dataset and scope.

text:
We construct a controlled hard-token variant using a frozen LLMLingua-2 scorer, sharing Qwen3.5-9B, Tool compression, protection rules, the Stage-3 boundary, and generation settings with ASTC. For a common input prefix, if ASTC aggregates a span of m positions into k soft representatives, the control retains the hidden states of k original positions according to LLMLingua-2 scores. title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: L Adapted FastKV and KVzip Baselines
text:
We extend the AppWorld comparison to FastKV (Jo et al., 2026) and KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), adapted to the frozen Qwen3.5-9B model. We evaluate all 168 Test-Normal tasks with official scoring, greedy decoding, at most 50 agent steps, 768 output tokens per action, and a 32,768-token context, following the AppWorld protocol in Appendix M.2. Both adapted baselines are training-free, with no weight updates, and apply their KV operations only to the eight full-attention layers at indices 3,7,11,15,19,23,27,31.
FastKV uses capacity 512, a Token-Selective Propagation (TSP) layer of 15, and TSP length 2,048, with window size 8, max pooling, and kernel size 7. KVzip uses retention ratio 0.3 and reconstruction chunk size 2,000. Its adaptation protects the system instructions and current user task while compressing earlier actions and tool observations. Workload is normalized to Base (100%). FastKV and KVzip results correspond to the Qwen3.5-9B adaptations described above.
Table 12 reports 0 and 19 successes for the adapted FastKV and KVzip baselines, compared with 56 for ASTC. Both baselines reduce Decode KV, but their end-to-end Attention Pairs rise to 561.23% and 5,976.41% of Base, respectively. ASTC improves task success while reducing all three workload measures. Under this closed-loop protocol, reducing the decoding cache alone is insufficient to preserve task quality or reduce total attention work; the comparison evaluates complete agent trajectories under the stated adaptation settings.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: M.1 General Setup
text:
Benchmarks. We evaluate ASTC on three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with distinct interaction structures. AppWorld provides a simulated ecosystem of everyday applications and APIs for interactive coding agents; we use its full 168-task Test-Normal split (Trivedi et al., 2024). OfficeBench covers realistic office-automation workflows that require planning, application switching, and grounded actions across productivity software (Wang et al., 2024). 8-Objective QA groups eight Natural Questions into each task and requires an agent to gather evidence with a Wikipedia search tool before returning all eight answers (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019;Zhou et al., 2026;Kang et al., 2026). Together, they test compression across API interaction, office automation, and multi-question information gathering.
Implementation. The three main benchmarks start from Qwen3.5-9B. Base and ASTC keep its parameters frozen and share the agent scaffold, prompts, decoding policy, context limit, and action budget. External compressors use the benchmark task splits and evaluators; their model services and adaptation-specific limits are detailed in Appendix M.3. In particular, LCLM adds trained Bridge and decoder LoRA parameters, so its evaluated decoder is adapted rather than identical to the frozen Base.

heading: Model checkpoints.
text:
The main experiments use Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at Hugging Face revision c202 236235762e1c871ad0ccb60c8ee5ba337b9a (Qwen Team, 2026). The transfer study also uses moonshotai/Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct at revision e1df551a447157d4658b573f 9a695d57658590e9 (Moonshot AI, 2025).
Bounded pooling. Selected positions are divided into at most M groups in causal order. In each group, an existing member closest to the mean direction anchors an initial trim by relative ℓ 2 error. ASTC then averages the remaining states in FP32, casts the mean to the runtime dtype, and accepts a group of at least two members only if its maximum post-cast relative error is at most τ h . Rejected and trimmed positions remain hard tokens. This check bounds hidden-state reconstruction, not downstream attention scores.
Baselines. Base is the uncompressed acting LLM. We compare ASTC with representative hard-token approaches, including prompt-based deletion (Prompting), LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023), LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024), and the UT and UTCO variants of ACON (Kang et al., 2026), as well as LCLM, a trained soft-token compressor (Li et al., 2026)

The main experiments use Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at Hugging Face revision c202 236235762e1c871ad0ccb60c8ee5ba337b9a (Qwen Team, 2026). The transfer study also uses moonshotai/Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct at revision e1df551a447157d4658b573f 9a695d57658590e9 (Moonshot AI, 2025).
Bounded pooling. Selected positions are divided into at most M groups in causal order. In each group, an existing member closest to the mean direction anchors an initial trim by relative ℓ 2 error. ASTC then averages the remaining states in FP32, casts the mean to the runtime dtype, and accepts a group of at least two members only if its maximum post-cast relative error is at most τ h . Rejected and trimmed positions remain hard tokens. This check bounds hidden-state reconstruction, not downstream attention scores.
Baselines. Base is the uncompressed acting LLM. We compare ASTC with representative hard-token approaches, including prompt-based deletion (Prompting), LLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2023), LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024), and the UT and UTCO variants of ACON (Kang et al., 2026), as well as LCLM, a trained soft-token compressor (Li et al., 2026)

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: M.3 Baseline Reproduction and Cost Accounting
text:
We adapt the public baseline implementations to the Qwen3.5-9B acting checkpoint and the benchmark evaluators described above. We distinguish three forms of preparation: using an already pretrained scoring model, optimizing a textual compression guideline on training tasks, and updating compressor or decoder parameters. These have different costs and should not all be described as parameter training.
The settings below describe our implementations rather than assert identity with every setting in the original papers. The matched-scope, matched-protection, and matched-length LLMLingua-2 comparison is a separate control in Appendix J.
ACON: guideline optimization and fixed test-time inference. We use ACON's UT and UTCO guideline-optimization procedures (Kang et al., 2026), with Qwen3.5-9B serving the acting and online compression roles in our reproduction; the retained observation-policy optimizer calls also identify the model as qwen35-9b. Training-task trajectories and the initial guideline provide the optimizer inputs.
The UT procedure proposes revised guidelines from trajectory analyses, evaluates the candidates with agent rollouts, and selects a guideline using the retained regression results. UTCO starts from the selected UT guideline and additionally optimizes the length of compressed histories or observations, with candidate generation, evaluation, and selection. The selected guideline is then fixed for Test; test-time compression still requires model calls to rewrite the eligible history or observation as text.
Neither the UT nor UTCO reproduction updates the acting model or compressor weights. We do not run ACON's optional compressor/agent LoRA distillation stages for these two baselines.

heading: M.3 Baseline Reproduction and Cost Accounting
text:
Neither the UT nor UTCO reproduction updates the acting model or compressor weights. We do not run ACON's optional compressor/agent LoRA distillation stages for these two baselines.
Offline preparation therefore includes trajectory collection, guideline optimizer calls, and candidate evaluation/selection; online inference includes the agent and its actual compression calls. We account for these phases separately. For a concrete retained preparation record, the AppWorld observationpolicy UTCO optimizer logged 69 calls with 665,733 input and 50,487 output tokens, totaling 716,220 tokens. This is an optimizer-only subtotal, not the complete cost of UTCO from initialization: it excludes the reused UT stage, training-task rollouts, and candidate evaluations. The corresponding initial-guideline Train90 rollout alone logged 7,611,026 input-plus-output tokens. History-policy and observation-policy search runs have separate logs and must not be combined as if they were the same run.
LLMLingua v1: causal token scoring. We use the public PromptCompressor implementation (Jiang et al., 2023), replacing its causal scoring backbone with Qwen3.5-9B. The scoring service loads this model in BF16 and performs no additional parameter training. It retains discrete tokens rather than producing soft representations. The recorded service calls compress_prompt with a requested retention rate of 0.30, iterative_size equal to the input's token count (at least one), token-level filtering enabled, and sentence-and context-level filtering disabled. These are explicit reproduction choices; in particular, using Qwen3.5-9B as the scorer is an adaptation of the public method. The observation-policy integration leaves ineligible short observations unchanged; the AppWorld and OfficeBench observation thresholds are 1,024 and 64 tokens, respectively. Requested retention is a local compressor setting, not a claim that the complete agent context or end-to-end workload is 30% of Base.

heading: M.3 Baseline Reproduction and Cost Accounting
text: LLMLingua-2: pretrained token classification. We use the public implementation (Pan et al., 2024) with a frozen pretrained classifier. Specifically, we enable use_llmlingua2=True and load microsoft/llmlingua-2-xlm-roberta-large-meetingbank. The checkpoint is an XLM RobertaForTokenClassification model with 24 layers, hidden size 1,024, and 16 attention heads. It was already trained by its authors; we do not fine-tune it on our benchmark tasks. Our service uses retention rate 0.30 and passes newline and question mark as force_tokens. The observation-policy runs use the same 1,024-token AppWorld and 64-token OfficeBench triggers as above. Their compressed text is returned to the agent; ASTC's recurrent-state selector, protectedposition mask, and soft-token pooling are not invoked by these ordinary baseline services. The separate matched-length control intentionally supplies ASTC's target positions and protection mask before applying LLMLingua-2 scores, and is labeled as such.

heading: M.3 Baseline Reproduction and Cost Accounting
text:
LCLM: pretrained components and Qwen adaptation. We initialize from the archived public latent-context/0.6b-4b-LCLM-4x compressor (Li et al., 2026). We retain and freeze its 0.6B encoder and pretrained 1,024 → 2,560 adapter. The trigger is at least 12 older turns eligible for archiving, excluding the most recent three turns; these three turns remain verbatim, compression is applied at most once per task, and interactions added afterward remain verbatim. The nominal 4× factor therefore applies to encoded older history, not the complete context. This archived launcher permits 50 interactions and 128 new tokens per action, rather than ASTC's 768-token action limit; its action parsing and progress guards are part of the adapter implementation. The runner-shaped training encodes archived events separately, whereas this one-shot inference runner encodes their concatenation, so the input constructions are not identical. These settings should be considered when interpreting the adaptation result, which does not by itself establish a general limitation of LCLM. Auxiliary Attention Pairs: definition and coverage. In particular, retained QA8 LLMLingua service logs do not record every internal q, c pair or classifier window length. Their available agent-side Attention counts are lower bounds until those scorer traces are included. heading: M.5 Additional-Dataset Protocols
text: RULER. We evaluate the same 32K inputs in Base and ASTC with the frozen Qwen3.5-9B model and a 32,768-token context limit. RULER scores answers by task-specific string matching and averages over its 13 task configurations. We use 20 examples per task, rather than the reference configuration's 500. Thus the reported accuracy is a 260-example aggregate; matching aggregate scores do not imply identical results on every task or at the larger default sample size. ASTC uses the Stage-3 data branch with (χ, ψ) = (0.60, 0.80) and merge-error threshold 0.50. Decode KV and Attention Pairs are analytical query-cache and causal-pair counts; Gen. is generated tokens, all normalized to Base.

title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
heading: LongBench v2.
text:
We use all 503 four-choice questions in the public train split (Bai et al., 2024). Base and ASTC share the frozen Qwen3.5-9B model and a 262,144-token context limit; examples that exceed the limit are truncated before either method processes them. Of the 503 examples, 100 require truncation. The inference configuration permits at most 16 new tokens; the recorded runs generate two tokens per example in both variants. ASTC uses the Stage-3 catalog branch with (χ, ψ) = (0.55, 0.74), merge-error threshold 0.55, and minimum net removal of one token. Overall and subgroup accuracy are exact-match rates for the extracted choice. Reported KV counts and cache bytes are analytical logical workload measures, not latency or measured peak device memory.
For MBPP, we use the sanitized task snapshot from Archer (He et al., 2026).
MBPP. We use its 427 sanitized MBPP problems (Austin et al., 2021). This interactive code-repair protocol is not numerically comparable with one-shot MBPP evaluations. The model submits a complete Python program, receives public-test feedback, and revises it; a third attempt is allowed if the second fails. The final program is scored once. Both variants use greedy decoding, at most 768 generated tokens per attempt, and a 32,768-token context limit. ASTC uses its Stage-3 calibration, thresholds, and 16-soft-token bound. Initial prompts, completed code, and public-test feedback are eligible for compression, while special control tokens remain explicit. Both variants re-prefill the full transcript before each turn; workload includes these repeated prefills and all decoding calls.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Abstract
text: Privacy leakage in LLM agents is commonly evaluated within individual components such as memory, retrieval, or tool-use pipelines, which makes it difficult to distinguish internal exposure from information that an external observer can actually recover. We present CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channel-aware evaluation framework for black-box privacy leakage in LLM agents. CIPL represents a target through sensitive source, selection, assembly, execution, observation, and extraction stages and evaluates the transition from selected sensitive units to attacker-recoverable output under a shared protocol. Experiments across memory-based, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated targets, together with a BrowserUse live-agent case study, show that storage labels alone do not determine recoverability. Memory targets form a near-saturated reference case, retrieval-mediated leakage is frequently partial, and tool-mediated and live-agent leakage varies strongly with observation surface, prompt-to-channel alignment, retrieval depth, and provider behavior. A stratified semantic audit further identifies attacker-useful disclosures that canonical exact matching misses. CIPL therefore provides a common framework for comparing how internal sensitive dependence is realized as externally recoverable leakage across heterogeneous agent pipelines.

CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
section: Abstract (abstract)

Privacy leakage in LLM agents is commonly evaluated within individual components such as memory, retrieval, or tool-use pipelines, which makes it difficult to distinguish internal exposure from information that an external observer can actually recover. We present CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channel-aware evaluation framework for black-box privacy leakage in LLM agents. CIPL represents a target through sensitive source, selection, assembly, execution, observation, and extraction stages and evaluates the transition from selected sensitive units to attacker-recoverable output under a shared protocol. Experiments across memory-based, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated targets, together with a BrowserUse live-agent case study, show that storage labels alone do not determine recoverability. Memory targets form a near-saturated reference case, retrieval-mediated leakage is frequently partial, and tool-mediated and live-agent leakage varies strongly with observation surface, prompt-to-channel alignment, retrieval depth, and provider behavior. A stratified semantic audit further identifies attacker-useful disclosures that canonical exact matching misses. CIPL therefore provides a common framework for comparing how internal sensitive dependence is realized as externally recoverable leakage across heterogeneous agent pipelines.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over prior interactions, retrieved documents, and tool outputs that may contain sensitive information [1,2,3]. Once such information enters active computation, privacy risk depends on more than the component in which it is stored. Sensitive units can be selected internally yet remain absent from the final answer, appear only in structured fields, be echoed through tool returns, or surface in process-level execution artifacts. Evaluating only the storage component therefore leaves open the question that matters to a black-box observer: which internally selected units become recoverable, through which visible channel, and under what conditions?
Existing memory, RAG, and tool-agent studies provide strong evidence that individual components can leak, but their target-specific prompts, observation surfaces, and extraction criteria make cross-channel interpretation difficult. A memory extraction result, for example, does not by itself establish how the same sensitive dependence would behave under a retrieval-conditioned answer or a tool-mediated observation surface. Likewise, changes in measured leakage can arise from upstream selection, provider behavior, prompt-tochannel alignment, or the extraction rule rather than from the storage label itself. This motivates an evaluation framework that separates the stages connecting sensitive source to external recovery while retaining each target's execution semantics.
We introduce CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channelaware framework for black-box privacy leakage evaluation. CIPL represents heterogeneous agent targets with a common source-selection-assemblyexecution-observation-extraction decomposition. For each trial it records the sensitive units selected into active computation and the units recoverable from the attacker-visible artifact. This exposure-to-recovery formulation makes it possible to compare leakage regimes across targets while attributing differences to explicit channel conditions instead of treating "memory", "retrieval", or "tool use" as leakage identifiers.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Introduction
text:
We organize the empirical study around three questions. RQ1 asks which leakage regimes appear across memory, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated targets under a shared black-box protocol. RQ2 examines how observation surface, prompt-to-channel alignment, retrieval depth, and provider behavior govern leakage realization. RQ3 measures attacker-useful disclosure that canonical exact matching fails to capture.
The resulting evidence separates several regimes that component labels obscure. Memory behaves as a near-saturated reference case under the evaluated conditions, while retrieval-mediated targets frequently expose some sensitive content without complete recovery. Tool-mediated targets and the BrowserUse case vary substantially across visible surfaces and providers, and cleaned operational controls sharply reduce leakage when adversarial alignment is removed. The semantic audit adds a second measurement layer by identifying non-verbatim but operationally useful disclosure among exactnegative outputs.
The contributions are threefold:
• Exposure-to-recovery formulation. We formalize black-box agent privacy evaluation around the transition from internally selected sensitive units to externally recoverable units, with explicit trial conditions and comparable recovery events.
• Channel-aware evaluation framework. We introduce CIPL's sourceselection-assembly-execution-observation-extraction decomposition and a shared evaluation protocol that applies to memory-based, retrievalmediated, tool-mediated, and live-agent settings.
• Cross-channel empirical characterization. Using the framework, we identify distinct leakage regimes, quantify target-dependent mainversus-naive realization behavior, and show that semantic auditing captures attacker-useful leakage missed by exact-only extraction.

heading: Privacy Leakage in Memory and Retrieval-Augmented Systems
text: Memory-equipped agents can reveal retrieved records through ordinary user-facing interaction; black-box memory extraction attacks such as MEX-TRA demonstrate that stored or retrieved records may be recoverable from the agent's response surface [4]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) studies likewise show that private or proprietary evidence can be extracted, leaked, or localized from generated responses [5,6,7,8]. These studies establish important component-level risks, but their measurement objects are usually tied to a particular retrieval or response interface.

Memory-equipped agents can reveal retrieved records through ordinary user-facing interaction; black-box memory extraction attacks such as MEX-TRA demonstrate that stored or retrieved records may be recoverable from the agent's response surface [4]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) studies likewise show that private or proprietary evidence can be extracted, leaked, or localized from generated responses [5,6,7,8]. These studies establish important component-level risks, but their measurement objects are usually tied to a particular retrieval or response interface.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Tool-Integrated and Web-Agent Security
text: Tool-integrated and web agents create additional visible surfaces because model decisions may be serialized into tool arguments, returned as structured outputs, or exposed through multi-step execution traces. Work on indirect prompt injection, tool misuse, and agent exfiltration demonstrates how attacker-controlled inputs can redirect these surfaces toward sensitive information [9,10,11,12]. CIPL uses tool and live-browser settings to measure how the choice of observation surface changes recoverability under a common exposure-to-recovery vocabulary.

text:
A complementary line of work studies prompt-level safeguards, privacypreserving generation, and safety guardrails for language models and retrieval systems [13,14,15,16,17]. Agent benchmarks, meanwhile, often emphasize end-to-end task success or attack success across heterogeneous environments. These approaches motivate practical controls and broad system evaluation, while CIPL focuses on the measurement structure needed to distinguish internal exposure, externally recoverable leakage, and the channel factors that connect them.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Exposure-to-Recovery Decomposition
text: Component labels such as "memory", "retrieval", or "tool use" identify where sensitive content may reside, but they do not determine how that content becomes visible to an external observer. The same sensitive unit may be selected into computation yet remain absent from the final answer, appear only in a structured field, be echoed in a tool return, or surface in intermediate process artifacts. CIPL therefore separates internal exposure, represented by U j , from external recovery, represented by V j . Changes in V j can then be analyzed with respect to upstream selection, observation surface, provider behavior, prompt-to-channel alignment, and extraction criteria.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Target Signature and Factor Separation
text:
Each element of τ isolates a distinct part of the exposure-to-recovery path. S identifies the source or storage context; Sel captures retrieval or other upstream selection; Asm and Exec describe how selected content enters and influences computation; Obs specifies the visible channel; and Ext defines the recovery rule. The same framework can therefore represent targets with different execution semantics without collapsing their differences into a single component label.
For controlled prompt construction, γ j records three lightweight descriptors used throughout the study: a locator for the sensitive content being measured, an alignment choice describing the intended visible surface or output form, and a diversification policy for allocating the query budget across sensitive units. These descriptors define an evaluation condition rather than a privileged attack recipe; Section 5.2 empirically compares the main construction with naive alternatives.

heading: Cross-Target Comparability Conditions
text: Cross-target comparisons are reported only when four protocol conditions are satisfied. Unit normalization requires a declared canonical sensitiveunit representation and target-specific ground truth. Budget parity requires the same query budget, retry interpretation, and seed aggregation for the compared main settings. Observation and extraction specification requires each attacker-visible surface and recovery rule to be explicit and held fixed within a comparison cell. These conditions make recovery events comparable without assuming that the underlying target executions are identical.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Target Instantiations and Observation Surfaces
text:
We instantiate CIPL on four controlled targets spanning memory-based, retrieval-mediated, and tool-mediated settings: memory_ehr, memory_rap, rag_ctrl, and tool_ctrl. The controlled targets isolate sensitive source, selection behavior, observable surface, and execution semantics while preserving the same black-box target signature. Full target definitions are reported in the Appendix. We additionally evaluate BrowserUse as a live-agent case study to test whether the same channel-sensitive patterns remain visible in a live multi-step environment.
Memory-based instantiations.. memory_ehr is adapted from the EHRAgentstyle setting [18], where retrieved records are used as demonstrations for code generation and the attacker-visible artifact is the generated answer. memory_rap is adapted from a RAP-style web-agent setting [19,20], where retrieved records guide action generation and leakage is exposed through an action-mediated output channel. These settings serve as continuity points with prior memory-extraction evidence while being evaluated under the shared CIPL protocol. Retrieval-mediated instantiation.. rag_ctrl isolates leakage through a retrievalconditioned answer channel. It retrieves the top-k documents from a 50-record corpus using string similarity, injects the embedded private_fact fields into the LLM context, and exposes a generated answer conditioned on the retrieved evidence. The construction provides a controlled retrieval-mediated channel in which upstream selection and external recovery can be measured separately.

heading: Target Instantiations and Observation Surfaces
text: Tool-mediated instantiation.. tool_ctrl isolates leakage through tool-visible artifacts while holding the surrounding task structure fixed. It retrieves the top-k records from a 50-record database containing secret_value fields and evaluates two observation modes: args_exfil, where the model inserts the secret into a tool-call payload, and return_echo, where the model echoes the raw JSON tool result. title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: Setup and Metrics
text:
We evaluate all controlled targets under a shared black-box protocol with attack budget n = 30, one retry per query, and five seeds {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. To avoid favorable variance from short prompt pools, we expand the prompt files of rag_ctrl and tool_ctrl to the same 30-query budget. Default source sizes are 200 for the memory targets and 50 for rag_ctrl and tool_ctrl. Default retrieval depths are k = 4 for memory_ehr, k = 3 for memory_rap, and k = 2 for rag_ctrl and tool_ctrl. Unless explicitly varied, the retriever uses edit-distance matching.
Our main experiments measure adversarially realizable black-box leakage: whether a black-box observer can convert internal sensitive dependence into attacker-recoverable output through ordinary user-facing interaction. The reported quantities therefore characterize recoverability under the stated query budget, prompts, observation surfaces, and extraction rules.
We evaluate five API-based providers: MiniMax-M2.5, MiniMax-M2.7, qwen3.5-plus, DeepSeek, and GPT-4o under a shared black-box protocol. Unless otherwise stated, each controlled-target setting uses n = 30 attack queries, one retry per query, five pipeline repetitions indexed by seeds {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}, and edit-distance retrieval. The default retrieval depths are k = 4 for memory_ehr, k = 3 for memory_rap, and k = 2 for rag_ctrl and tool_ctrl; default source sizes are 200 for the memory targets and 50 for rag_ctrl and tool_ctrl. No API-level generation seed is supplied, and top-p follows the provider default. Target-specific model identifiers, endpoints, access-date windows, and decoding details are reported in the Appendix Reproducibility Details.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: RQ1: Cross-Target Leakage Regimes
text:
Table 2 and Figure 1 show that, under the shared black-box protocol, externally recoverable leakage does not follow directly from storage-component labels alone. Instead, the targets occupy distinct leakage realization regimes.
Memory is the near-saturated reference case.. The two memory targets remain saturated across all five providers, with CER = AER = 1.0 throughout. Under the shared protocol, memory therefore serves as a near-saturated reference case in which internal exposure is almost perfectly converted into externally recoverable leakage. Retrieval-mediated leakage appears as a frequent-but-partial regime.. The clearest deviation from the memory pattern appears in rag_ctrl. Leakage remains frequent but is incomplete across providers: CER ranges from 0.33 to 0.55 and AER from 0.78 to 0.95. MiniMax-M2.7 has the highest CER (0.55), while DeepSeek has the lowest AER (0.78). Under the shared protocol, retrieval-mediated leakage therefore remains a frequent-but-partial regime rather than a complete-extraction regime.

title: CIPL: A Channel-Aware Framework for Recoverable Privacy Leakage in LLM Agents
heading: RQ2: What Governs Leakage Realization?
text:
We next ask what governs whether internal exposure becomes externally recoverable leakage. The central result is that internal exposure alone is not sufficient: leakage depends on how exposure is realized through attackervisible channels. Figure 2 highlights two effects. First, for tool_ctrl, cleaned weak controls sharply suppress leakage, showing that the main-effect leakage depends on prompt-to-channel alignment rather than ordinary task completion. Second, for rag_ctrl, increasing retrieval depth k does not monotonically increase leakage; greater internal exposure can preserve any-leakage while weakening complete extraction.
Leakage is channel-conditioned rather than recipe-universal.. The boundary analyses reinforce the same interpretation. In memory and tool-mediated settings, the main prompt family is often strong, but rag_ctrl provides a clear counterexample: a dump-style naive baseline can outperform the main prompt family, and component ablations show that the full locator/aligner/diversification configuration is not uniformly optimal. The detailed baseline and component-ablation results in the Appendix quantify this target dependence. The comparison separates the framework from any particular prompt recipe: CIPL normalizes measurement across heterogeneous channels, while the strongest realization condition remains target-dependent.

heading: RQ2 Extension: BrowserUse as a Live-Agent Case Study
text:
To test transfer beyond controlled targets, we instantiate CIPL on BrowserUse, a live Playwright-driven browser agent with two attacker-visible observation The BrowserUse results preserve the controlled lesson in a live multi-step agent. Leakage depends strongly on observation surface, but the ordering is not universal: DeepSeek and GPT-4o leak much more through process, the MiniMax models leak through both surfaces but peak on process, and qwen3.5-plus leaks more through final_result. Thus, the observed leakage pattern depends on which surface is exposed and how the provider realizes that surface.
The standard operational-task control further separates internal exposure from external leakage. As shown in Table 5, leakage collapses to near-zero on both observation modes under ordinary operational instructions, even though retrieved sensitive content still enters the agent's initial context. This supports the same conclusion as tool_ctrl: severe leakage in live agents is not merely a byproduct of internal exposure, but depends on alignment between the input condition and a leakable observation surface.
